paragraphs.text: Physics states its results as relations between measured quantities, so it starts with measurement. This chapter fixes what a measured value means: a number with a unit from an agreed system, scales compared by powers of ten, equations checked by their dimensions, and results reported with their uncertainty. Every later chapter relies on these tools.

Physics studies matter, energy, space and time, and looks for a small number of laws that cover a wide range of phenomena. In this text a *model* is a simplified description of a system that keeps only the features that matter for a given question; a *theory* is a tested explanation that links many observations; a *law* is a concise statement, usually an equation, of a regularity that has held in every test within its range of validity. That range is wide: lengths in physics run from about 10⁻¹⁵ m, the size of a proton, to nearly 10²⁷ m, the diameter of the observable universe.

Scales this different are compared by ratios rather than differences. The [[omag|order of magnitude]] of a quantity is the power of ten nearest to its value on a logarithmic scale, found by rounding the base-10 logarithm: n = round(log₁₀ Q), with Q expressed in a chosen unit. The mass of an electron, 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, has order of magnitude 10⁻³⁰ kg; the age of the universe, about 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s, has order of magnitude 10¹⁸ s. Quantities one order of magnitude apart differ by a factor of about ten.

Every *physical quantity* is a number multiplied by a unit, and measuring it means comparing it with that unit. The [[si|SI system of units]] (Système International d'Unités) chooses seven *base quantities*: time, length, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity, with base units the second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. All other units are *derived* as products of powers of base units: speed is measured in m/s, and force in newtons, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten, for example kilo- (10³), mega- (10⁶), milli- (10⁻³), micro- (10⁻⁶) and nano- (10⁻⁹). Other unit systems, such as English units, remain in use; this text works in SI.

Mechanics uses three of these base quantities. [[t|Time]] is read from a clock; the second is defined by fixing the frequency of a hyperfine transition of the caesium-133 atom at exactly 9 192 631 770 Hz. [[L|Length]] is read from a ruler; the metre is the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299 792 458 of a second. [[m|Mass]] is read from a balance; since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by fixing Planck's constant at exactly h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Together with the ampere, kelvin, mole and candela, these units are the base on which the [[si|SI]] builds every other unit.

A quantity is expressed in other units by multiplying it by a [[conv|conversion factor]], a ratio of two equal quantities written in different units, such as (1000 m)/(1 km). Since the ratio equals one, the number changes but the quantity does not, and units cancel like algebraic factors: 80.0 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 22.2 m/s. Each factor follows from the definitions of the [[si|SI]] units and prefixes. Unconverted units cause real failures: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because ground software supplied thruster impulse in pound-force seconds where newton seconds were expected.

[[dim|Dimensional analysis]] records which base quantities a unit is built from, and with what powers. Writing L, M and T for the dimensions of length, mass and time, a speed has dimension [v] = LT⁻¹ and a force has dimension MLT⁻². The dimension of a quantity follows from its unit in the [[si|SI]]. Only quantities of the same dimension can be added or equated, so in a *dimensionally consistent* equation every term has the same dimension: in x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², each term has dimension L. Arguments of functions such as sin, exp and log must be *dimensionless*. A consistent equation can still be wrong, but an inconsistent one cannot be right.

An [[est|estimate]] aims at the right order of magnitude when precise inputs are not available. Rough values are combined so that the dimensions come out right, by [[dim|dimensional analysis]], and the result is rounded to its [[omag|order of magnitude]]. The number of heartbeats in a lifetime, for example, is about (1 beat/s) × (80 years) × (3.2 × 10⁷ s/year) ≈ 3 × 10⁹, of order 10⁹. Because only the power of ten is wanted, inputs that are uncertain by a factor of two are acceptable. Such estimates, often called Fermi calculations after Enrico Fermi, are used to check calculations and to judge whether an effect is large enough to matter.

A measured value is useful only together with a statement of how good it is. *Accuracy* is closeness to the accepted value and is measured by the [[disc|discrepancy]], the measured value minus the accepted value, both in the same [[si|SI]] unit. *Precision* is the agreement of repeated measurements with each other and is described by the [[unc|uncertainty]] δA, so that a result is reported as A ± δA. The percent uncertainty compares the uncertainty with the value. A measurement can be precise but inaccurate, for example when a balance consistently reads high.

Uncertainties carry over into quantities calculated from measured values. For a product, (A + δA)(B + δB) = AB(1 + δA/A + δB/B + δA·δB/(AB)). The last term is a product of two small fractions and can be dropped, so to first order the percent [[unc|uncertainties]] of the factors add; the same holds for a quotient. This rule of [[prop|uncertainty propagation]], the method of adding percents, gives a conservative bound. A rectangle measured as (2.00 ± 0.02) m by (3.00 ± 0.06) m has percent uncertainties 1 % and 2 %, so its area is 6.00 m² ± 3 %, that is, (6.00 ± 0.18) m².

[[sigfig|Significant figures]] apply the same idea digit by digit: a result should not carry more digits than its inputs support. In multiplication and division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor, so 2.5 m × 3.47 m = 8.7 m². In addition and subtraction, it keeps the decimal places of the least precise term, so 12.1 m + 0.523 m = 12.6 m. Zeros that only locate the decimal point, as in 0.0052, are not significant. Rounding is done once, at the end of a calculation; the rule is a coarse form of [[prop|uncertainty propagation]].

Problems in physics are solved in a stable sequence. Identify the physical principles involved and the system they apply to, draw a sketch, and list the known and unknown quantities with their units. Choose the equations that connect them and solve symbolically before substituting numbers, so that each step can be checked by [[dim|dimensional analysis]]. Then substitute values in [[si|SI]] units and keep the [[sigfig|significant figures]] the data support. Finally, judge the result: compare its [[omag|order of magnitude]] with an [[est|estimate]] and check that its sign, units and size are reasonable.

Chapter 1 treated a measured quantity as a number times a unit. Many quantities in mechanics also have a direction: a displacement of 5 m to the east differs from one of 5 m to the north, and two such quantities combine according to their directions as well as their sizes. This chapter develops the mathematics of directed quantities. It adds and scales them geometrically, writes them in components along the axes of a coordinate system, and defines two kinds of product. A relation between directed quantities then becomes one ordinary equation per axis, each checked by [[dim|dimensional analysis]] as before.

A [[scal|scalar quantity]], or scalar, is fixed by one real number and a unit, such as a mass of 2.0 kg, a time interval of 3.5 s or a temperature of 300 K. Scalars obey ordinary arithmetic, and an equation between scalars is a *scalar equation*. A [[vec|vector quantity]], or vector, has a *magnitude* and a direction. Its model case is *displacement*, the change of position from a starting point to an end point, drawn as an arrow from the one to the other whatever path was taken between them. The magnitude A = |A⃗| is the length of the arrow and is never negative. Vectors that point the same way are *parallel*, vectors that point in opposite directions are *antiparallel*, and perpendicular vectors are *orthogonal*. A *vector equation* such as A⃗ = B⃗ asserts equal magnitudes and the same direction at once.

Two [[vec|vectors]] are added by the *tail-to-head geometric construction*: place the tail of B⃗ at the head of A⃗, and their [[vadd|vector sum]], the *resultant vector* R⃗ = A⃗ + B⃗, runs from the tail of A⃗ to the head of B⃗. Successive displacements combine in exactly this way. Drawn from a common point, A⃗ and B⃗ span a parallelogram whose diagonal is the same R⃗; this is the *parallelogram rule*. The sum is *commutative*, A⃗ + B⃗ = B⃗ + A⃗, and *associative*, (A⃗ + B⃗) + C⃗ = A⃗ + (B⃗ + C⃗), and its magnitude is at most A + B, with equality only for parallel vectors. The *difference of two vectors* adds the antiparallel vector: A⃗ − B⃗ = A⃗ + (−B⃗). Along one line, vectors add like signed numbers: 4.0 m east followed by 6.0 m west gives 2.0 m west.

[[vscale|Multiplication by a scalar]] turns a [[vec|vector]] A⃗ and a [[scal|scalar]] α into the vector B⃗ = αA⃗, of magnitude B = |α|A. For α > 0 the direction is kept and for α < 0 it is reversed; either way B⃗ lies along the line of A⃗, and α = −1 gives the antiparallel vector −A⃗. The operation is *distributive* over both kinds of sum: α(A⃗ + B⃗) = αA⃗ + αB⃗ and (α₁ + α₂)A⃗ = α₁A⃗ + α₂A⃗. Dividing a vector by its own magnitude gives the *unit vector* Â = A⃗/A, which has magnitude 1, carries no unit and only marks a direction. Every vector is therefore its magnitude times its unit vector, A⃗ = AÂ.

A Cartesian *coordinate system* has an origin and three mutually perpendicular axes, with *unit vectors of the axes* î, ĵ and k̂. Every [[vec|vector]] A⃗ is the [[vadd|sum]] of three vectors parallel to the axes, each a unit vector [[vscale|multiplied by a scalar]]. This gives the *component form* A⃗ = A_x î + A_y ĵ + A_z k̂. The terms A_x î, A_y ĵ and A_z k̂ are the [[comp|vector components]] of A⃗, and the signed numbers A_x, A_y and A_z are its *scalar components*. A vector drawn from a point b to a point e has A_x = x_e − x_b, and likewise for y and z. By the Pythagorean theorem its magnitude is A = √(A_x² + A_y² + A_z²). Two vectors are equal exactly when all their components are equal, so one vector equation stands for three scalar equations, one per axis.
eqs: A⃗ = A_x î + A_y ĵ + A_z k̂,   A = √(A_x² + A_y² + A_z²)

paragraphs.text: A vector in a plane is also fixed by its magnitude A and its *direction angle* θ_A, measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis: A_x = A cos θ_A, A_y = A sin θ_A and tan θ_A = A_y/A_x. With A_x = 3.00 m and A_y = 4.00 m, A = 5.00 m and θ_A = 53.1°. The inverse tangent returns only angles between −90° and +90°, so the signs of the components fix the quadrant: reversing both components gives θ_A = 233.1°, not 53.1°. For the vector from the origin to a point, magnitude and direction angle are the [[polar|polar coordinates]] (r, φ), related to the [[comp|Cartesian components]] by x = r cos φ and y = r sin φ. In this *polar coordinate system* the *radial coordinate* r is never negative, φ is fixed only up to whole turns, and φ is undefined at r = 0.

[[comp|Components]] turn vector algebra into arithmetic done axis by axis. A resultant's x-component is the sum of the x-components of the vectors added, R_x = A_x + B_x + C_x + …, and likewise for y and z. Subtraction and [[vscale|multiplication by a scalar]] also act component by component. *Equal vectors* have equal components; the *null vector* 0⃗ has all its components zero and is the [[vadd|sum]] of any vector and its antiparallel vector. Vector equations are solved like ordinary ones. If three displacements return a walker to her start, A⃗ + B⃗ + C⃗ = 0⃗, so C⃗ = −(A⃗ + B⃗); with A⃗ = (2.0 î + 3.0 ĵ) m and B⃗ = (1.0 î − 5.0 ĵ) m, C⃗ = (−3.0 î + 2.0 ĵ) m.

Two vectors can be multiplied together in two ways. The [[dot|scalar product]], or *dot product*, of A⃗ and B⃗ is the scalar A⃗·B⃗ = AB cos φ, where φ is the *angle between the two vectors*, from 0° to 180°, measured with their tails together. It equals A times the projection of B⃗ on the direction of A⃗: positive for an acute angle, zero for orthogonal vectors, negative for an obtuse one. The product is commutative and distributive, and A⃗·A⃗ = A². Because î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 and î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0, expanding A⃗·B⃗ in [[comp|components]] leaves only products of matching components. Then cos φ = A⃗·B⃗/(AB) gives the angle between two vectors from their components: for A⃗ = î + 2ĵ + 2k̂ and B⃗ = 2î + k̂, A⃗·B⃗ = 4, A = 3 and B = √5, so φ = 53.4°.
eqs: A⃗·B⃗ = AB cos φ = A_{x}B_{x} + A_{y}B_{y} + A_{z}B_{z}

paragraphs.text: The [[cross|vector product]], or *cross product*, A⃗×B⃗ is a vector perpendicular to both A⃗ and B⃗ with magnitude AB sin φ, the area of the parallelogram the two vectors span. It vanishes for parallel and antiparallel vectors, so A⃗×A⃗ = 0⃗. The *corkscrew right-hand rule* fixes its sense: turn A⃗ toward B⃗ through the smaller angle, and A⃗×B⃗ points the way a right-handed screw advances under that turn. Reversing the order reverses the turn, which is the *anticommutative property* A⃗×B⃗ = −B⃗×A⃗. The product is distributive but not associative: î×(î×ĵ) = −ĵ, while (î×î)×ĵ = 0⃗. Using î×ĵ = k̂, ĵ×k̂ = î and k̂×î = ĵ and distributing over the [[comp|components]] gives the component formula. For the two vectors above, A⃗×B⃗ = 2î + 3ĵ − 4k̂, whose magnitude √29 ≈ 5.39 equals AB sin φ.

*Kinematics* describes how bodies move, without asking why. This chapter treats the simplest case: a body whose size and orientation do not matter, so that it can be treated as a point, moving along a straight line. Its position is a signed [[L|length]] from a chosen origin, and following that position in [[t|time]] gives the motion. Velocity and acceleration are rates of change of the motion. Along one line a [[vec|vector]] has a single [[comp|component]], so each vector quantity of the chapter is a signed number. The chapter ends with constant acceleration, free fall near Earth's surface, and the recovery of a motion from its acceleration by integration.

A position is always stated relative to something. A [[frame|frame of reference]] supplies an origin, a set of axes along which [[comp|components]] are taken, and a clock that reads the [[t|time]]. The origin and the directions of the axes are free choices, and in classical mechanics all frames share the same time. For motion along a line one axis is enough. The [[x|position]] x of a body is then its signed distance from the origin: a [[L|length]] measured along the axis, positive on one side of the origin and negative on the other. With the origin at a lamppost and east chosen positive, a car 25 m east of the post has x = +25 m and one 10 m west of it has x = −10 m. Moving the origin shifts every position by the same amount.

Recording the [[x|position]] at every instant of [[t|time]] gives the [[xt|motion on a line]], the function x(t); its graph against t is a complete record of the motion. The [[dx|displacement]] over an interval is the change of position, Δx = x_f − x_i, read from the motion at the end and at the start of the interval. It is signed: positive for a net move toward larger x, negative for a net move back. For a motion in several stages, the *total displacement* is the sum of the displacements of the stages, Δx_{total} = ΣΔx_i, which reduces to the last position minus the first. A runner who goes from x = 2.0 m to x = 9.0 m and then back to x = 5.0 m has displacements of +7.0 m and −4.0 m, and a total displacement of +3.0 m.

Opposite displacements cancel in that sum, so the total displacement does not show how far a body went. The [[dist|distance traveled]] adds the magnitudes of the [[dx|displacements]] instead, d = Σ|Δx_i|, with the stages taken between the points where the body reverses. It is never negative and never smaller than the magnitude of the total displacement; the two are equal only if the body never turns back. The runner above traveled 7.0 m + 4.0 m = 11.0 m, although her total displacement was 3.0 m.

The [[dtm|elapsed time]] of an interval is the difference between two readings of the same clock, Δt = t_f − t_i, where t_i and t_f are the [[t|times]] at its start and end. The [[vavg|average velocity]] over the interval is the [[dx|displacement]] divided by the elapsed time, in metres per second. It has the sign of the displacement and depends only on the end points: every motion with the same start, end and duration has the same average velocity. On the graph of x(t) it is the slope of the straight line joining the two end points. If the runner's trip took 5.0 s, her average velocity was (+3.0 m)/(5.0 s) = +0.60 m/s, although she covered 11.0 m and spent part of the time moving backwards.

As the interval shrinks, the average velocity approaches a limit, the velocity at one instant. Such a limit is the [[ddt|time derivative]]: for a quantity f known at every instant, df/dt = lim_{Δt→0} [f(t + Δt) − f(t)]/Δt. The derivative is linear, obeys the product rule, gives zero for a constant and turns tⁿ into ntⁿ⁻¹. Applied to the [[xt|motion]] x(t), it defines the [[v|instantaneous velocity]] v(t) = dx/dt, the slope of the tangent to the x(t) graph at time t. For x(t) = (4.0 m/s)t − (1.0 m/s²)t², the velocity is v(t) = 4.0 m/s − (2.0 m/s²)t. It is +2.0 m/s at t = 1.0 s, zero at t = 2.0 s, where the body turns around, and −2.0 m/s at t = 3.0 s.

Speed ignores direction. The [[savg|average speed]] is the [[dist|distance traveled]] divided by the [[dtm|elapsed time]], s̄ = d/Δt, and is never negative. It is not in general the magnitude of the average velocity: the runner of the previous section had s̄ = (11.0 m)/(5.0 s) = 2.2 m/s but v̄ = +0.60 m/s. Over an interval short enough that the body does not reverse, however, the distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement, so the [[speed|instantaneous speed]] is the magnitude of the [[v|instantaneous velocity]], |v(t)|. In the example above, at t = 3.0 s the velocity is −2.0 m/s and the speed is 2.0 m/s. A speedometer shows instantaneous speed.

A changing velocity is described by acceleration. The [[aavg|average acceleration]] over an interval is the change of [[v|instantaneous velocity]] divided by the [[dtm|elapsed time]], ā = Δv/Δt = (v_f − v₀)/(t_f − t₀), in (m/s)/s = m/s². A car that goes from rest to 27 m/s in 9.0 s has an average acceleration of 3.0 m/s². Along a line, acceleration is signed like velocity. When the two have the same sign the speed grows, and when their signs are opposite it falls. A negative acceleration therefore does not by itself mean slowing down: a body moving in the negative direction with a negative acceleration speeds up.

Letting the interval shrink gives the [[a|instantaneous acceleration]], the [[ddt|time derivative]] of the [[v|velocity]]. On a graph of v against t it is the slope of the tangent at time t. On the graph of x against t it is the second derivative, which sets how the curve bends: concave up where a > 0 and concave down where a < 0. For the motion x(t) = (4.0 m/s)t − (1.0 m/s²)t² of the previous section, v(t) = 4.0 m/s − (2.0 m/s²)t and a = −2.0 m/s² at every instant. The body slows until t = 2.0 s and then speeds up in the negative direction, with the same acceleration throughout, including the instant at which v = 0.

If the acceleration a is constant, the [[aavg|average acceleration]] over every interval equals a. Starting the clock at t = 0 with velocity v₀ then gives v = v₀ + at, a velocity linear in time. For a linear velocity the [[vavg|average velocity]] is the mean of the end values, v̄ = (v₀ + v)/2, so the position is x = x₀ + v̄t = x₀ + ½(v₀ + v)t. Substituting v = v₀ + at gives x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², and eliminating t gives v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). These are the equations of [[kin|constant-acceleration kinematics]]. They hold only while a stays constant: a car that accelerates and then brakes is treated in stages, the final values of one stage serving as the initial values of the next.
eqs: v = v₀ + at,   x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²

paragraphs.text: Each of the four [[kin|kinematic equations]] leaves out one quantity: v = v₀ + at contains no position, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² no final velocity, v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) no time, and x = x₀ + ½(v₀ + v)t no acceleration. The equation to use contains the unknown and otherwise only known quantities. A car braking from 30.0 m/s at 6.00 m/s² stops in (30.0 m/s)²/(2 × 6.00 m/s²) = 75.0 m. In a *two-body pursuit problem* both bodies are described in one [[frame|frame of reference]] with one clock, and they meet when x₁(t) = x₂(t). A car that starts from rest at 2.0 m/s² just as a truck passes it at a constant 20 m/s draws level when (1.0 m/s²)t² = (20 m/s)t, at t = 20 s and x = 400 m, when the car is moving at 40 m/s.

Near Earth's surface, when *air resistance* is negligible, all bodies fall with the same constant acceleration whatever their mass, as Galileo argued. Its magnitude is the [[g|acceleration due to gravity]], g = 9.80 m/s², which varies by about half a percent with latitude and altitude. Motion with this acceleration alone is [[ffall|free fall]], whether the body is dropped, thrown down or thrown up. With y positive upward the acceleration is a = −g, and substituting it into the [[kin|constant-acceleration equations]] gives v = v₀ − gt, y = y₀ + v₀t − ½gt² and v² = v₀² − 2g(y − y₀). These equations assume heights small compared with Earth's radius, so that g stays constant, and speeds low enough for the drag of the air to be ignored.
eqs: y = y₀ + v₀t − ½gt²,   v = v₀ − gt

paragraphs.text: A ball thrown straight up at 14.7 m/s is in [[ffall|free fall]] from the moment it leaves the hand and loses 9.80 m/s of upward velocity each second. It reaches the top at t = v₀/g = 1.50 s, at a height v₀²/(2g) = 11.0 m above the launch point, and is back at the launch point at t = 3.00 s with velocity −14.7 m/s: the same speed, reversed. The acceleration is −g throughout. At the top the velocity is momentarily zero, but it is still changing at 9.80 m/s per second, which is why the ball does not stay there. A body dropped from rest falls ½gt²: 4.90 m in the first second and 19.6 m in the first two.

Integration reverses differentiation. The [[integ|time integral]] accumulates a rate over an interval, and by the fundamental theorem of calculus the integral of df/dt from 0 to t equals f(t) − f(0). Applied first to the [[a|acceleration]] and then to the velocity, it gives the velocity and position at time t from their initial values v₀ and x₀. For constant a the first integral is at, so v = v₀ + at; integrating again gives x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at². The [[kin|constant-acceleration equations]] thus follow without the argument about averages. Geometrically, the displacement over an interval is the signed area under the v(t) graph, and the change of velocity is the area under the a(t) graph.
eqs: v(t) = v₀ + ∫₀ᵗ a(t′) dt′,   x(t) = x₀ + ∫₀ᵗ v(t′) dt′

paragraphs.text: The same two integrations work for any acceleration known as a function of time. An indefinite integral is fixed only up to a constant, v(t) = ∫a(t) dt + C₁ and x(t) = ∫v(t) dt + C₂, and the two constants are set by the initial velocity and the initial position. The [[a|acceleration]] at all times, together with these two initial values, therefore determines the whole [[xt|motion]] x(t) through the [[integ|time integral]]. For a(t) = (2.0 m/s³)t, starting from rest at the origin, v(t) = (1.0 m/s³)t² and x(t) = (1.0 m/s³)t³/3. At t = 3.0 s the body moves at 9.0 m/s and has covered 9.0 m.

Chapter 3 followed a body along a line with a single coordinate. In a plane or in space, position, displacement, velocity and acceleration become [[vec|vectors]]. This chapter defines them and shows that, in [[comp|components]], a motion in three dimensions is three motions along perpendicular axes, each obeying the rules of Chapter 3 and all sharing one clock. Two motions are treated in detail: projectile flight, in which gravity acts on the vertical motion only, and motion on a circle, in which the acceleration has a part directed toward the centre. The chapter ends by relating the descriptions of one motion in two [[frame|frames of reference]] moving relative to each other.

In space, a body is located by its [[r|position vector]] r⃗ = x î + y ĵ + z k̂, the arrow from the origin of the frame to the body. Its [[comp|components]] are three coordinates, each a [[x|position]] measured along one axis exactly as in Chapter 3. As the body moves, the tip of r⃗ traces a curve, the [[rt|trajectory]] r⃗(t). Each coordinate is a function of time, so the trajectory is made of three [[xt|motions on a line]], one per axis: r⃗(t) = x(t) î + y(t) ĵ + z(t) k̂. Results about motion on a line therefore apply to each component separately.

The [[dr|displacement vector]] between two instants is the change of the position vector along the [[rt|trajectory]], Δr⃗ = r⃗(t₂) − r⃗(t₁). Like a displacement on a line, it depends only on the two end positions. A particle that moves from r⃗(t₁) = (1.0 î + 2.0 ĵ) m to r⃗(t₂) = (4.0 î − 2.0 ĵ) m has Δr⃗ = (3.0 î − 4.0 ĵ) m, of magnitude 5.0 m, whatever path it took. The difference between path and displacement is large in *Brownian motion*: a small particle suspended in a liquid is knocked about by molecular impacts and follows an erratic path of many short steps, yet its net displacement, the [[vadd|vector sum]] of the steps, stays far shorter than the path.

The [[vvec|velocity vector]] is the [[ddt|time derivative]] of the position vector, v⃗ = dr⃗/dt = lim_{Δt→0} Δr⃗/Δt. As Δt shrinks, the chord Δr⃗ lines up with the path, so v⃗ is tangent to the [[rt|trajectory]]. The unit vectors of the frame are constant, so differentiating r⃗(t) means differentiating its components: v⃗ = v_x î + v_y ĵ + v_z k̂, with v_x = dx/dt, v_y = dy/dt and v_z = dz/dt. Each [[comp|component]] is thus a one-dimensional [[v|instantaneous velocity]], and the [[vavg|average velocity]] over an interval becomes the vector Δr⃗/Δt. For r⃗(t) = (2.0 m/s)t î + (1.0 m/s²)t² ĵ, the velocity is v⃗(t) = (2.0 m/s) î + (2.0 m/s²)t ĵ; at t = 1.5 s it is (2.0 î + 3.0 ĵ) m/s, of magnitude 3.6 m/s.
eqs: v⃗ = dr⃗/dt = v_x î + v_y ĵ + v_z k̂

paragraphs.text: The [[avec|acceleration vector]] is the [[ddt|time derivative]] of the [[vvec|velocity vector]], a⃗ = dv⃗/dt = d²r⃗/dt². In [[comp|components]], a⃗ = a_x î + a_y ĵ + a_z k̂ with a_x = dv_x/dt = d²x/dt², and likewise for y and z, so each component is a one-dimensional [[a|instantaneous acceleration]]. A velocity vector can change in magnitude, in direction, or in both, and a⃗ records either change. A car rounding a bend at constant speed is therefore accelerating. For the velocity v⃗(t) = (2.0 m/s) î + (2.0 m/s²)t ĵ of the previous section, a⃗ = (2.0 m/s²) ĵ, constant and directed along the y-axis.

When a⃗ is constant, each of its components is constant, and the [[kin|constant-acceleration equations]] hold along each axis separately: x = x₀ + v_{0x}t + ½a_{x}t² and y = y₀ + v_{0y}t + ½a_{y}t², and likewise for z, all with the same t. The motions along perpendicular axes are independent and share only the clock. In the example above, x = (2.0 m/s)t is uniform and y = (1.0 m/s²)t² is uniformly accelerated; eliminating t gives y = x²/(4.0 m), a parabola. Whenever a constant acceleration is neither parallel nor antiparallel to a nonzero initial velocity, the [[rt|trajectory]] is a parabola in the plane of the two vectors.

[[proj|Projectile motion]] is the motion of a body launched into the air and then acted on by gravity alone, with air resistance neglected. With x horizontal and y vertically up, the acceleration is constant, a⃗ = −g ĵ, where g is the [[g|free-fall acceleration]]. Applying the [[kin|constant-acceleration equations]] to each [[comp|component]] splits the motion in two: uniform motion horizontally and free fall vertically, independent of each other and linked only by the common time. For a launch from the origin at speed v₀ and angle θ₀ above the horizontal, x = (v₀ cos θ₀)t and y = (v₀ sin θ₀)t − ½gt². Eliminating t gives the [[rt|trajectory]], a parabola.

On level ground the [[proj|projectile]] lands when y returns to zero. Writing y = t(v₀ sin θ₀ − ½gt) shows the nonzero root, the [[tof|time of flight]] T_{tof} = 2v₀ sin θ₀/g. The horizontal distance covered in that time is the [[rng|range]], R = (v₀ cos θ₀)T_{tof} = v₀² sin 2θ₀/g, since 2 sin θ₀ cos θ₀ = sin 2θ₀. For a given launch speed the range is largest at θ₀ = 45°, and complementary angles such as 30° and 60° give equal ranges. At the top of the path the vertical velocity is zero, which gives the maximum height H = v₀² sin²θ₀/(2g). A ball launched at 20.0 m/s and 30.0° stays in the air for 2.04 s, rises 5.10 m and lands 35.3 m away.
eqs: T_{tof} = 2v₀ sin θ₀/g,   R = v₀² sin 2θ₀/g

paragraphs.text: If the landing point is at a different height, the [[tof|time of flight]] is the later root of y(t) = h, where h is the height of the landing point relative to the launch point, and the horizontal distance is v₀ cos θ₀ times that time. At impact the horizontal velocity is still v₀ cos θ₀ and the vertical velocity is v₀ sin θ₀ − gt. A stone thrown horizontally at 15.0 m/s from a cliff 20.0 m high reaches h = −20.0 m after t = √(2 × 20.0 m / 9.80 m/s²) = 2.02 s and lands 30.3 m from the foot of the cliff. Its vertical velocity is then −19.8 m/s, so it strikes the ground at 24.8 m/s, 52.9° below the horizontal.

A body moving on a circle of radius r about the origin follows a special [[rt|trajectory]]: in [[polar|polar coordinates]] its radial coordinate stays fixed and only the angle changes. Its position is r⃗(t) = r cos φ(t) î + r sin φ(t) ĵ, so the [[circ|circular motion]] is described completely by the one function φ(t). With φ in radians, the arc length covered from φ = 0 is s = rφ. When the body covers equal arcs in equal times, its speed is constant and the motion is uniform circular motion; otherwise the motion is nonuniform.

Even at constant [[speed|speed]] v, the velocity in [[circ|circular motion]] keeps turning, so the body accelerates. With constant speed and φ = 0 at t = 0, the angle grows as φ = vt/r. Differentiating r⃗(t) once gives v⃗ = −v sin φ î + v cos φ ĵ, tangent to the circle; differentiating again gives a⃗ = −(v²/r)(cos φ î + sin φ ĵ). This vector points from the body toward the centre and has magnitude a_C = v²/r, the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]]. A car taking a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s has a_C = 8.0 m/s², about 0.8g. At a fixed speed, halving the radius doubles a_C; at a fixed radius, doubling the speed quadruples it.

The rate at which the angle of a [[circ|circular motion]] advances is the [[omega|angular frequency]] ω = dφ/dt, the [[ddt|time derivative]] of φ, measured in radians per second. In uniform circular motion ω is constant, φ = ωt, and one turn takes 2π/ω. Since the arc length is s = rφ, the speed is v = rω, and the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] becomes a_C = v²/r = rω². Earth turns once in about 8.6 × 10⁴ s, so ω ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, and a point on the equator, at r = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, has a_C ≈ 0.034 m/s², about 0.35 % of g.

If the speed changes as well, the circular motion is nonuniform and the acceleration gains a second part. The [[at|tangential acceleration]] a_T = d|v⃗|/dt, the [[ddt|time derivative]] of the [[speed|speed]], points along the path and is zero in uniform circular motion. The *total acceleration* a⃗ = a⃗_C + a⃗_T is the [[vadd|vector sum]] of this part and the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]], which is still v²/r at each instant. The two parts are perpendicular, so the [[avec|acceleration vector]] has magnitude √(a_C² + a_T²). The same split applies to any curved path, with r the radius of the circle that best fits the path at that point. A car at 10 m/s on a curve of radius 50 m, speeding up at 2.0 m/s², has a_C = a_T = 2.0 m/s² and a total acceleration of 2.8 m/s², directed 45° ahead of the inward radius.

The same motion is described differently in different [[frame|reference frames]]. Let a frame S′ move relative to a frame S, with r⃗_{S′S} the position of the origin of S′ in S. A particle P has the [[r|position vector]] r⃗_{PS′} in S′ and r⃗_{PS} in S, and the [[vadd|vector sum]] of the arrows gives r⃗_{PS} = r⃗_{PS′} + r⃗_{S′S}. Differentiating with respect to the time common to both frames gives the rule of [[galrel|relative motion]] for velocities, v⃗_{PS} = v⃗_{PS′} + v⃗_{S′S}, and the same rule for accelerations. If S′ moves at constant velocity relative to S, then a⃗_{S′S} = 0⃗ and both frames measure the same acceleration. The rules rest on one time for all frames; for speeds approaching the speed of light they fail, and special relativity replaces them.

Solved for the velocity in the moving frame, the rule of [[galrel|relative motion]] gives the [[vrel|relative velocity]] v⃗_{PS′} = v⃗_{PS} − v⃗_{S′S}: the [[vvec|velocity vector]] measured in S minus the velocity of S′. Rain falling vertically at 8.00 m/s relative to the ground, seen from a car driving at 15.0 m/s, moves at 17.0 m/s relative to the car, slanting backward at 61.9° from the vertical. A boat heading straight across a river at 4.00 m/s relative to the water, in a current of 3.00 m/s, moves relative to the shore at 5.00 m/s, at 36.9° downstream from its heading. With more than two frames, relative velocities chain: v⃗_{PC} = v⃗_{PA} + v⃗_{AB} + v⃗_{BC}.

Chapters 3 and 4 described motion without asking what produces it: from the acceleration and the initial position and velocity, [[integ|integration in time]] returns the [[rt|trajectory]]. This chapter supplies the cause. Other bodies exert forces, and the forces determine the acceleration. Newton's three laws state how: the first identifies the frames in which the laws hold, the second relates net force, mass and acceleration, and the third pairs every force with an equal and opposite force on another body. With the common forces of mechanics (weight, the normal force, tension and the spring force), these laws turn the description of motion into its prediction.

*Dynamics* is the part of mechanics that asks why motion changes. Its central quantity is [[F|force]], a push or a pull exerted on a body by another body. A force has a magnitude and a direction. *Contact forces* act where surfaces touch, as when a hand pushes a cart or a floor supports a box; *field forces*, such as gravity and the electric force, act across a distance. Forces are measured with a calibrated spring. A stretched spring exerts a *restoring force* that pulls back toward its relaxed length, and the same stretch always signals the same force; two identical springs pulling side by side at that stretch exert twice the force. The SI unit of force is the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², named after Isaac Newton, whose Principia of 1687 set out the laws of this chapter.

To find how forces affect one body, isolate it. A [[fbd|free-body diagram]] represents the body by a point and draws from that point every external force, that is, every force exerted on the body by something outside it. Each is drawn as a [[vec|vector]], with its true direction and a length proportional to its magnitude. [[F|Forces]] that the body exerts on other objects are left out, and so are forces between its own parts. One diagram is drawn for each body of interest, and drawing it is the first step of every problem in this chapter.

The forces on a [[fbd|free-body diagram]] combine by [[vadd|vector addition]] into the [[Fnet|net external force]], F⃗_{net} = ΣF⃗ = F⃗₁ + F⃗₂ + ⋯. The order of the terms does not matter, and in practice the sum is taken in [[comp|components]] along chosen axes. A crate on a smooth floor, pulled with 3.0 N toward the east and 4.0 N toward the north, has a horizontal net force of 5.0 N, directed 53.1° north of east. For a body treated as a particle, only this sum matters: two different sets of forces with the same sum have the same effect on its motion.

A puck pushed across rough concrete soon stops, while the same puck on smooth ice slides much farther. The difference is friction, a force exerted by the surface; it is an external force like any other. As friction is reduced, the puck keeps its velocity for longer, and the idealised limit is [[n1|Newton's first law]]: a body on which the [[Fnet|net external force]] is zero keeps a constant velocity, remaining at rest or moving uniformly in a straight line. This tendency to keep the present velocity is *inertia*, and the law is also called the *law of inertia*. [[m|Mass]] is the measure of inertia. A body with zero net force has zero acceleration and is said to be in *equilibrium*; large forces may act on it, but they cancel.

The first law does not hold in every [[frame|reference frame]]. Seen from a car that brakes hard, a bag on the seat starts to slide forward although nothing pushes it forward. The law therefore singles out the [[inframe|inertial reference frames]], the frames in which a body free of net force has zero acceleration, and [[n1|Newton's first law]] asserts that such frames exist. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial; accelerating and rotating frames are not. A frame fixed to the ground is inertial to good approximation: Earth's rotation gives a point on the equator a [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] of only 0.034 m/s², about 0.35 % of the [[g|free-fall acceleration]].

Experiments with carts on a low-friction track, pulled by calibrated springs, show two proportionalities: at fixed mass the acceleration is proportional to the net force, and at fixed net force it is inversely proportional to the mass. [[n2|Newton's second law]] combines them: the [[Fnet|net external force]] on a body equals its [[m|mass]] times its [[avec|acceleration]]. Solved for the acceleration, a⃗ = F⃗_{net}/m, the law says that the acceleration points along the net force and that the mass sets how strongly the body responds. Only external forces enter; forces between parts of the body cancel. As a vector equation it stands for one scalar equation per axis, ΣF_x = ma_x and likewise for y and z. It also fixes the newton: 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². A net force of 3000 N gives a 1200 kg car an acceleration of 2.50 m/s².

The second law also determines motion. Writing the acceleration as the second time derivative of position gives m d²r⃗/dt² = F⃗_{net}, a differential equation of second order. When the [[Fnet|net force]] is known as a function of position, velocity and time, the equation can be solved, in the simplest cases by [[integ|integrating]] the acceleration twice, first to the velocity and then to the position. The solution is the [[rt|trajectory]], and its two constants of integration are fixed by the initial position r⃗(0) and the initial velocity v⃗(0). A constant net force gives constant acceleration and hence the [[kin|constant-acceleration kinematics]] of Chapter 3. In this form [[n2|Newton's second law]] holds in inertial frames, for a body of constant [[m|mass]] moving much slower than light. Newton framed the law around the change of mass times velocity, his quantity of motion, now called momentum; Chapter 9 returns to that form.

Near Earth's surface every body in [[ffall|free fall]] has the same acceleration g⃗, directed downward, of magnitude g = 9.80 m/s². In free fall the only force on the body is the gravitational pull of the Earth, so [[n2|Newton's second law]] identifies that force: it is the [[w|weight]], w⃗ = m g⃗, of magnitude w = mg. A body of [[m|mass]] 70.0 kg weighs 686 N. Mass and weight are different quantities. Mass is a property of the body, measured in kilograms and the same everywhere; weight is a force, measured in newtons, which depends on the local value of the [[g|free-fall acceleration]]. On the Moon, where g = 1.62 m/s², the same body weighs 113 N, but it resists changes of velocity just as much.

Strictly, a body falling through air is never in free fall: air resistance acts as well and grows with speed until it nearly balances the weight, as Chapter 6 shows. It is negligible only for short drops of compact, dense objects. A bathroom scale does not measure weight directly; it measures the force with which it pushes up on whatever stands on it. In a freely falling elevator or an orbiting spacecraft, scale and body fall together, the scale reads zero, and the body is called weightless. Gravity has not vanished: 400 km above the ground g is still about 8.7 m/s², nearly 90 % of its surface value. Weightlessness is [[ffall|free fall]], not the absence of [[w|weight]].

Every force arises from an interaction between two bodies. [[n3|Newton's third law]] states that if body A exerts a force F⃗_{AB} on body B, then B exerts a force F⃗_{BA} = −F⃗_{AB} on A, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and simultaneous. Two spring scales hooked together read the same however hard they are pulled. The two forces of a pair are of the same kind and act on different bodies, so they never appear together in the [[fbd|free-body diagram]] of one body and never cancel each other. A book resting on a table is pulled down by the Earth and pulls the Earth up with an equal force. The table's upward push on the book is a different force; its partner is the book's downward push on the table.

Which forces cancel depends on the system chosen. For a system of several bodies, the forces between its members occur in third-law pairs inside the system, and their sum is zero; the [[Fnet|net force]] on the system is the sum of the external forces alone. To move forward, a body must therefore push on something else. A swimmer pushes water backward and the water pushes the swimmer forward. A car's tyres push backward on the road, and the road pushes the car forward. A rocket engine expels gas backward at high speed, and the gas pushes the engine forward with a force called *thrust*. In each case the forward force is exerted by another body; internal forces alone cannot accelerate a system.

A book on a table does not sink into it. The table deforms very slightly and pushes back with a contact force perpendicular to its surface, the [[Nf|normal force]] N⃗, where normal means perpendicular. It grows as needed to prevent penetration, up to the point where the surface breaks. Its magnitude follows from [[n2|Newton's second law]] applied across the surface: if the body does not accelerate perpendicular to the surface and no other force acts in that direction, the normal force balances the perpendicular component of the [[w|weight]]. On a level surface N = mg. On a plane inclined at angle θ, only the component mg cos θ presses into the surface, so N = mg cos θ; for a 10.0 kg block on a 30.0° slope, N = 84.9 N.

A string, rope or cable pulled taut transmits a pulling force along its length, the [[T|tension]] T. A rope can only pull, never push. If its mass is negligible, the tension is the same along its whole length, and a frictionless pulley changes the direction of the rope without changing the tension. For a body hanging at rest from a vertical rope, [[n2|Newton's second law]] with zero acceleration gives T = mg: the rope balances the [[w|weight]]. If a load hangs from the middle of a wire that sags by an angle θ below the horizontal on each side, the two halves together must supply mg vertically, so T = mg/(2 sin θ). A 5.00 kg load on a wire sagging by 5.0° produces a tension of 281 N, almost six times its weight.

Hanging increasing loads from a spring shows that, for moderate loads, its extension grows in proportion to the load. A spring stretched or compressed by x from its relaxed length therefore pulls or pushes back with a force proportional to x. This is [[hooke|Hooke's law]], F = −kx. The force constant k, in N/m, measures the stiffness of the spring, and the minus sign says that the force opposes the displacement. The law is an approximation that holds while the deformation stays small, below the proportional limit of the material. Because the spring's [[F|force]] follows from its deformation, a calibrated spring is the standard way to measure forces: a spring scale with k = 500 N/m stretched by 2.00 cm reads 10.0 N. Each force in this section has an agent and a third-law partner. Forces that appear only because motion is described from an accelerating frame have neither; such *fictitious forces* are treated in Chapter 6.

A [[fbd|free-body diagram]] is drawn in a fixed order. Represent the chosen body by a dot. Find everything that touches or pulls it: a surface gives a [[Nf|normal force]] and possibly friction, a rope a [[T|tension]], a spring a force given by [[hooke|Hooke's law]], and the Earth the [[w|weight]]. Draw each external force as an arrow from the dot in its true direction. Leave out forces the body exerts on other things, and never add ma as a force; it is the result of the forces, not one of them. Choose axes, ideally one along the expected acceleration, and resolve the forces into components. For interacting bodies draw one diagram each: the two forces of a pair related by [[n3|Newton's third law]] always appear on different diagrams.

Newton's laws are general, but to solve a problem one also needs the forces themselves. This chapter adds force laws for two contact forces met everywhere: friction between solid surfaces and drag in a fluid. Both are empirical and valid only over limited ranges. It then applies [[n2|Newton's second law]] to [[circ|circular motion]], where a net force toward the centre must produce the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] of Chapter 4, and shows how the laws must be modified when motion is described from an accelerating or rotating frame.

Newton's laws of motion are applied in a fixed order: a [[fbd|free-body diagram]] for each body, axes, then [[n2|Newton's second law]] for each axis. In *particle equilibrium* every component of the [[Fnet|net force]] vanishes; in *particle acceleration* the components equal ma_x and ma_y, and [[kin|kinematics]] then gives positions and times. In an *Atwood machine*, masses m₁ > m₂ hang from a light rope over a light, frictionless pulley; the second law for each mass gives the magnitude of their acceleration, a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂). A person of mass m in an *elevator* accelerating upward at a is pushed by the floor with a [[Nf|normal force]] N = m(g + a). A velocity-dependent force, such as the drag force, makes the second law a differential equation.

When one solid surface slides, or tends to slide, over another, the contact force between them has a component along the surfaces that opposes the relative motion or its onset. This component is [[frict|friction]]. Pulling a block across a table with a spring scale shows that doubling the load on the block doubles the friction, while turning the block onto a smaller face hardly changes it: friction is roughly proportional to the [[Nf|normal force]], f ∝ N, and nearly independent of the apparent area of contact. The reason is microscopic. Even polished surfaces touch only at the tips of their irregularities, and pressing harder enlarges this true contact area roughly in proportion to the load. Sliding requires shearing these junctions, and the force per unit area needed is a *shear stress* characteristic of the materials. The law is empirical, and its constants must be measured for each pair of surfaces.

A heavy crate pushed gently does not move, because [[fs|static friction]] matches the push. Static friction takes whatever value equilibrium requires, up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_s N, where μ_s is the *coefficient of static friction* and N the [[Nf|normal force]]. The [[frict|friction law]] fixes only this maximum. It also yields a simple measurement on an *inclined plane*. On a slope of angle θ, a block has N = mg cos θ and a weight component mg sin θ along the slope; static friction can hold it as long as mg sin θ ≤ μ_s mg cos θ, so the block starts to slide when tan θ reaches μ_s. The mass cancels. If sliding begins at 26.6°, then μ_s = tan 26.6° = 0.50.

Once the surfaces slide, the [[frict|friction law]] gives a force of fixed magnitude, the [[fk|kinetic friction]] f_k = μ_k N, with N the [[Nf|normal force]]. It opposes the body's velocity relative to the surface. The *coefficient of kinetic friction* μ_k is usually smaller than μ_s, so a sliding object is easier to keep moving than to start. Both coefficients are dimensionless; they range from a few hundredths for ice sliding on ice to about 1 for rubber on dry concrete, and an *artificial joint* is designed to be near the low end. A 20.0 kg crate on a level floor with μ_s = 0.50 and μ_k = 0.40 has N = 196 N. It stays at rest under any horizontal push up to 98 N; once sliding, it is opposed by 78.4 N, and a 100 N push accelerates it at 21.6 N/20.0 kg = 1.08 m/s².

A body moving at speed v on a circle of radius r has the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] a_C = v²/r, directed toward the centre. By [[n2|Newton's second law]], a net force toward the centre must produce it. This is the [[Fc|centripetal force]], F_c = mv²/r = mrω², where m is the body's [[m|mass]] and ω the [[omega|angular frequency]]. It is not a new kind of force but a role that some force fills: tension for a stone whirled on a string, gravity for a satellite, [[fs|static friction]] for a car on a flat curve. Friction can supply at most μ_s mg there, so the car can take the curve only if v²/r ≤ μ_s g. A 1200 kg car rounding a curve of radius 50.0 m at 15.0 m/s needs a centripetal force of 5400 N, and the road must provide μ_s ≥ 0.46.

On a [[bank|banked curve]] the road is tilted toward the centre by an angle θ, so the [[Nf|normal force]] has an inward horizontal component. Without friction, the vertical component balances the [[w|weight]] and the horizontal component supplies the [[Fc|centripetal force]]: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r. Dividing the two equations gives tan θ = v²/(rg). At this design speed a car needs no friction to take the curve, a condition called *ideal banking*. The angle does not depend on the mass, but each angle suits only one speed. A curve of radius 100 m designed for 20.0 m/s should be banked at 22.2°; cars that are faster or slower rely on friction to hold their path.

All forces so far have been described from an [[inframe|inertial frame]]. Consider a frame whose origin accelerates at a⃗_{frame} without rotating. By the rules of [[galrel|relative motion]], the acceleration of a body measured in this frame is a⃗′ = a⃗ − a⃗_{frame}, so [[n2|Newton's second law]] becomes m a⃗′ = F⃗_{net} − m a⃗_{frame}. In such a [[noninert|noninertial frame of reference]] the second law holds only if an *inertial force* −m a⃗_{frame} is added to the real forces. This force is proportional to the mass and has neither an agent nor a third-law partner. In a car accelerating forward at 2.45 m/s², a pendulum hangs tilted backward by 14.0° from the vertical, with tan θ = a/g = 0.250. A passenger explains the tilt by a backward inertial force; an observer on the ground sees the string's tension accelerating the bob forward.

In a frame rotating steadily with angular velocity ω⃗, whose magnitude is the [[omega|angular frequency]] ω of the rotation, two inertial forces are needed. A body at rest in the frame, at distance r from the axis, is subject to the outward *centrifugal force* mrω². A *centrifuge* spins samples so fast that this force exceeds their weight many times over and drives the denser parts of a mixture outward. A body moving with [[vvec|velocity]] v⃗′ relative to the frame is also subject to the [[Fcor|Coriolis force]], F⃗ = −2m ω⃗ × v⃗′, a [[cross|vector product]] perpendicular to v⃗′ that bends the path without changing the speed. Earth turns at ω = 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, so at 100 m/s the Coriolis acceleration is at most 2ωv′ = 0.0146 m/s², yet over hours it turns storms counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. Both forces belong to the [[noninert|noninertial frame]] and vanish in an inertial one.

A body moving through a fluid such as air or water is resisted by the [[FD|drag force]], which points opposite to its velocity relative to the fluid and grows with its [[speed|speed]]. For most motions through air, from a thrown ball to a car on a highway, the body leaves a turbulent wake and the drag is close to F_D = ½CρAv². Here ρ is the density of the fluid, A the cross-sectional area that faces the flow and C the dimensionless *drag coefficient*, which depends on the shape of the body. The coefficient is measured in a *wind tunnel*; a sphere has C ≈ 0.5 and a streamlined modern car about 0.3. For slow motion of a small sphere of radius r through a fluid of viscosity η, the flow stays smooth and the drag is instead linear in the speed, given by Stokes' law, F_s = 6πrηv.

A body falling from rest speeds up, and the growing drag reduces its acceleration until the drag balances the weight. From then on the net force is zero, [[n2|Newton's second law]] gives zero acceleration, and the body falls at constant speed, its [[vT|terminal velocity]]. Equating the [[FD|drag force]] ½CρAv² with the [[w|weight]] mg gives v_T = √(2mg/(ρCA)). A hailstone 2.0 cm across, of mass 3.8 g, with C = 0.50 and A = 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ m², falls through air of density 1.21 kg/m³ at about 20 m/s. For bodies of the same shape and density, m grows as the cube of the size and A as its square, so v_T grows as the square root of the size: dust drifts down while large bodies fall fast. In the slow, viscous regime, neglecting buoyancy, the balance 6πrηv_T = mg gives v_T = mg/(6πrη) instead.

The second law predicts motion by following the [[F|forces]] from instant to instant. Often only the speeds at two positions are wanted, and the forces are known as functions of position rather than of time. This chapter therefore integrates [[n2|Newton's second law]] along the path instead of over time. Three quantities result: work, the integral of a force along a displacement; kinetic energy, ½mv²; and power, the rate at which work is done. The second law then takes a scalar form: the net work done on a body equals the change of its kinetic energy.

A force transfers energy to a body that moves along the direction of the force. For a constant [[F|force]] and a straight [[dr|displacement]] Δr⃗, the [[W|work]] done by the force is the [[dot|scalar product]] W = F⃗·Δr⃗ = F Δr cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is a scalar. It is positive when the force has a component along the motion, negative when that component is opposite to the motion, and zero when the force is perpendicular to it, like the [[Nf|normal force]] on a body sliding on a level floor. For a varying force or a curved path, the path is divided into small steps dr⃗ and the contributions F⃗·dr⃗ are added, which in the limit is an [[integ|integral]] along the path. The SI unit of work is the *joule*, 1 J = 1 N·m.

Three forces recur in practice. The [[w|weight]] is constant, so its work depends only on the change in height, W = −mg(y_B − y_A), whatever the path; while a 2.00 kg book is lifted by 1.50 m, gravity does −29.4 J of work on it. The spring force of [[hooke|Hooke's law]], F = −kx, varies with position, and integrating it gives W = −½k(x_B² − x_A²). A spring with k = 200 N/m, stretched from its relaxed length by 0.100 m, does −1.00 J of work on the hand that stretches it. A *bungee cord* behaves roughly like such a spring once it is taut. [[fk|Kinetic friction]] of constant magnitude always opposes the motion, so its work is −f_k times the length of the path, and a longer route between the same two points means more negative work.

The quantity that work changes is the [[K|kinetic energy]] of a body, K = ½mv², built from its [[m|mass]] and its [[speed|speed]]. It is a scalar, never negative, and measured in joules, since 1 kg·m²/s² = 1 N·m = 1 J. Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy, while doubling the mass only doubles it. A 0.145 kg baseball thrown at 40.0 m/s has K = 116 J, and a 1500 kg car at 25.0 m/s has 469 kJ. The expression holds for speeds much smaller than the speed of light; at higher speeds special relativity replaces it with a formula that reduces to ½mv² when v/c is small.

Kinetic energy depends on the [[frame|reference frame]], because speed does. A 1.00 kg parcel resting on a seat in a train that moves at 30.0 m/s has zero kinetic energy in the train's frame and 450 J in the ground frame. If a passenger throws it forward at 10.0 m/s relative to the train, its kinetic energy becomes 50.0 J in the train frame and 800 J in the ground frame. The two observers disagree about the gain, 50.0 J against 350 J, and therefore about the work done by the passenger's hand, which during the throw moves farther in the ground frame. Each account is consistent within its own frame. For a system of particles, the [[K|kinetic energy]] is the sum of ½m_j v_j² over its particles, all measured in one frame.

Several forces usually act on a body at once. Each does its own [[W|work]], and their sum is the [[Wnet|net work]]. For a particle all forces share the same displacement, and the scalar product is distributive, so the net work also equals the work of the [[Fnet|net external force]]: W_{net} = ∫F⃗_{net}·dr⃗ = ΣW_i. A 5.00 kg box dragged 3.00 m across a level floor by a horizontal 40.0 N pull, against 25.0 N of kinetic friction, receives +120 J from the pull and −75.0 J from friction, while the normal force and the weight, both perpendicular to the motion, do no work. Then W_{net} = 45.0 J, the same as (40.0 N − 25.0 N) × 3.00 m.

Net work changes speed. Take [[n2|Newton's second law]], m dv⃗/dt = F⃗_{net}, and form the scalar product of both sides with the displacement dr⃗ = v⃗ dt. The right side becomes F⃗_{net}·dr⃗, the work of the net force in that step. The left side becomes m v⃗·dv⃗ = d(½mv²), the change of [[K|kinetic energy]]. Integrating from A to B gives the [[wet|work–energy theorem]]: the [[Wnet|net work]] done on a particle equals the change of its kinetic energy. It holds for any forces, constant or not, because it is the second law in integrated form. If the box of the last example started from rest, it ends with K = 45.0 J and a speed of √(2 × 45.0 J / 5.00 kg) = 4.24 m/s.

The theorem relates forces, distances and speeds without involving time. A car skidding to a stop on a level road with locked wheels loses its kinetic energy to the work of kinetic friction, μ_k mgd = ½mv², so its stopping distance d = v²/(2μ_k g) grows as the square of the speed: twice as fast takes four times as far. On a frictionless *loop-the-loop* track of radius R, the [[Nf|normal force]] is perpendicular to the motion and does no work, so between the bottom and the top only the [[w|weight]] changes K, through the work −mg(2R). At the top the car stays on the track only if its weight does not exceed the [[Fc|centripetal force]] required there, mg ≤ mv_{top}²/R. The [[wet|work–energy theorem]] then requires v_{bottom}² = v_{top}² + 4gR ≥ 5gR, that is, at least 4.43 m/s at the bottom for R = 0.40 m.

Engines and muscles are rated less by how much work they can do than by how fast they do it. [[P|Power]] is the rate at which work is done. Over a finite interval Δt, the *average power* is the work divided by the time, W/Δt; the *instantaneous power* is the limit of this ratio as the interval shrinks, the [[ddt|time derivative]] P = dW/dt of the [[W|work]]. The SI unit is the watt, 1 W = 1 J/s; an older unit, the horsepower, is about 746 W. A motor that lifts a 500 kg load through 12.0 m in 20.0 s at constant speed does 58 800 J of work, an average power of 2940 W, or about 3.9 hp.

For a force acting on a moving body, the work in a time dt is dW = F⃗·dr⃗ = F⃗·v⃗ dt. Dividing by dt expresses the [[P|power]] delivered by the [[F|force]] as its [[dot|scalar product]] with the [[vvec|velocity]], P = F⃗·v⃗. Only the component of the force along the velocity delivers power. At constant speed the driving force balances the resistance, so the power needed is the resistance times the speed: a cyclist holding 10.0 m/s against 25.0 N of air [[FD|drag]] and rolling resistance must supply 250 W. Because drag grows as v², the power needed to overcome it grows as v³, and doubling the speed takes eight times the power.

The [[W|work]] done by the [[w|weight]] or by a spring between two points does not depend on the path taken between them. This chapter turns that observation into a new quantity, potential energy, which stores the work of such forces in the configuration of a system. Added to the [[K|kinetic energy]], it gives the mechanical energy, which stays constant when only these forces do work and otherwise changes by the work of the remaining forces. Conservation of energy then solves many problems without reference to time, and a graph of potential energy shows where a body can move and where it can rest.

For some forces the [[W|work]] done as a body moves from A to B depends only on the end points, not on the path. For such a force one can define a function of position, the [[U|potential energy]], whose decrease equals the work done: ΔU_{AB} = U_B − U_A = −W_{AB}. Only this *potential energy difference* has physical meaning. The zero of U can therefore be placed at any convenient configuration; another choice adds the same constant everywhere and changes no prediction. Potential energy belongs to a system of interacting bodies, such as a body and the Earth or a block and a spring, not to one body alone. When the force does positive work, U decreases by the same amount; when it does negative work, energy is stored.

Near Earth's surface the [[w|weight]] is constant, and its work between heights y_A and y_B is −mg(y_B − y_A) along any path. The definition of [[U|potential energy]] then gives the [[Ugrav|gravitational potential energy]] of the body–Earth system, U(y) = mgy + const, with y measured upward. The constant is usually chosen so that U is zero at the floor or the ground, but any choice works. Raising a 5.00 kg box from the floor to a shelf 2.00 m higher increases U by 98.0 J, whatever route the box takes; if it falls back, it regains those 98.0 J as [[K|kinetic energy]] when air resistance is negligible. The formula assumes heights small compared with Earth's radius, so that g stays constant.

A spring obeying [[hooke|Hooke's law]] does work −½k(x_B² − x_A²) when its end moves from x_A to x_B, again independent of the path. Its [[U|potential energy]], the [[Uel|elastic potential energy]], is therefore U(x) = ½kx² + const, and the natural choice puts U = 0 at the relaxed length, x = 0. Stretch and compression by the same amount store the same energy; a spring with k = 400 N/m compressed by 5.0 cm stores 0.50 J. A *bungee jumper* shows both kinds of potential energy at work. During the free fall, [[Ugrav|gravitational potential energy]] becomes kinetic energy. Once the cord is taut it stretches, storing elastic energy, until at the lowest point the jumper stops and, if losses are neglected, all the gravitational energy lost so far is stored in the cord.

A [[cons|conservative force]] is one whose [[W|work]] between any two points is the same along every path. Equivalently, its work around every closed path is zero, ∮F⃗·dr⃗ = 0: going from A to B along one path and back along another, the two contributions cancel. Gravity near the Earth and the force of an ideal spring are conservative, and a potential energy can be defined only for forces of this kind. [[fk|Kinetic friction]] is not conservative. On any closed path its work is −f_k times the path length, which is never zero. [[FD|Drag]], which also always opposes the motion, is not conservative either.

Since the work of a [[cons|conservative force]] is minus the change of [[U|potential energy]], the [[F|force]] can be recovered from U. For a small displacement dℓ in any direction, F_{ℓ} dℓ = −dU, so the component of the force along that direction is F_{ℓ} = −dU/dℓ, and in three dimensions F⃗ = −∇U: the force points down the steepest slope of U. From U = ½kx² this returns F = −kx, and from U = mgy it returns F_y = −mg. Conversely, a force F⃗ = F_x î + F_y ĵ can be conservative only if F_x dx + F_y dy is an *exact differential*, which requires ∂F_x/∂y = ∂F_y/∂x. In arbitrary units, the force (2xy, x²) passes this test and has U = −x²y; the swirling force (−y, x) fails it and does work 2π once around the unit circle counterclockwise.

Kinetic friction, air drag and the push of a muscle or a motor are *non-conservative forces*: their [[W|work]] depends on the path, and no potential energy describes it. The work done on a body therefore splits into two parts: the work of the [[cons|conservative forces]], which equals −ΔU, and the rest, the [[Wnc|work of nonconservative forces]], W_{nc} = W_{net} − W_{cons}. Friction and drag make W_{nc} negative and turn mechanical energy into thermal energy of the surfaces or the air. A motor or a muscle can make it positive, drawing on energy stored in fuel, food or a battery.

The sum of the [[K|kinetic energy]] of a system and its [[U|potential energy]] is its [[Emech|mechanical energy]], E = K + U. Because the zero of U is a matter of choice, E is defined only up to an additive constant, but its changes are not affected. A ball thrown straight up shows the two terms trading places: on the way up K decreases while the gravitational potential energy grows, at the top K is zero, and on the way down the exchange runs in reverse.

Split the [[Wnet|net work]] in the [[wet|work–energy theorem]] into the work of conservative forces, which is minus the change of [[U|potential energy]], and the [[Wnc|nonconservative work]] W_{nc}: then ΔK = −ΔU + W_{nc}, or Δ(K + U) = W_{nc}. The [[Emech|mechanical energy]] changes only through the work of nonconservative forces. When they do no work, mechanical energy is a conserved quantity, the same at every point of the motion. This is the [[econs|conservation of mechanical energy]]. Energy removed by friction is not destroyed: it reappears as thermal energy of the surfaces, and when every form of energy is counted, the total energy of an isolated system does not change.

[[econs|Energy conservation]] replaces a calculation in time by a comparison of two states. A block released from rest 1.00 m up a frictionless ramp reaches the bottom with ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = 4.43 m/s for any shape of ramp and any mass. It then slides onto a level floor where μ_k = 0.25. [[fk|Kinetic friction]] does work −μ_k mgd, and the block stops when this has removed the whole mgh, after d = h/μ_k = 4.0 m. *Bar graphs of total energy* make such accounts visible: at each stage, bars for K, U and the energy converted by friction stand side by side, and their total height stays the same.

For motion along a line, plotting U(x) together with the total energy E, a horizontal line, gives a [[pediag|potential energy diagram]]. By [[econs|conservation of mechanical energy]], K = E − U(x) at every position, and because K cannot be negative, the body can be found only where E ≥ U(x). The vertical gap between the line and the curve is the kinetic energy. Where the curve meets the line, K = 0: the body stops momentarily and reverses, so such a position is a *turning point*. A mass on a spring with energy E oscillates between the turning points x = ±√(2E/k), where ½kx² = E. The force is minus the slope of the [[U|potential energy]] curve, so on the graph the body is always pushed downhill.

Where the curve is flat, dU/dx = 0, the [[F|force]] F = −dU/dx vanishes, and a body placed there at rest stays at rest. Such an [[eqpt|equilibrium point]] can be read off the [[pediag|potential energy diagram]], and its stability is decided by the curvature of U. At a minimum, a small displacement produces a force back toward the equilibrium, and the body oscillates about it: the equilibrium is stable. Near a minimum at x₀, U(x) ≈ U(x₀) + ½U″(x₀)(x − x₀)², which apart from a constant is the [[Uel|elastic potential energy]] of a spring with force constant k = U″(x₀). At a maximum, the force pushes the body farther away, and the equilibrium is unstable. For U(x) = ax⁴ − bx² with a, b > 0, x = 0 is unstable and x = ±√(b/(2a)) are stable.

[[Emech|Mechanical energy]] is one of several forms of energy, and only the total over all forms is conserved. *Thermal energy* is the random kinetic and potential energy of atoms and molecules; *chemical energy* is stored in molecular bonds; *electrical energy* is carried by charges and currents; *radiant energy* travels as light and other electromagnetic waves; *nuclear energy* is stored in atomic nuclei. Sources replenished on human timescales, such as *hydropower*, *wind power*, *geothermal* heat and *solar power*, are *renewable*; *fossil fuels* such as coal, oil and natural gas, and the uranium used for fission, are *non-renewable*. Every conversion obeys [[econs|energy conservation]], yet some energy always ends up as thermal energy at low temperature, which is hard to use again. The rate of conversion is a [[P|power]].

Forces between bodies often act for short or poorly known times, as in a collision or an explosion. This chapter introduces a quantity that can be followed without such details: momentum, mass times velocity. [[n2|Newton's second law]] says that the net force on a body is the rate of change of its momentum, and [[n3|Newton's third law]] makes the internal forces of a system cancel, so the total momentum of an isolated group of bodies cannot change. Momentum conservation, combined with the [[econs|energy conservation]] of Chapter 8, describes collisions, and the centre of mass reduces the motion of a whole system to that of a single point.

The [[p|momentum]] of a particle is the product of its [[m|mass]] and its [[vvec|velocity]], p⃗ = m v⃗. It is a vector pointing along the velocity, measured in kg·m/s. Momentum and kinetic energy both grow with mass and speed, but they are different measures of motion. A 10.0 g bullet at 400 m/s and a 2.00 kg ball at 2.00 m/s have the same momentum, 4.00 kg·m/s, yet the bullet carries 800 J of kinetic energy and the ball only 4.00 J. Stopping either of them in the same time requires the same average force; stopping them in the same distance does not.

Newton framed his second law around the change of the quantity of motion, mass times velocity, which is the momentum. In this form [[n2|Newton's second law]] reads F⃗_{net} = dp⃗/dt: the net external force equals the [[ddt|time derivative]] of the [[p|momentum]]. For constant mass, d(mv⃗)/dt = m a⃗, which is the form of Section 5.3. The momentum form is the more general one. It keeps its shape in special relativity, where momentum is no longer m v⃗, and applied to a closed system it handles bodies that gain or lose mass, as Section 9.7 shows. Eliminating v between p = mv and K = ½mv² expresses the [[K|kinetic energy]] of a particle of [[m|mass]] m through its momentum: K = p²/(2m).

A [[F|force]] acting over a time interval changes momentum, and the measure of its accumulated effect is the [[J|impulse]], the [[integ|time integral]] of the force, J⃗ = ∫F⃗(t) dt from t_i to t_f. In a collision the force rises and falls within milliseconds and is rarely known in detail, but the impulse can be written as the average force times the duration, J⃗ = F⃗_{ave}Δt; for each component it is the area under the graph of force against time. Impulse is a vector, measured in N·s, which equals kg·m/s. It accumulates a force over time as [[W|work]] accumulates a force over displacement.

Integrating [[n2|Newton's second law]], F⃗_{net} = dp⃗/dt, over the interval gives the [[imt|impulse–momentum theorem]]: the [[J|impulse]] of the net force equals the change of [[p|momentum]], J⃗ = Δp⃗, however the force varies in between. The theorem explains *seatbelts* and *airbags*. In a crash the passenger's momentum must fall to zero whatever happens, so the impulse is fixed; spreading it over a longer time lowers the average force. A 70.0 kg passenger stopping from 15.0 m/s has Δp = 1050 kg·m/s. Stopped in 0.0100 s by a hard surface, the average force is 105 000 N, about 150 times the passenger's weight; stopped in 0.150 s by a belt and airbag, it is 7000 N. Padding, crumple zones and bent knees on landing work the same way.

To treat several bodies together, draw a boundary around them, as for a [[fbd|free-body diagram]], but enclosing all of them. What lies inside is a [[sys|system of particles]], described by the [[m|masses]] m_j and [[rt|trajectories]] r⃗_j(t) of its members. Forces between members are internal to the system; forces exerted from outside the boundary are external. The boundary is a free choice and decides which forces are which: when two skaters push off each other, the push is internal to the two-skater system but external to each skater alone. A system whose members stay the same and on which the net external force is zero is a *closed system* in the sense used here; many texts call it an isolated system.

Write [[n2|Newton's second law]] in momentum form, dp⃗_j/dt = F⃗_j, for each member of the [[sys|system]] and add the equations. The left sides add up to the rate of change of the total [[p|momentum]], P⃗ = Σp⃗_j; the right sides add up to all forces on all members. By [[n3|Newton's third law]] the internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs and cancel in the sum, so dP⃗/dt = F⃗_{ext}, the net external force. If it is zero, the total momentum is constant: this is the [[pcons|law of conservation of momentum]]. It holds whatever the internal forces are, and component by component; if the external forces have no horizontal component, the horizontal momentum is conserved even while the vertical momentum changes.
eqs: P⃗ = p⃗₁ + p⃗₂ + ⋯ + p⃗_N = constant when F⃗_{ext} = 0

paragraphs.text: [[pcons|Momentum conservation]] also applies to brief events such as collisions and explosions when external forces act but are small compared with the internal ones: over the short duration their [[J|impulse]] is negligible. A 60.0 kg skater at rest on smooth ice throws a 2.00 kg ball forward at 15.0 m/s. The total momentum was zero and stays zero, so (60.0 kg)v + (2.00 kg)(15.0 m/s) = 0, and the skater recoils at v = −0.500 m/s. The same reasoning gives the recoil of a gun and the push a spacecraft receives from a thruster.

In a collision the forces between the bodies are large and brief, so [[pcons|conservation of momentum]] holds for the colliding bodies taken together. It does not fix the outcome alone: in one dimension, two final velocities must be found from a single equation. The missing information is what happens to the [[K|kinetic energy]], and [[coll|collisions]] are classified by it. In an *elastic* collision K is conserved, as nearly happens for hard steel balls and exactly for atoms that collide without being excited. In an *inelastic* collision part of K becomes thermal energy, sound or permanent deformation. A *perfectly inelastic* collision, in which the bodies stick together, loses the most kinetic energy that momentum conservation allows. In an *explosion*, stored energy is released and K increases.

When m₁, moving at v₁, sticks to m₂ at rest, momentum alone gives the common final velocity v = m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂), and the fraction of the kinetic energy lost is m₂/(m₁ + m₂). In a head-on elastic collision with m₂ at rest, momentum and kinetic energy together give v₁′ = (m₁ − m₂)v₁/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂′ = 2m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂). Equal masses exchange velocities. A neutron hitting a *deuteron*, the nucleus of heavy hydrogen with about twice its mass, passes on 8/9 of its kinetic energy, which makes heavy water an effective neutron moderator. A projectile can bounce straight back only from a heavier target; when Geiger and Marsden saw a few alpha particles rebound from gold foil, Rutherford concluded in 1911 that nearly all of an atom's mass sits in a tiny nucleus, far heavier than an alpha particle.

In two or three dimensions [[pcons|conservation of momentum]] is a vector law, and it splits into one equation per axis with [[comp|vector components]]: the x components of the [[p|momenta]] add to the same total before and after, and so do the y components. Each equation holds separately, so a planar collision gives two conditions instead of one. A useful case is an elastic glancing [[coll|collision]] of two equal masses, one initially at rest. Momentum gives v⃗₁ = v⃗₁′ + v⃗₂′, and [[K|kinetic energy]] gives v₁² = v₁′² + v₂′². Squaring the first equation and comparing shows that the [[dot|scalar product]] v⃗₁′·v⃗₂′ is zero: unless the collision is head-on, the two bodies move off at right angles, as billiard balls nearly do.

Every [[sys|system of particles]] has a special point, the [[rcm|centre of mass]], whose [[r|position vector]] is the mass-weighted average of the positions of its members, r⃗_{CM} = (1/M)Σm_j r⃗_j, where M = Σm_j is the total [[m|mass]]. Each coordinate is averaged separately. For 2.00 kg at x = 0 and 6.00 kg at x = 4.00 m, x_{CM} = (6.00 kg × 4.00 m)/(8.00 kg) = 3.00 m, nearer the heavier mass. The centre of mass need not lie inside any material: for a ring it is the empty centre. Differentiating with respect to time gives the velocity of the centre of mass, v⃗_{CM} = (1/M)Σm_j v⃗_j, and its acceleration, a⃗_{CM} = (1/M)Σm_j a⃗_j.

Multiply a⃗_{CM} by M and apply [[n2|Newton's second law]] to each member: M a⃗_{CM} = Σm_j a⃗_j is the sum of all forces on all members. The *internal forces* between members cancel in pairs by [[n3|Newton's third law]], and only the *external forces* remain. The result is the [[n2sys|second law for a system]], F⃗_{ext} = M a⃗_{CM} = dP⃗/dt, with total momentum P⃗ = M v⃗_{CM}. The [[rcm|centre of mass]] of any [[sys|system]] moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the external forces alone, whatever the members do among themselves. A firework shell that bursts in flight scatters fragments in all directions, yet until the first fragment lands, their centre of mass continues along the parabola of [[proj|projectile motion]], air resistance neglected.

For a continuous body the sum becomes an integral over mass elements dm, r⃗_{CM} = (1/M)∫r⃗ dm. For a thin rod or string along the x axis, an element of length dx has mass dm = λ dx, where λ = dm/dx is the [[lmd|linear mass density]], the [[m|mass]] per unit [[L|length]]; a uniform rod of mass M and length L has λ = M/L. The [[rcm|centre of mass]] is then x_{CM} = (1/M)∫xλ dx, an ordinary [[integ|integral]] along the rod. A uniform rod balances at its midpoint. A rod from x = 0 to x = L whose density grows in proportion to x, λ = λ₀x/L, has M = λ₀L/2 and x_{CM} = 2L/3, two thirds of the way toward its heavier end.

A rocket in empty space has nothing to push against; it gains speed by throwing mass backward. Treat the rocket and the gas it ejects in a short time dt as one closed [[sys|system]]. At time t the rocket has mass m and speed v; it then ejects gas that leaves at speed u relative to the rocket, and its mass changes by dm, a negative amount. [[pcons|Conservation of momentum]] for this system gives, to first order, m dv = −u dm. Integrating from the initial mass m_i to the current mass m gives the [[rocket|rocket equation]], Δv = u ln(m_i/m). The gain in speed depends only on the exhaust speed and the mass ratio, not on how quickly the fuel is burned.

With an exhaust speed of 3.0 km/s, typical of chemical rockets, burning fuel until the mass ratio m_i/m reaches 10 gives Δv = 3.0 km/s × ln 10 = 6.9 km/s.
