Because the logarithm grows slowly, high speeds demand very large mass ratios, and multistage rockets discard empty tanks and engines to keep the ratio favourable. The force of the exhaust on the rocket, the thrust, has magnitude u|dm/dt|. For a rocket climbing vertically near the Earth, the [[w|weight]] is an external force, and if air resistance is neglected the speed gained after a burn of duration t becomes Δv = u ln(m_i/m) − gt.

Chapters 4 to 9 treated bodies as points, or as systems whose centre of mass moves like a point. Wheels, rotors, doors and planets also turn. A [[rigid|rigid body]] is a [[sys|system of particles]] whose mutual distances never change. When it turns about an axis fixed in a reference frame, each particle off the axis performs [[circ|circular motion]] in a plane perpendicular to the axis, and all particles turn through the same angle in the same time. One angle θ(t) therefore describes the whole body. This chapter develops the kinematics of that angle, then the moment of inertia, torque, Newton's second law for rotation, and rotational work and power.

The orientation of a [[rigid|rigid body]] turning about a fixed axis is given by one number, its [[theta|angular position]] θ: the angle between a reference line fixed in the body, perpendicular to the axis, and a fixed direction in the frame. Angles are measured in radians. A point at distance r from the axis that moves through an arc of length s along its circle turns through θ = s/r. A full turn is an arc of length 2πr, so 1 rev = 2π rad = 360°, and 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. As a ratio of two lengths the radian is dimensionless, which is why the unit rad can be written or dropped, as in rad/s or s⁻¹. By convention θ increases for counterclockwise rotation seen from the positive end of the axis.

The [[angvel|angular velocity]] is the rate of change of the angular position. Its average over an interval is Δθ/Δt, and its limit as Δt → 0, the *instantaneous angular velocity*, is the [[ddt|time derivative]] ω = dθ/dt of [[theta|θ]]. Since all points of a rigid body turn through the same angle, ω is the same for each of them. It is the [[omega|angular frequency]] of circular motion given a direction: the vector ω⃗ lies along the axis, with its sense fixed by the *right-hand rule*. When the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of rotation, the thumb points along ω⃗. With the origin on the axis, a point at position r⃗ has velocity v⃗ = ω⃗ × r⃗, a [[cross|vector product]], and [[speed|speed]] v_t = rω, where r is its distance from the axis.

[[alpha|Angular acceleration]] measures how fast the [[angvel|angular velocity]] changes. Its average over an interval is Δω/Δt, and the *instantaneous angular acceleration* is the [[ddt|time derivative]] α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt², measured in rad/s². For rotation about a fixed axis the vector α⃗ also lies along the axis, parallel to ω⃗ when the rotation speeds up and antiparallel when it slows down. Differentiating v_t = rω at fixed r shows that a point at distance r from the axis gains speed along its circle at the rate a_t = rα, its [[at|tangential acceleration]]. A wheel that reaches 1200 rev/min, or 126 rad/s, 4.0 s after starting from rest has an average angular acceleration of 31.4 rad/s². A point 0.10 m from its axis then moves at 12.6 m/s, and if α is constant it gains speed at 3.14 m/s².

When the [[alpha|angular acceleration]] is constant, θ, ω and α obey the same equations as x, v and a in [[kin|constant-acceleration kinematics]], and the derivation carries over line by line. Integrating dω/dt = α gives ω = ω₀ + αt; integrating dθ/dt = ω gives θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt²; eliminating t gives ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ, with Δθ = θ − θ₀. The average angular velocity over an interval is (ω₀ + ω)/2. These relations are the [[rotkin|kinematics of rotational motion]], and they hold only while α is constant. On a graph of ω against t the motion is a straight line of slope α, and the area under the line is Δθ. A fan turning at 30.0 rad/s that is switched off and slows at a constant 2.00 rad/s² stops after 15.0 s, having turned through ω₀²/(2|α|) = 225 rad, or 35.8 revolutions.
eqs: θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt²,   ω = ω₀ + αt,   ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ

paragraphs.text: Angular variables describe the whole body, while the motion of one point depends on its distance r from the axis. Multiplying by r converts one into the other: arc length s = rθ, tangential speed v_t = rω and [[at|tangential acceleration]] a_t = rα. Dividing the kinematic equations of a point along its circle by r gives the rotational ones. Each point also has a [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] a_c = v_t²/r = rω² toward the axis, even at constant [[angvel|angular velocity]]. Its [[avec|total linear acceleration]] a⃗ = a⃗_c + a⃗_t is the vector sum of these perpendicular parts, of magnitude √(a_c² + a_t²). For a wheel of radius 0.40 m that starts from rest with α = 5.0 rad/s², a rim point after 2.0 s, when ω = 10 rad/s, has a_t = 2.0 m/s² and a_c = 40 m/s², so its acceleration points nearly straight at the axis.

A spinning wheel whose axle is at rest still has kinetic energy, because its particles move. Particle j of a [[rigid|rigid body]], at distance r_j from the axis, moves at v_j = r_j ω, where ω is the common [[angvel|angular velocity]]. Adding the [[K|kinetic energies]] ½m_j v_j² of all the particles gives the [[Krot|rotational kinetic energy]] K = Σ ½m_j(r_j ω)² = ½(Σ m_j r_j²)ω². The angular velocity comes out of the sum because it is the same for every particle, and the masses enter only through the combination Σ m_j r_j². Rotational kinetic energy is not a new form of energy. It is the ordinary kinetic energy of the particles, written in the variable that suits rotation.

The sum Σ m_j r_j² is the [[I|moment of inertia]] of the body about the axis. It is built from the [[m|masses]] m_j of the particles of the [[rigid|rigid body]] and their distances r_j from the axis; for a continuous body it becomes I = ∫ r² dm. Its SI unit is kg·m². In terms of I, the [[Krot|rotational kinetic energy]] takes the compact form K = ½Iω², the analogue of ½mv² with I in place of m and the [[angvel|angular velocity]] ω in place of v. Mass counts with the square of its distance from the axis, so I depends on the axis chosen. Two small 1.0 kg balls joined by a light rod 1.0 m long have I = 2 × 1.0 kg × (0.50 m)² = 0.50 kg·m² about the centre of the rod, but 1.0 kg·m² about an axis through one of the balls.
eqs: K = ½Iω²,   I = Σ m_j r_j²

paragraphs.text: Rotational kinetic energy enters the conservation of energy like any other kinetic energy. A *flywheel* is a wheel built to store it: one with most of its 50 kg mass in a rim of radius 0.40 m has I ≈ MR² = 8.0 kg·m², and at 200 rad/s it holds ½Iω² = 1.6 × 10⁵ J. The rotor of a helicopter and a twirled baton carry rotational kinetic energy in the same way. When a system both rotates and translates, [[econs|conservation of mechanical energy]] counts both kinds of kinetic energy. A block of mass m that falls from rest through a height h while unwinding a string from a pulley of radius R gives mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω², with ω = v/R if the string does not slip, so v = √(2mgh/(m + I/R²)). Energy dissipated by friction at the axle is subtracted from mgh.

For a continuous body the sum over particles becomes an [[integ|integral]] over mass elements, I = ∫ r² dm. For a thin rod along the x axis, a slice of length dx has mass dm = λ dx, where λ is the [[lmd|linear mass density]], equal to M/L for a uniform rod of mass M and length L. About an axis perpendicular to the rod through its centre, the [[I|moment of inertia]] is I = ∫_{−L/2}^{L/2} x²λ dx = λL³/12 = ML²/12. About a parallel axis through one end, the limits 0 and L give I = ML²/3, four times as much, because more of the mass lies far from the axis. The same procedure gives the moment of inertia of any body whose mass distribution is known.

The two results for the rod are related by the [[paxis|parallel-axis theorem]]. Let I_{CM} be the moment of inertia about an axis through the [[rcm|centre of mass]], and take a *parallel axis* at distance d from it. Measure the position of particle j from the first axis by r⃗′_j, perpendicular to that axis. Its distance from the second axis is |r⃗′_j + d⃗|, where d⃗ is the perpendicular vector from the second axis to the first. Expanding Σ m_j|r⃗′_j + d⃗|² gives Σ m_j r′_j² + 2d⃗·Σ m_j r⃗′_j + Md². The middle term vanishes because Σ m_j r⃗′_j = 0 by the definition of the centre of mass, so the [[I|moment of inertia]] about the new axis is I = I_{CM} + Md². For the rod, ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3. Among parallel axes, the one through the centre of mass has the smallest moment of inertia.

For a thin flat body the [[smd|surface mass density]] σ = dm/dA, a [[m|mass]] divided by an area, the square of a [[L|length]], plays the role of λ. A uniform disk of mass M and radius R has σ = M/(πR²). Cut it into thin rings of radius r and width dr: each ring has area 2πr dr and mass dm = 2πσr dr, and all of it lies at distance r from the central axis. [[integ|Integrating]] from r = 0 to R gives the [[I|moment of inertia]] I = ∫_{0}^{R} r²σ 2πr dr = πσR⁴/2 = ½MR². A thin hoop of the same mass and radius has all its mass at distance R, so I = MR², twice as much. Moments of inertia of the parts of a compound body about the same axis add: a wheel is a hoop plus spokes plus a hub.

How strongly a force turns a body depends on where and in which direction it acts. A door pushed at the handle, at right angles to the door, swings easily; the same push applied at the hinge, or directed along the door toward the hinge, does not turn it at all. The [[tau|torque]] of a [[F|force]] F⃗ applied at [[r|position]] r⃗ relative to a point O is the [[cross|vector product]] τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗. Its magnitude is τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between r⃗ and F⃗. This can be read in two ways: as r times the component F sin θ of the force perpendicular to r⃗, or as F times the *lever arm* r⊥ = r sin θ, the perpendicular distance from O to the line along which the force acts. Torque is measured in newton metres, N·m.
eqs: τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗,   τ = rF sin θ = r⊥F

paragraphs.text: For rotation about a fixed axis only the component of the [[tau|torque]] along the axis matters, and it is treated as a signed number. It is positive if the force alone would turn the body counterclockwise as seen from the positive end of the axis, and negative if clockwise; this is the right-hand rule again. A force parallel to the axis, or one whose line of action passes through the axis, exerts no torque about it. Torques about the same axis add, and their sum is the net torque. A 40 N force applied 0.25 m from the hinge of a door, at 60° to the door, produces a torque of 0.25 m × 40 N × sin 60° = 8.7 N·m. The same force at the edge of the door, 0.80 m from the hinge and at right angles to it, gives 32 N·m.

Apply [[n2|Newton's second law]] to particle j of a [[rigid|rigid body]] turning about a fixed axis. Along the particle's circle it reads F_{j,⊥} = m_j a_{j,t} = m_j r_j α, where F_{j,⊥} is the component of the net force on the particle along the circle, perpendicular to its radius r_j. Multiplying by r_j turns the left side into the [[tau|torque]] r_j F_{j,⊥} about the axis and the right side into m_j r_j²α. Summing over all particles gives Σ r_j F_{j,⊥} = (Σ m_j r_j²)α. Internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs along the lines joining the particles, so their torques cancel and only external torques remain. The sum on the right is the [[I|moment of inertia]], and the result is [[n2rot|Newton's second law for rotation]]: the net external torque about a fixed axis equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration.

The second law for rotation is the basic equation of [[n2rot|rotational dynamics]]. A net torque produces an angular acceleration inversely proportional to the moment of inertia, as a net force produces an acceleration inversely proportional to mass. The torques and the moment of inertia must refer to the same axis, and that axis must be fixed in an inertial frame or pass through the centre of mass without changing direction. A string wound on a pulley, a uniform disk of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m with I = ½MR² = 0.010 kg·m², is pulled with a constant force of 5.0 N. If friction at the axle is negligible, the torque is 0.50 N·m and the angular acceleration is α = τ/I = 50 rad/s². A pulley with twice the moment of inertia would turn with half the angular acceleration under the same pull.

A force acting on a body that turns about a fixed axis moves its point of application along a circle. In a small rotation dθ that point moves a distance r dθ along the tangent, so the [[W|work]] of the force is dW = F⃗·dr⃗ = F_{⊥}r dθ = τ dθ, where τ is the [[tau|torque]] about the axis and θ the [[theta|angular position]]. The radial component of the force does no work. [[integ|Integrating]] over a finite rotation gives the [[Wrot|rotational work]] W = ∫ τ dθ, taken from θ_A to θ_B. For a constant torque W = τΔθ: a torque of 10 N·m applied through two full turns, 4π rad, does about 126 J of work.

The [[wet|work–energy theorem]] holds in rotational form. With Στ = Iα and α = dω/dt = ω dω/dθ, the net work is ∫ Στ dθ = ∫ Iω dω. The [[Wrot|rotational work]] done by all the torques therefore equals the change of [[Krot|rotational kinetic energy]]: W_{AB} = ½Iω_B² − ½Iω_A². The theorem gives the angular velocity after a given rotation without solving for the time. If the 126 J of the previous example is delivered to a wheel with I = 0.50 kg·m² that starts from rest, and friction is negligible, the wheel ends with ω = √(2W/I) ≈ 22.4 rad/s.

[[P|Power]] is the rate at which work is done. Dividing dW = τ dθ by dt gives P = τω, the product of the [[tau|torque]] and the [[angvel|angular velocity]]. An engine delivers a given power either as a large torque at a low angular velocity or as a small torque at a high one, and gears trade one for the other. A motor exerting 30 N·m at 3000 rev/min, that is, at ω = 100π rad/s ≈ 314 rad/s, delivers about 9.4 kW.

Each quantity of fixed-axis rotation corresponds to one of linear motion. Angular position θ, angular velocity ω and angular acceleration α correspond to x, v and a; the moment of inertia I corresponds to the mass m; torque τ corresponds to force F. The laws carry over with these replacements: the [[n2rot|second law for rotation]] Στ = Iα corresponds to F = ma, the [[Krot|rotational kinetic energy]] ½Iω² to ½mv², the [[Wrot|rotational work]] ∫τ dθ to ∫F dx, and the power τω to Fv. The correspondence is exact for rotation about a fixed axis, where each rotational quantity reduces to one component along that axis. The next chapter extends it to the counterpart of linear momentum.

Chapter 10 held the axis of rotation fixed. Many rotations are less constrained: a rolling wheel turns while its axle moves forward, and the axis of a spinning top swings slowly around. To treat such motion, this chapter introduces angular momentum, the rotational counterpart of linear [[p|momentum]]. Its rate of change equals the net [[tau|torque]], as the rate of change of momentum equals the net force. It is conserved when no net external torque acts, as [[pcons|momentum is conserved]] when no net external force acts. The chapter begins with rolling without slipping and ends with the precession of a gyroscope.

A wheel of radius R rolling on a surface combines translation of its [[rcm|centre of mass]], at its centre, with rotation about an axis through that point. Each point of the wheel, a [[rigid|rigid body]] turning at [[angvel|angular velocity]] ω, moves with the velocity v⃗_{CM} of the centre plus its velocity of rotation about the centre. At the bottom the rotational part has magnitude Rω and points backward, so the contact point moves at v_{CM} − Rω. In [[roll|rolling motion]] without slipping the contact point is instantaneously at rest: v_{CM} = Rω, and by differentiation a_{CM} = Rα. The top of the wheel then moves forward at 2v_{CM}. The force that holds the contact point is [[fs|static friction]], which takes whatever value this requires, up to μ_s N. If more is needed, the wheel slips, and kinetic friction acts instead.

A body of mass m and moment of inertia I_{CM} that rolls without slipping down an incline of angle θ is acted on by its weight, the normal force and static friction f_s up the slope. The second law along the slope, ma_{CM} = mg sin θ − f_s, and the second law for rotation about the centre, f_s R = I_{CM}α = I_{CM}a_{CM}/R, give a_{CM} = g sin θ/(1 + I_{CM}/(mR²)). A uniform solid cylinder, with I_{CM} = ½mR², rolls down with a_{CM} = (2/3)g sin θ and needs f_s = (1/3)mg sin θ; static friction can supply this only if tan θ ≤ 3μ_s. Since the contact point does not move, static friction does no work, and mechanical energy is conserved, with K = ½mv_{CM}² + ½I_{CM}ω². After descending a height h from rest, the cylinder moves at v_{CM} = √(4gh/3).

The [[Lang|angular momentum]] of a particle about a point O is the [[cross|vector product]] of its [[r|position vector]] r⃗, measured from O, and its [[p|momentum]] p⃗: l⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗. It is perpendicular to the plane of r⃗ and p⃗, and its magnitude rp sin φ, with φ the angle between them, equals p times the perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion. Angular momentum therefore depends on the choice of O. A particle moving at constant velocity along a straight line has a constant, nonzero angular momentum about any point off that line, and zero about points on it. For a system of particles the total angular momentum L⃗ = Σ l⃗_j is the sum over all particles about the same point. Its SI unit is kg·m²/s.
eqs: l⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗,   L⃗ = Σ l⃗_j

paragraphs.text: For a [[rigid|rigid body]] turning about a fixed axis, each particle moves on a circle with speed r_j ω, perpendicular to its radius r_j from the axis. The component of its angular momentum along the axis is therefore r_j m_j r_j ω, and summing over the particles gives L = (Σ m_j r_j²)ω = Iω. The [[Lang|angular momentum]] about the axis is the [[I|moment of inertia]] times the [[angvel|angular velocity]], the analogue of p = mv. If the body is symmetric about the axis, the components of the l⃗_j perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs, and L⃗ = Iω⃗ points along the axis. A *pulsar* is a rotating neutron star about 20 km across, the collapsed core of a massive star. Some pulsars turn hundreds of times per second, and their beamed radio emission sweeps past Earth once per turn.

The rate of change of l⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗ follows from the product rule: dl⃗/dt = (dr⃗/dt) × p⃗ + r⃗ × (dp⃗/dt). The first term is v⃗ × mv⃗ = 0, since the vector product of parallel vectors vanishes. By [[n2|Newton's second law]] dp⃗/dt is the net force, so the second term is the net [[tau|torque]] r⃗ × F⃗ about O. This is the [[dLdt|torque law]]: the rate of change of [[Lang|angular momentum]] equals the net torque, both taken about the same point fixed in an inertial frame. For a system of particles, internal forces that act along the lines joining pairs of particles exert torques that cancel in pairs, so dL⃗/dt equals the net external torque. The torque law is the rotational counterpart of F⃗_{net} = dp⃗/dt. For a rigid body on a fixed axis, where L = Iω, it reduces to Στ = Iα.

If the net external torque on a system is zero, the [[dLdt|torque law]] gives dL⃗/dt = 0, and the total angular momentum stays constant in magnitude and direction. This is the [[Lcons|law of conservation of angular momentum]]. Internal forces cannot change the total: by [[n3|Newton's third law]] they come in equal and opposite pairs, and when each pair acts along the line joining the two particles, their torques about any point cancel. The law holds component by component. If only the torque about one fixed axis vanishes, the angular momentum about that axis is conserved even if other components change.

A body that changes its shape changes its moment of inertia, and with its [[Lang|angular momentum]] Iω conserved, I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. A skater spinning with outstretched arms who pulls them in reduces I and turns faster. If I falls from 3.0 kg·m² to 1.0 kg·m², an angular velocity of 2.0 rad/s rises to 6.0 rad/s. The kinetic energy L²/(2I) rises from 6.0 J to 18 J; the extra 12 J is work done by the skater's muscles in pulling the arms inward. A diver tucks to spin faster, and a collapsing stellar core spins up into a pulsar. Gravity exerts no torque about Earth's centre, so a satellite on an elongated *Molniya orbit*, used for communications at high northern latitudes, moves slowly far from Earth and fast close to it, and spends most of its period of about 12 hours over the northern hemisphere.

A *gyroscope* is a wheel spinning rapidly about its symmetry axis, mounted so that the axis can turn freely. Rest one end of the horizontal axis on a pivot, with the centre of mass at distance r from it. The [[w|weight]] Mg then exerts a torque of magnitude rMg about the pivot, horizontal and perpendicular to the axis. By the [[dLdt|torque law]], in a time dt the spin [[Lang|angular momentum]] L = Iω changes by dL⃗ = τ⃗ dt, perpendicular to L⃗. A change perpendicular to a vector turns the vector without changing its length, so the axis swings around in a horizontal circle instead of falling. This motion is [[omegaP|precession]]. In the time dt the axis turns through dφ = dL/L = τ dt/L, so the precession rate is ω_P = τ/L = rMg/(Iω).

The result assumes that the spin angular momentum is much larger than the angular momentum of the slow precession itself. Under that condition, the faster the wheel spins, the slower it precesses. As friction slows the spin, the precession speeds up until the simple picture fails and the gyroscope falls. A wheel with I = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² spinning at 300 rad/s, in a gyroscope of mass 0.15 kg whose centre of mass is 4.0 cm from the pivot, precesses at ω_P = (0.040 m × 0.15 kg × 9.80 m/s²)/(0.060 kg·m²/s) = 0.98 rad/s. Earth precesses in the same way: the Sun and the Moon exert torques on its equatorial bulge, and its axis traces a cone about once every 26 000 years.

A bridge, a bookshelf or a ladder leaning on a wall is meant to stay at rest. Its centre of mass must not accelerate and it must not start to rotate, so the [[n2sys|second law for a system]] and the [[dLdt|torque law]] both apply with zero on one side. This chapter turns them into conditions on the forces and torques that act on an extended body, and uses those conditions to find unknown support forces. It then asks what the forces do to the body itself. Real materials deform under load, and for small deformations they respond like the springs of [[hooke|Hooke's law]].

A body is in equilibrium when neither its translation nor its rotation changes: its centre of mass does not accelerate and its angular velocity stays constant. A [[rigid|rigid body]] is in [[staticeq|static equilibrium]] when, in addition, it is at rest, with v⃗_{CM} = 0 and ω⃗ = 0, and stays at rest. Buildings, bridges and furniture are designed to be in static equilibrium under every load they are expected to carry. The task of statics is to find the forces this requires and to check that the supports and materials can provide them.

The conditions follow from two laws of motion. The [[n2sys|second law for a system]], Ma⃗_{CM} = ΣF⃗, requires the first equilibrium condition, zero net external force. The [[dLdt|torque law]], dL⃗/dt = Στ⃗, requires the second, zero net external torque. Together they are the [[eqcond|equilibrium conditions]]: six scalar equations in three dimensions, and three for forces in a plane, ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0 and Στ_z = 0. When the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point, so the torque condition may be applied about any *pivot point*. A good choice is a point through which unknown forces act, since their torques then vanish. For a [[rigid|rigid body]] at rest, solving these equations for the unknown forces solves the problem of [[staticeq|static equilibrium]].

Gravity acts on every particle of a body. In a uniform field g⃗ the [[tau|torques]] of the particle [[w|weights]] about a point O add up to Σ r⃗_j × m_j g⃗ = (Σ m_j r⃗_j) × g⃗ = r⃗_{CM} × Mg⃗, by the definition of the [[rcm|centre of mass]]. This *gravitational torque* is the same as if the whole weight Mg acted at a single point, the [[rcg|centre of gravity]]. In a uniform field the centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass, and in statics problems the weight of each body is drawn there. A body hanging from a single pivot can be at rest only with its centre of gravity directly below or directly above the pivot; the equilibrium is stable below and unstable above.

Statics problems follow a routine. Choose the body, draw its [[fbd|free-body diagram]] with each external force at its point of application, and place each weight at its [[rcg|centre of gravity]]. Write the [[eqcond|equilibrium conditions]] in components, taking torques about a point where an unknown force acts. Solve, then check by taking torques about a second point. A uniform plank 4.0 m long and weighing 300 N rests on supports at its ends, and a person weighing 600 N stands 1.0 m from the left end. Torques about the left support give F_R × 4.0 m = 300 N × 2.0 m + 600 N × 1.0 m, so the right support pushes up with F_R = 300 N, and the force balance leaves 600 N for the left support.

Forces that keep a body in equilibrium also deform it. A *deformation* is described by quantities that do not depend on the size of the sample. [[stress|Stress]] is the [[F|force]] per unit area of the surface on which it acts, with the area A = ℓ² measured as a [[L|length]] squared. A *tensile stress* F⊥/A pulls perpendicular to a cross-section and stretches the body; a *compressive stress* pushes and shortens it. A *shear stress* F∥/A acts parallel to the surface. A *bulk stress*, or *volume stress*, presses inward on every face. A beam bent under load carries tensile stress on one side and compressive stress on the other, largest at its top and bottom faces, so *I-beams* put most of their material there.

[[strain|Strain]] is the fractional deformation that a stress produces: ΔL/L₀ for a tensile or compressive strain, ΔV/V₀ for a bulk or *volume strain*, and Δx/L₀ for a shear strain, where Δx is the sideways shift of a face relative to the opposite face at distance L₀. As a ratio of two [[L|lengths]], strain is dimensionless. For small deformations, experiment shows that strain is proportional to stress and disappears when the load is removed; the deformation is *elastic*. This is [[hooke|Hooke's law]] F = −kx stated per unit size: dividing force by area and extension by original length removes the dimensions of the sample. [[elin|Linear elasticity]] states that [[stress|stress]] = elastic *modulus* × strain, with one modulus for each kind of deformation, fixed by the material alone.

For tension and compression the modulus is [[Ymod|Young's modulus]], the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in [[elin|linear elasticity]]: Y = (F⊥/A)/(ΔL/L₀). A rod of length L₀ and cross-section A therefore behaves as a spring of constant k = YA/L₀. Steel has Y ≈ 2.0 × 10¹¹ N/m². A steel wire 2.0 m long with a cross-section of 1.0 mm² that holds a load of 100 N stretches by ΔL = FL₀/(YA) = (100 N × 2.0 m)/(2.0 × 10¹¹ N/m² × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²) = 1.0 mm. Its strain is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, within the linear range.

The [[Smod|shear modulus]] S = (F∥/A)/(Δx/L₀) is the modulus of [[elin|linear elasticity]] for *shear*, one face sliding sideways over the opposite one. Compression from all sides is set by the [[pres|pressure]] or normal pressure p = F⊥/A, the normal [[F|force]] per unit area of a surface, area being a [[L|length]] squared. Pressure is a scalar: at a point of a fluid at rest it is the same in all directions. Its unit is the pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m²; 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. The bulk [[stress|stress]] is a change of pressure Δp, and the [[Bmod|bulk modulus]] is B = −Δp/(ΔV/V₀), positive since the volume falls as the pressure rises; 1/B is the *compressibility*. Water has B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa, so an extra 100 atm reduces its volume by about 0.5 %. Fluids have no shear modulus: they cannot resist a steady shear.

How far the linear law holds is found by testing. A sample is stretched in a machine while its [[stress|stress]] and [[strain|strain]] are recorded, and the plot of one against the other is the [[ssdiag|stress–strain diagram]]. It starts as a straight line, the region of [[elin|linear elasticity]], whose slope is [[Ymod|Young's modulus]]. The line ends at the *proportionality limit*, or linearity limit. Beyond it the curve bends, but the deformation remains *elastic* up to the *elastic limit*: the sample returns to its original length when unloaded. Past that point the sample shows *plastic behaviour*: unloading follows a line roughly parallel to the initial one and leaves a permanent strain. The highest point of the curve is the *ultimate stress*, the largest stress the material can sustain; beyond it the sample soon breaks.

Materials differ in the shape of the diagram. Brittle materials such as glass and cast iron break soon after the elastic limit, with little plastic deformation. Ductile materials such as copper and mild steel deform plastically far beyond it before they break, which is why they can be drawn into wire or bent into shape. Rubber stays elastic up to strains of several hundred percent, but its stress–strain curve is not a straight line. Structures are designed so that working stresses stay well below the elastic limit, usually by a safety factor of several, so that no expected load leaves a permanent deformation.

Until now gravity near Earth was a constant force, the [[w|weight]] mg, with g measured rather than explained. This chapter replaces it with a single force law between any two masses. Together with [[n2|Newton's second law]], that law accounts for the measured [[g|free-fall acceleration]], for the energy needed to leave Earth, for the orbits of satellites and planets, and for the tides. [[econs|Conservation of mechanical energy]] and [[Lcons|conservation of angular momentum]] do much of the work. The chapter ends with Einstein's general theory of relativity, in which gravity becomes a property of space and time.

The motions of the planets were among the first precise data of science. Ptolemy, in the second century, described them by combinations of circles around a fixed Earth. Copernicus, in a book published in 1543, put the Sun at the centre. The careful naked-eye measurements of Tycho Brahe allowed Kepler to find three empirical laws of planetary motion, published in 1609 and 1619, and in 1610 Galileo's telescope showed moons orbiting Jupiter. In 1687 Newton explained the fall of bodies on Earth and the orbits of the Moon and the planets with a single law of force.

[[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]] states that any two point particles attract each other along the line joining them, with a [[F|force]] proportional to the product of their [[m|masses]] and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Let r⃗ be the [[r|position]] of particle 2 relative to particle 1, with r = |r⃗| and r̂₁₂ = r⃗/r. The force that particle 1 exerts on particle 2 is F⃗₁₂ = −Gm₁m₂/r² r̂₁₂; the minus sign makes it point back toward particle 1. Particle 2 pulls on particle 1 with the opposite force. The constant G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is the [[G|universal gravitational constant]], the same for all bodies. The law also holds for spherically symmetric bodies that do not overlap, with r the distance between their centres, and the forces of several bodies add as vectors.

Newton tested the law on the Moon. Its distance from Earth's centre is about 60 Earth radii, so the inverse square predicts an acceleration toward Earth of g/60² ≈ 2.7 × 10⁻³ m/s². This matches the centripetal acceleration 4π²r/T² of its orbit, with r = 3.84 × 10⁸ m and T = 27.3 days. Between laboratory masses the force is tiny: two 1.0 kg masses 1.0 m apart attract each other with 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N. Henry Cavendish measured such a force in 1798 with a torsion balance, in which the twist of a thin wire balanced the attraction between lead spheres; his result, stated as the mean density of Earth, is equivalent to a value of G. The same law holds the stars of the Milky Way together and draws it and the Andromeda galaxy toward each other.

Dividing the gravitational force on a small test mass m by m removes the test mass from [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]] and leaves the [[gfield|gravitational field]] of the attracting body, g⃗(r⃗) = −GM/r² r̂. Here M is the mass of the body, r̂ points away from its centre, and G is the [[G|gravitational constant]]. The field is defined at every point, whether or not a mass is there, and a mass m placed at r⃗ feels the force mg⃗. At Earth's surface the field strength is the [[g|free-fall acceleration]], g = GM_E/R_E² = (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/(6.37 × 10⁶)² m/s² = 9.82 m/s², close to the measured value. Since g does not depend on m, all bodies fall alike. Read the other way, a measured g and radius give the mass of a planet, M = gR²/G.

A scale does not measure gravity directly. It measures the [[Nf|normal force]] N with which it supports a body, and this is the [[wapp|apparent weight]]. For a person on a scale in an elevator whose acceleration a is directed downward, [[n2|Newton's second law]] gives mg − N = ma, so N = m(g − a). The scale reads less than the [[w|weight]] mg when the elevator accelerates downward, more when a < 0, that is, when it accelerates upward, and zero in free fall, a = g. In the elevator's own frame, a [[noninert|noninertial frame]], the same result appears as an inertial force −ma⃗ added to the weight. Earth's surface is such a frame: at the equator part of the gravitational pull supplies the centripetal acceleration ω²R_E ≈ 0.034 m/s², and a scale reads about 0.35 % less than the pull.

Astronauts on the International Space Station, about 400 km above the surface, are not beyond the reach of gravity. There the field is still g = 9.82 m/s² × (6.37/6.77)² ≈ 8.7 m/s². They float because the station and everything in it fall freely together around Earth: their acceleration equals the local field, so their apparent weight is zero. What is called weightlessness is free fall, not the absence of weight. On Earth's surface g varies by about half a percent between the equator and the poles, because of Earth's rotation and its slightly flattened shape, and by smaller amounts with altitude and local density.

Near the surface the weight is nearly constant and the potential energy is mgy. Over large distances the force falls off as 1/r², and the potential energy must be obtained from [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]] itself. Gravity is a [[cons|conservative force]]: it is central and its magnitude depends only on r, so its work depends only on the initial and final separations. Taking U = 0 at infinite separation, the [[U|potential energy]] at separation r is minus the work done by gravity while the bodies come in from infinity: U(r) = −∫_{∞}^{r} F_r dr′ with F_r = −GMm/r′². This gives the [[Ugr|gravitational potential energy]] U(r) = −GMm/r. It is negative at every finite separation and rises toward zero as the bodies move apart.

Near Earth's surface the new expression reduces to the old one. Put r = R + y, where R is Earth's radius and y the height, with y ≪ R. To first order in y/R, U = −GMm/(R + y) = −(GMm/R)(1 + y/R)⁻¹ ≈ −GMm/R + (GMm/R²)y = −GMm/R + mgy, since GM/R² = g. The constant −GMm/R drops out of every energy difference, so the [[Ugrav|near-surface potential energy]] mgy is the limit of the [[Ugr|gravitational potential energy]] −GMm/r for heights much smaller than Earth's radius. At a height of 640 km, about a tenth of R, mgy already overestimates the change of potential energy by about 10 %.

A body launched from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R escapes if it can reach infinite distance. Without air resistance, [[econs|mechanical energy is conserved]]: ½mv² − GMm/R = ½mv_∞², where v_∞ is the speed left at infinity. The smallest launch speed leaves v_∞ = 0, so its [[K|kinetic energy]] exactly cancels the [[Ugr|gravitational potential energy]] at launch, ½mv_{esc}² = GMm/R. The [[vesc|escape velocity]] v_{esc} = √(2GM/R) does not depend on the mass of the body or on the direction of launch, as long as the path clears the planet. For Earth it is √(2 × 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/(6.37 × 10⁶)) m/s = 1.12 × 10⁴ m/s, about 11.2 km/s, if Earth's rotation is ignored.

The sign of the total [[Emech|mechanical energy]] E = ½mv² − GMm/r decides whether two bodies can separate. The kinetic energy is never negative, so the [[Ugr|potential energy]] −GMm/r can never exceed E. If E < 0, this requires r ≤ GMm/|E|: the separation has an upper bound, and the system is [[bound|gravitationally bound]]. If E ≥ 0, the bodies can move arbitrarily far apart. Earth and the Moon, and each planet with the Sun, form bound systems. A body that arrives from far away with E > 0 swings past once and leaves again, unless another interaction takes energy from it.

A satellite of mass m on a circular orbit of radius r about a planet of mass M ≫ m is pulled toward the centre by gravity alone. The force given by [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]] must therefore supply the [[Fc|centripetal force]]: GMm/r² = mv²/r. Solving for v gives the [[vorb|orbital speed]] v = √(GM/r), the same for every satellite at that radius, whatever its mass. Its kinetic energy is then ½mv² = GMm/(2r), half the magnitude of the potential energy, so the total energy is E = −GMm/(2r), negative as for any [[bound|bound orbit]]. For Earth GM_E = 3.98 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². The International Space Station, about 400 km up, has r ≈ 6.77 × 10⁶ m and v ≈ 7.67 × 10³ m/s.

The [[Torb|orbital period]] is the circumference divided by the [[vorb|orbital speed]]: T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM). For the space station T ≈ 5.55 × 10³ s, about 92 minutes. Higher orbits are slower and take longer. A *geosynchronous* orbit has a period of one sidereal day, 86 164 s, the time in which Earth turns once relative to the stars. Solving for the radius gives r = (GMT²/(4π²))^{1/3} ≈ 4.22 × 10⁷ m, about 35 800 km above the surface. A satellite on such an orbit above the equator stays over one point of the ground, which is why communication and weather satellites use it.

From Tycho Brahe's observations Kepler found that every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. This is [[kep1|Kepler's first law]]. Newton derived it. Solving [[n2|Newton's second law]] for a body attracted toward a much heavier one by the inverse-square force of [[ngrav|gravitation]] shows that the path is a conic section with the heavy body at a focus. Which conic it is depends on the energy. A [[bound|bound orbit]], with E < 0, is an ellipse, a circle being the special case of zero eccentricity. With E = 0 the path is a parabola, and with E > 0 a hyperbola; on these open paths the body passes once and escapes, as some comets and the spacecraft sent out of the solar system do.

In polar coordinates centred on the Sun, the [[rt|trajectory]] that [[kep1|Kepler's first law]] describes is the [[orbit|elliptical orbit]] r(θ) = α/(1 + e cos θ). The eccentricity satisfies 0 ≤ e < 1, and the length α = L²/(GMm²) is set by the [[Lang|angular momentum]] L. The planet is closest to the Sun at the *perihelion*, θ = 0, where r = α/(1 + e), and farthest at the *aphelion*, θ = π, where r = α/(1 − e). The semimajor axis a, half the longest diameter, is the mean of these two distances, a = α/(1 − e²). Earth's orbit, with e ≈ 0.017, is nearly a circle. A *Hohmann transfer* takes a spacecraft from Earth's orbit to that of Mars along half an ellipse whose perihelion touches Earth's orbit and whose aphelion touches Mars's, with one engine burn at each end.

[[kep2|Kepler's second law]] states that the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In a time dt the planet moves by v⃗ dt, and the line sweeps a thin triangle of area dA = ½|r⃗ × v⃗| dt = (L/2m) dt, so dA/dt = L/(2m). The gravitational force on the planet points along r⃗, toward the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero and the [[Lcons|angular momentum is conserved]]. The area swept per unit time is therefore constant along the [[orbit|orbit]]. The planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion; at both points its velocity is perpendicular to r⃗, so r_p v_p = r_a v_a. The argument uses only the fact that the force is central, so the second law holds for any central force.

For a circular orbit, squaring the [[Torb|orbital period]] gives T² = 4π²r³/(GM). [[kep3|Kepler's third law]] extends this to an [[orbit|elliptical orbit]], with r replaced by the semimajor axis a. The constant 4π²/(GM) depends only on the mass of the central body, provided the orbiting mass is much smaller, so all planets of the Sun share it. With T in years and a in astronomical units (1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, the semimajor axis of Earth's orbit), the law reads T² = a³ for the planets. Halley's comet, named after Edmond Halley, who predicted its return, has a period of about 76 years, so a ≈ 76^{2/3} AU ≈ 18 AU, and its aphelion lies beyond the orbit of Neptune.

A body of finite size is not pulled uniformly. The gravitational force of a mass M falls off with distance, so a mass m at distance r and an equal mass a distance Δr farther away feel different pulls. Differentiating [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]] gives dF/dr = −2GMm/r³, so to first order in Δr/r the difference is ΔF = 2GMmΔr/r³. This is the [[Ftide|tidal force]], and it falls off as 1/r³, faster than the force itself. The Moon pulls the near side of Earth more strongly than Earth's centre, and the far side more weakly. In the freely falling frame of Earth's centre both sides are therefore pulled outward along the Earth–Moon line, and in the simplest picture the oceans rise in two bulges, one facing the Moon and one opposite.

Earth turns under the two bulges, so most coasts have two high tides a day, about 12 h 25 min apart, since the Moon moves along its orbit while Earth turns. The Sun is far more massive than the Moon but much farther away, and its tidal effect on Earth is about half as large. At new and full Moon, when Sun, Earth and Moon lie in a line, the two effects add and give large *spring tides*. At the quarter Moons, when the Sun and the Moon are at right angles as seen from Earth, they partly cancel and give small *neap tides*. Tidal forces also act in binary stars and on moons. Jupiter's moon Io is flexed continually by Jupiter's tides, and the heat dissipated drives the strongest volcanism in the solar system.

[[ngrav|Newton's law]] gives the force between two masses but no mechanism: each mass acts on the other instantly across empty space, an *action-at-a-distance force*. Yet no signal is observed to travel faster than the [[c|speed of light]] in vacuum, c = 299 792 458 m/s, about 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; the value is exact because the metre is defined through it. Einstein's [[GR|theory of general relativity]], completed in 1915, removes the action at a distance. Mass and energy curve *space-time*, the four-dimensional union of space and time, and a body on which no other force acts follows the straightest possible path of the curved geometry. That geometry is a *non-Euclidean geometry*: the angles of a large triangle need not add up to 180°, and clocks at different heights run at different rates.

The theory starts from the [[equiv|principle of equivalence]]: no experiment in a small region of space and time can distinguish a uniform gravitational field from an acceleration of the frame. Objects released in a closed cabin at rest on Earth fall exactly as in a cabin accelerating at g far from all masses, and a freely falling cabin is locally an inertial frame. The principle extends the observed equality of gravitational and inertial mass, the reason all bodies fall alike. Applied everywhere, it makes gravity a property of space-time, and [[GR|general relativity]] ties the curvature to the density of energy and momentum. The coupling, 8πG/c⁴, contains the [[c|speed of light]] and is fixed by requiring that weak fields obey ∇²Φ = 4πGρ, the field form of [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]]. For weak fields and speeds v ≪ c, as in the solar system, the theory reduces to Newton's law.

In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the exact field outside a spherical mass in [[GR|general relativity]]. It contains a critical radius, the [[RS|Schwarzschild radius]] R_S = 2GM/c², built from the mass, the [[G|gravitational constant]] and the [[c|speed of light]]. It is also the radius at which the Newtonian [[vesc|escape velocity]] √(2GM/R) would equal c, although only general relativity describes what happens there. A body compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius becomes a [[bh|black hole]]. The sphere r = R_S is its *event horizon*: inside it every possible path, even that of light, leads inward, so nothing that crosses the horizon can return or send a signal out. For the Sun, with M = 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg, R_S = 2.95 km; for Earth it is 8.9 mm. The name black hole was popularised by John Wheeler.

The evidence for black holes is indirect but strong. A *neutron star*, the collapsed core left by some exploding stars, holds more than a solar mass within a radius of about 10 km, and no such star can be heavier than roughly two to three solar masses; compact objects that are heavier must be black holes. Gas falling onto a compact companion in a binary star system heats up and emits X-rays. Stars at the centre of the Milky Way orbit an unseen object of about four million solar masses. In 2015 detectors recorded gravitational waves from two merging black holes. The orbital speeds of stars in galaxies also reveal more mass than is seen; the nature of this *dark matter* is still unknown.

Solids keep their shape because they resist shear [[stress]]. Liquids and gases cannot resist it, so they flow. This chapter describes both as continuous media with a density, a pressure and a velocity at every point. It starts with fluids at rest, where [[n2|Newton's second law]] applied to a small volume of fluid shows how [[pres|pressure]] grows with depth and explains hydraulics and buoyancy. It then treats fluids in motion: conservation of mass gives the continuity equation, and the [[wet|work–energy theorem]] gives Bernoulli's equation. It ends with viscosity, which resists flow, and with turbulence.

Matter occurs in several *phases of matter*. In a *solid* the atoms stay near fixed positions, so a solid keeps its shape. In a *liquid* the molecules remain close together but can slide past one another; in a *gas* they are far apart and move almost freely; a *plasma* is a gas of ions and free electrons. Liquids and gases are [[fluid|fluids]]: a fluid at rest cannot sustain a shear [[stress]], so any shear makes it flow. At rest it exerts only a normal force on a surface, described by the [[pres|pressure]] p = F/A, the force per unit area, in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). In a *static fluid* the pressure at a point is the same in all directions. *Atmospheric pressure* at sea level is about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.

The [[rho|density]] of a material is its [[m|mass]] per unit volume, ρ = m/V, in kg/m³; volume has the dimension of [[L|length]] cubed. In a *homogeneous substance* the density is the same everywhere, so any sample gives the same ratio m/V. In a *heterogeneous substance*, such as granite, it varies from point to point and is defined locally as ρ = dm/dV. Water has ρ = 1.00 × 10³ kg/m³, air at sea level about 1.2 kg/m³, and lead 1.13 × 10⁴ kg/m³. Liquids and solids are nearly incompressible, while the density of a gas changes readily with pressure. The [[sg|specific gravity]] is the density divided by that of water, a pure number. Lead, at 11.3, sinks in water; ice, at 0.917, floats.

Most gauges measure pressure relative to the surrounding air. A tyre gauge reads the [[pabs|gauge pressure]] p_g, the excess over atmospheric pressure; the absolute pressure is the total, p_{abs} = p_g + p_{atm}. Gauge pressure is negative in a partial vacuum, but absolute [[pres|pressure]] cannot be. An open-tube *manometer* is a U-shaped tube of liquid with one arm connected to the gas and the other open to the air; a difference h in the heights of the two columns means a gauge pressure ρgh, as the next section shows. A mercury *barometer*, introduced by Evangelista Torricelli, is a tube closed at the top with almost empty space above the mercury, so its column height measures the absolute pressure of the atmosphere, about 760 mm at sea level. Besides the *pascal*, the *torr*, 1/760 of an atmosphere or about 133 Pa, is still used.

Take a [[fluid]] at rest, with the y axis pointing up, and a thin horizontal layer of it with area A and thickness dy. The layer does not accelerate, so by [[n2|Newton's second law]] the forces on it balance. The [[pres|pressure]] below pushes up with pA, the pressure above pushes down with (p + dp)A, and the weight of the layer is ρgA dy, with [[rho|density]] ρ and [[g|free-fall acceleration]] g. Balance gives dp/dy = −ρg: pressure falls with height and grows with depth. This is [[hydro|hydrostatic equilibrium]]. For constant density, the pressure at depth h below a point at pressure p₀ is p = p₀ + ρgh, whatever the shape of the container. At 10.0 m below the surface of a lake the gauge pressure is (1.00 × 10³ kg/m³)(9.80 m/s²)(10.0 m) = 9.80 × 10⁴ Pa, almost one atmosphere.

In a fluid at rest, the pressure profile is fixed only up to its value at one point. If the pressure at the surface of an enclosed liquid is raised by Δp, it therefore rises by the same Δp everywhere in the liquid. This consequence of [[hydro|hydrostatic equilibrium]] is [[pascal|Pascal's principle]], and it is the basis of *hydraulics*. In a *hydraulic jack*, a force F₁ on a small piston of area A₁ raises the pressure by F₁/A₁, and the same increase pushes on a large piston of area A₂ at the same level, so F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁. With A₂/A₁ = 100, a push of 200 N supports a load of 2.00 × 10⁴ N. No energy is gained: the liquid is incompressible, so the large piston moves one hundredth as far as the small one, and the two works are equal.

A body immersed in a [[fluid]] is pushed upward by the fluid around it. This net upward force is the [[FB|buoyant force]], and it arises because [[pres|pressure]] grows with depth. Consider a submerged block of height h whose top and bottom faces have area A. The horizontal forces on its sides cancel. Its bottom face is deeper than its top face by h, so by [[hydro|hydrostatic equilibrium]] the pressure there is larger by ρ_{fl} gh, where ρ_{fl} is the density of the fluid. The net upward force is ρ_{fl} ghA = ρ_{fl} V g, with V = hA the volume of the block. It depends neither on the depth of the block nor on the material it is made of.

The result holds for a body of any shape. Imagine the body replaced by fluid filling the same space. That fluid would be in [[hydro|hydrostatic equilibrium]], so the pressure forces on its surface would exactly support its [[w|weight]]. The pressure on each part of the surface depends only on depth, not on what lies inside, so the real body feels the same total force. This is [[archi|Archimedes' principle]], named after Archimedes of Syracuse: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. With the [[rho|density]] of the fluid and the [[g|free-fall acceleration]], the [[FB|buoyant force]] is F_B = ρ_{fl} V_{disp} g, where V_{disp} is the submerged volume. A body sinks if its mean density exceeds that of the fluid; otherwise it floats with the fraction ρ_{body}/ρ_{fl} of its volume submerged, 91.7 % for ice in fresh water.

Moving fluids are first described by a simplified model. An [[ideal|ideal fluid]] is a [[fluid]] that is incompressible, with constant density, and has no internal friction. Liquids, and gases moving much more slowly than sound, change density very little, so the model is a good first approximation for them. Internal friction is measured by the [[eta|viscosity]] η. Place a layer of fluid of thickness L between two plates of area A, hold the lower plate fixed and drag the upper one at [[speed]] v. The force needed is F = ηvA/L, so η = (F/A)/(v/L), the shear [[stress]] divided by the velocity gradient. Its SI unit is the pascal second. Water at 20 °C has η = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s; honey is thousands of times more viscous.

The motion of a fluid, the [[flow|fluid flow]], is described by a [[vvec|velocity vector]] v⃗(r⃗, t) at every point of the [[fluid]]. Curves tangent to the velocity at each point are *streamlines*; in steady flow they do not change in time and are the paths of the fluid elements. In *laminar flow* neighbouring layers slide smoothly past one another; in *turbulent flow* irregular eddies mix them. The [[Q|flow rate]] Q = dV/dt is the volume crossing a surface per unit time, in m³/s. Through a pipe of cross-section A with mean speed v̄, Q = Av̄. A hose that fills a 10.0 L bucket in 20.0 s has Q = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s; if its cross-section is 2.00 cm², the mean speed is 2.50 m/s.

In steady flow, mass cannot pile up inside a section of a flow tube, so the mass entering per second equals the mass leaving per second. This *mass flow rate* is the [[rho|density]] times the [[Q|flow rate]], ρQ = ρAv, so along any flow tube of a steady [[flow|fluid flow]], ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂. This is the [[contin|equation of continuity]], a statement of conservation of mass. For an incompressible fluid the densities cancel and A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: the flow is faster where the tube is narrower. If the hose above ends in a nozzle of area 0.500 cm², a quarter of its cross-section, the water leaves at 10.0 m/s.

Bernoulli's equation applies the [[wet|work–energy theorem]] to an [[ideal|ideal fluid]] in steady flow. Follow the fluid in a thin flow tube between points 1 and 2 on a streamline. In a short time a small volume ΔV enters at 1 and, by the [[contin|continuity equation]], the same volume leaves at 2; the net effect is to carry a parcel ΔV from 1 to 2. The surrounding fluid does net work (p₁ − p₂)ΔV on it through the [[pres|pressure]] difference, and with no viscosity no work goes into friction. This work equals the gain in kinetic energy, Δ(½ρv²)ΔV, plus the gain in gravitational potential energy, Δ(ρgy)ΔV. Dividing by ΔV gives [[bern|Bernoulli's equation]], named after Daniel Bernoulli: along a streamline, p + ½ρv² + ρgy is constant.

At constant height the equation gives [[bern|Bernoulli's principle]]: where a fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower. In a *Venturi* meter a pipe narrows, [[contin|continuity]] makes the flow faster in the throat, and the pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts, read on a manometer, gives the flow speed. A *Prandtl tube* on an aircraft compares the pressure at an opening facing the airflow, where the air is brought to rest, with the pressure of the air streaming past; the difference is ½ρv², which gives the airspeed. *Entrainment*, the drawing of surrounding fluid into a fast stream, as in an atomiser or a Bunsen burner, uses the lower pressure in the stream. From a wide tank open to the air, water leaves a hole a depth h below the surface at v = √(2gh), the speed of free fall from height h.

In a real fluid viscosity resists the motion, and a pressure difference is needed to keep fluid moving through a pipe. In laminar flow through a tube of radius r and length l, the fluid at the wall is at rest and the speed rises to a maximum on the axis, with a parabolic profile. Integrating this profile over the cross-section gives [[poise|Poiseuille's law]], named after the physician Jean Poiseuille, for the [[Q|flow rate]]: Q = (p₂ − p₁)/R, where p₂ − p₁ is the [[pres|pressure]] difference between the ends and R = 8ηl/(πr⁴) is the resistance, set by the [[eta|coefficient of viscosity]] η. The pressure difference drives the [[flow|flow]] as a voltage drives an electric current, and the pressure falls steadily along the tube. Narrowing a blood vessel by 10 % in radius reduces the flow at fixed pressure difference to 0.9⁴ ≈ 0.66 of its value.

Laminar flow gives way to *turbulence* when inertia dominates viscosity. The [[Re|Reynolds number]] measures their ratio. For flow at mean [[speed]] v through a tube of radius r it is N_R = 2ρvr/η, with ρ the [[rho|density]] and η the [[eta|viscosity]] of the fluid; it is dimensionless. Experiments show that the flow is laminar for N_R below about 2000, turbulent above about 3000, and unstable in between. Blood, with ρ = 1.05 × 10³ kg/m³ and η = 3.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, flowing at 0.40 m/s through an aorta of radius 1.0 cm has N_R = 2800, near the transition. A body falling through a fluid speeds up until the [[FD|drag force]] balances its [[w|weight]] minus the [[FB|buoyant force]]; it then moves at its [[vT|terminal velocity]].

Many systems move back and forth about a stable position: a mass on a spring, a pendulum, the atoms of a crystal. Near a stable [[eqpt|equilibrium point]] the force on a displaced body is nearly proportional to the displacement, as in [[hooke|Hooke's law]], and [[n2|Newton's second law]] then gives one universal motion, described by a sine or cosine. This chapter studies that motion, then adds friction, which makes it die away, and a periodic push, which can build it up. A *tuned-mass damper*, a heavy mass on springs and dampers near the top of a tall building, uses both effects: driven by the sway, it swings against the building and absorbs energy from it.

A motion that repeats itself at regular intervals is *periodic motion*; a periodic motion back and forth about an equilibrium is an *oscillation*. The [[Tper|period]] T is the [[dtm|elapsed time]] for one complete cycle, after which the position and velocity have their earlier values again. The [[freq|frequency]] f = 1/T is the number of cycles per unit time, with SI unit the hertz, 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹. A heart beating 72 times per minute has f = 1.2 Hz and T = 0.83 s. The quartz crystal of a watch oscillates at 32 768 Hz, with a period of about 30.5 μs.

The model oscillator is a block of mass m on a frictionless horizontal surface, attached to a spring. Measure x from the position where the spring is relaxed. Within the elastic range the spring exerts the force F = −kx of [[hooke|Hooke's law]], and [[n2|Newton's second law]] gives m d²x/dt² = −kx. A system obeying this equation is a [[sho|simple harmonic oscillator]], and its motion is *simple harmonic motion*: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it. The equation is linear, so a sum of solutions is again a solution. A block hanging from a vertical spring obeys the same equation when x is measured from its new equilibrium position, where the spring force balances the weight.

The solutions are x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), where the [[omega|angular frequency]] ω is fixed by the spring and the mass, as shown below. This [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] is the general solution of the [[sho|oscillator equation]]. The *amplitude* A is the largest displacement from the *equilibrium position* x = 0, and the *phase shift* φ sets where the cycle stands at t = 0. Differentiating gives v(t) = −Aω sin(ωt + φ) and a(t) = −Aω² cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x. The speed is greatest, Aω, as the block passes through equilibrium, and the acceleration is greatest, Aω², at the ends of the motion. The constants A and φ are fixed by the initial position and velocity: a block released from rest at x = 0.10 m has A = 0.10 m and φ = 0.

The [[kspr|force constant]] k of a spring is the force per unit stretch, k = −F/x, the slope of the straight line of [[hooke|Hooke's law]]; it is measured by hanging known weights on the spring, and its unit is N/m. Substituting the solution into the [[sho|oscillator equation]] gives −mω²x = −kx, so the [[omega|angular frequency]] is ω = √(k/m), set only by k and the [[m|mass]]. The [[Tper|period]] is T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k), and the frequency is f = (1/2π)√(k/m). Neither depends on the amplitude. A stiffer spring makes the oscillation faster, and a larger mass makes it slower. A 0.500 kg block on a spring with k = 200 N/m has ω = 20.0 rad/s and T = 0.314 s.

Springs are not special. Near a stable [[eqpt|equilibrium point]] x₀ the [[U|potential energy]] U(x) has a minimum, so U′(x₀) = 0 and U″(x₀) > 0. Expanding the [[F|force]] F = −dU/dx to first order in the displacement gives F ≈ −U″(x₀)(x − x₀): a [[Frest|restoring force]] proportional to the displacement and directed back toward x₀, as from a spring of force constant U″(x₀). *Stability* is decided by the curvature: at a maximum of U the same expansion gives a force pointing away, and a displaced body does not return. Two atoms bound by the *Lennard-Jones 6-12 potential*, U = 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶], have their stable separation at r₀ = 2^{1/6}σ, and small vibrations of the bond are harmonic. Large displacements leave the linear range.

For the block on a spring, energy passes back and forth between the [[Uel|elastic potential energy]] ½kx² and the [[K|kinetic energy]] ½mv². Inserting the [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] x = A cos(ωt + φ), v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ) and using mω² = k gives the total ½kA²[cos²(ωt + φ) + sin²(ωt + φ)] = ½kA². The [[Emech|mechanical energy]] is constant and set by the amplitude. At the *turning points* x = ±A all of it is potential; at x = 0 all of it is kinetic, so v_{max} = A√(k/m). At any position, v = ±√((k/m)(A² − x²)). Doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy.

A point moving at constant [[omega|angular frequency]] ω on a circle of radius A is in uniform [[circ|circular motion]]. Its angle at time t is ωt + φ, so its x coordinate is A cos(ωt + φ), the same function as the [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] of a spring. Simple harmonic motion is the projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter. The projection works for the other quantities too. The *tangential velocity* of the point has magnitude Aω, and its x component is −Aω sin(ωt + φ); the [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] Aω² has x component −Aω² cos(ωt + φ). A peg on a turntable rotating at ω = √(k/m), lit from the side, casts a shadow that moves exactly like a mass m on a spring of force constant k.

A [[spend|simple pendulum]] is a small *pendulum bob* of mass m on a light, inextensible string of length L. At an angle θ from the vertical, the component of the bob's weight along its arc, −mg sin θ, pulls it back, and [[n2|Newton's second law]] along the arc gives mL d²θ/dt² = −mg sin θ. The mass cancels. For small angles sin θ ≈ θ in radians, and the equation becomes that of the [[sho|harmonic oscillator]] with k/m replaced by g/L. So ω = √(g/L) and T = 2π√(L/g), independent of the mass and, for small swings, of the amplitude. At 15° the approximation is off by about 1 %. Since T depends only on L and the [[g|free-fall acceleration]], timing a pendulum measures g: a pendulum 0.994 m long has T = 2.00 s where g = 9.80 m/s².

A [[ppend|physical pendulum]] is any rigid body swinging about a fixed pivot. Let L be the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass and I the [[I|moment of inertia]] about the pivot. The [[w|weight]] acts at the centre of mass and exerts the torque −mgL sin θ about the pivot, so the [[n2rot|second law for rotation]] gives I d²θ/dt² = −mgL sin θ ≈ −mgLθ for small angles. This is again the [[sho|oscillator equation]], with ω = √(mgL/I) and T = 2π√(I/(mgL)). For a point mass, I = mL² and the simple pendulum is recovered. A uniform rod of length ℓ pivoted at one end has I = mℓ²/3 and L = ℓ/2, so T = 2π√(2ℓ/(3g)); a rod 1.00 m long swings with T = 1.64 s.

A [[tpend|torsional pendulum]] is a body hung from a wire or fibre that twists instead of swinging. Twisting the wire through an angle θ produces a restoring torque τ = −κθ, where the *torsion constant* κ depends on the material and dimensions of the wire. The [[n2rot|second law for rotation]] gives I d²θ/dt² = −κθ, with I the [[I|moment of inertia]] of the body about the wire, the rotational form of the [[sho|oscillator equation]]. Hence T = 2π√(I/κ). The torque is linear for any twist within the elastic range of the wire, with no small-angle condition, so torsional pendulums serve as timekeepers and as sensitive torque balances.

Real oscillations die away because friction removes mechanical energy. The simplest model adds to the [[sho|harmonic oscillator]] a [[FD|drag force]] proportional to the velocity, −bv, as for slow motion through a viscous fluid. The equation of motion of this [[damp|damped oscillator]] is m d²x/dt² + b dx/dt + kx = 0, and the motion is *damped harmonic motion*. Without damping the system would oscillate at its *natural angular frequency* ω₀ = √(k/m). For weak damping, b² < 4mk, the motion is *underdamped*: x(t) = A₀e^{−bt/2m} cos(ωt + φ) with ω = √(ω₀² − (b/2m)²). The block still oscillates, a little more slowly than without damping, and its amplitude decays exponentially, falling by the factor 1/e in the time 2m/b.

Stronger damping removes the oscillation. When b² = 4mk the system is *critically damped*: displaced and released, it returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without overshooting. When b² > 4mk it is *overdamped* and creeps back more slowly, the more slowly the larger b is. The regime of a [[damp|damped oscillator]] is chosen by design. The shock absorbers of a car are set close to critical damping, so the car settles quickly after a bump without bouncing, while a door closer is usually overdamped so that the door never slams.

A swing pushed at the right moments goes higher and higher. To model this, add a *periodic driving force* F₀ sin ωt to the [[damp|damped oscillator]]. The equation m d²x/dt² + b dx/dt + kx = F₀ sin ωt describes the [[forced|driven oscillator]]. Once the initial transient has died out, the mass oscillates at the driving frequency ω, not at its own, with amplitude A = F₀/√(m²(ω² − ω₀²)² + b²ω²). The amplitude is largest when ω is close to the natural angular frequency ω₀ = √(k/m); this is *resonance*. At ω = ω₀ the amplitude is F₀/(bω₀), so the weaker the damping, the higher and narrower the resonance peak. Far below ω₀ the response approaches the static stretch F₀/k, and far above it the inertia of the mass keeps the amplitude small.

An oscillation stays in one place. When the parts of a medium are coupled, the oscillation of one part drives its neighbours, and the disturbance travels: this is a wave. The chapter describes waves on strings and in fluids. It defines wavelength and wave speed, writes the wave function, derives the wave equation from [[n2|Newton's second law]], finds the energy a wave carries, and shows how waves combine into interference patterns and standing waves. At each point of the medium the motion is the [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] of Chapter 15.

A [[wave]] is a disturbance that travels while the material carrying it stays, on average, where it was. In a *mechanical wave* the disturbance moves through a *medium*, a [[sys|system of particles]] such as a string, water or air, in which each part pushes or pulls on its neighbours. In a periodic wave each part performs a [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] about its equilibrium, slightly delayed relative to the part before it, and these delays make the pattern move. In a *transverse wave* the medium moves perpendicular to the direction of travel, as on a plucked string; in a *longitudinal wave* it moves along that direction, as in sound. *Electromagnetic waves* need no medium, and *matter waves* describe particles in quantum mechanics; both are treated in later volumes.

A periodic wave repeats in space as well as in time. Its [[lam|wavelength]] λ is the distance between neighbouring points in the same state of motion, such as two adjacent crests, read from a snapshot of the [[wave]]. Its *amplitude* is the largest displacement of the medium from equilibrium. Each point of the medium oscillates with the [[Tper|period]] T and [[freq|frequency]] f of the source. In one period the pattern advances by one wavelength, so the [[vwave|wave speed]], the magnitude of the wave velocity, is v = λ/T = λf. It is set by the medium, not by the source: on a given string a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength at the same speed. Water waves with crests 2.0 m apart passing a post every 0.50 s travel at 4.0 m/s.

A *wave function* y(x, t) gives the displacement of the medium at position x and time t. Suppose a shape y = f(x) at t = 0 moves in the +x direction at the [[vwave|wave speed]] v without changing. At time t it has shifted by vt, so the displacement at x is what it was at x − vt at t = 0: y(x, t) = f(x − vt). A shape moving toward −x is f(x + vt). This [[trav|traveling wave function]] describes any [[wave]] that keeps its form. A *pulse* is a single localised disturbance of this kind, such as one flick sent along a rope.

A periodic wave has the shape of a sine, y(x, t) = A sin(kx − ωt + φ). The sine repeats when kx grows by 2π, that is, after one [[lam|wavelength]], so the [[kwave|wave number]] is k = 2π/λ, in radians per metre. It plays the role in space that the [[omega|angular frequency]] ω = 2π/T plays in time. The argument kx − ωt + φ is the *phase of the wave*. Writing it as k(x − (ω/k)t) + φ shows that the wave speed is v = ω/k = λf. The velocity of a piece of the medium is a different quantity: for a transverse wave it is ∂y/∂t = −Aω cos(kx − ωt + φ), perpendicular to the direction of travel, with maximum Aω.

Differentiating y = f(x − vt) twice with respect to t gives v²f″, and twice with respect to x gives f″. The derivatives are partial: the [[ddt|time derivative]] is taken at fixed x, and the space derivative at fixed t. Every [[trav|traveling wave function]] therefore satisfies the [[waveeq|linear wave equation]]. Its general solution is f(x − vt) + g(x + vt), a sum of waves travelling in the two directions. The equation is linear, so the sum of any two solutions is again a solution. Conversely, whenever Newton's laws for a medium lead to this equation, the medium carries waves of any shape at the speed v.

Newton's laws give the speed of a wave on a stretched string. Take a short piece of string of length dx and [[lmd|linear mass density]] μ, so its mass is μ dx, under [[T|tension]] F_T. For small transverse displacements the tension has the same magnitude all along the string, but its direction at the two ends of the piece differs by the change in slope ∂y/∂x. The net transverse force is therefore F_T (∂²y/∂x²) dx, and [[n2|Newton's second law]] gives μ dx ∂²y/∂t² = F_T ∂²y/∂x² dx. This is the [[waveeq|linear wave equation]] with v² = F_T/μ, so the [[vwave|wave speed]] on a string is v = √(F_T/μ). A guitar string with μ = 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg/m under a tension of 180 N carries waves at 190 m/s.

The same reasoning works in other media, and the speed always has the form of the square root of an elastic property over an inertial property. For a compression wave in a fluid, the elastic property is the [[Bmod|bulk modulus]] B, the pressure increase per fractional decrease in volume, and the inertial property is the [[rho|density]] ρ. Newton's second law for a thin slab of fluid leads to the wave equation with [[vwave|wave speed]] v = √(B/ρ). For water, B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa and ρ = 1.00 × 10³ kg/m³ give v ≈ 1.5 × 10³ m/s. Other things being equal, stiffer media carry waves faster and denser media carry them more slowly.

A wave carries energy along the medium although the medium itself does not travel. Each piece of a string carrying the [[trav|traveling wave]] y = A sin(kx − ωt) has [[K|kinetic energy]] from its transverse motion and potential energy from its stretching. For a piece of mass μ dx, with [[lmd|linear mass density]] μ and [[omega|angular frequency]] ω, the kinetic energy averaged over a cycle is ¼μA²ω² dx, and the potential energy has the same average. One wavelength therefore holds the energy E_λ = ½μA²ω²λ. This energy passes a given point in one period, so the average [[Pwave|power of the wave]] is P_{ave} = E_λ/T = ½μA²ω²v, with v the [[vwave|wave speed]]. The power grows as the square of the amplitude and the square of the frequency.

A wave spreading in two or three dimensions is described by its [[Iint|intensity]] I, the power per unit area crossing a surface perpendicular to the direction of travel, I = P/A, in W/m². It follows from the [[Pwave|wave power]] by dividing by the area over which that power is spread. A point source emitting power P equally in all directions spreads it over a sphere of area 4πr², so I = P/(4πr²): without absorption, the intensity falls as 1/r². A source of 1.00 W gives I = 7.96 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 10.0 m, and a quarter of that at 20.0 m.

A wave that reaches the end of its medium is reflected, and the reflection depends on how the end is held. At a fixed end, such as a string tied to a wall, the displacement must stay zero; this is the *fixed boundary condition*. The reflected wave is the one that, added to the incident wave, cancels it at the end at every instant, so a pulse comes back inverted. At a free end, such as a string tied to a ring that slides without friction on a vertical rod, the slope ∂y/∂x must be zero; this is the *free boundary condition*, and a pulse comes back upright. Such [[bc|boundary conditions]] select the solutions of the [[waveeq|wave equation]] that are allowed. Where two different strings are joined, part of a wave is transmitted and part is reflected.

When two waves pass through the same part of a medium, the result is [[interf|interference]]. Two identical sinusoidal waves travelling the same way and in step, crest on crest, combine into a wave of twice the amplitude; this is *constructive interference*. If one is shifted by half a wavelength, crest meets trough, the displacements cancel and the medium stays at rest; this is *destructive interference*. Intermediate shifts give intermediate amplitudes. After overlapping, each wave continues as if the other had not been there.

These observations are explained by the [[superp|superposition principle]]: where waves overlap, the displacement of the medium is the sum of the displacements the waves would cause separately, y = y₁ + y₂. The principle is a consequence of the linearity of the [[waveeq|wave equation]]: if y₁ and y₂ are solutions, so is y₁ + y₂, since the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. It holds as long as the amplitudes are small enough for the medium to respond linearly. Adding two [[trav|traveling waves]] A sin(kx − ωt) and A sin(kx − ωt + φ), which differ by a *phase shift* φ, with the identity sin a + sin b = 2 sin((a + b)/2) cos((a − b)/2), gives the resultant below. The [[interf|interference]] is constructive for φ = 0, 2π, 4π, … and destructive for φ = π, 3π, ….

A wave on a string with a fixed end is reflected and travels back through the incoming wave. By the [[superp|superposition principle]], two [[trav|traveling waves]] of equal amplitude and frequency moving in opposite directions add to A sin(kx − ωt) + A sin(kx + ωt) = 2A sin kx cos ωt. This is a [[standw|standing wave]]: the pattern does not travel. Each point oscillates at angular frequency ω with its own amplitude 2A|sin kx|. At *nodes*, where kx = nπ, the medium never moves; midway between them, at *antinodes*, it oscillates with the full amplitude 2A. Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart. A fixed end satisfies its [[bc|boundary condition]] by being a node.
eqs: y(x, t) = [2A sin kx] cos ωt

paragraphs.text: A string of length L fixed at both ends must have a node at each end. With one node at x = 0, the other requires kL = nπ, so only the wavelengths λ_n = 2L/n fit, with n = 1, 2, 3, …. With the [[vwave|wave speed]] v = √(F_T/μ), the allowed frequencies are f_n = nv/2L = nf₁. These [[standw|standing waves]], selected by the [[bc|boundary conditions]], are the [[modes|normal modes]] of the string, and any motion of the string is a superposition of them. The lowest, f₁ = v/2L, is the *fundamental frequency*; the higher ones are *overtones*. Each mode acts as an oscillator, so a string driven at one of its frequencies f_n responds strongly; this is [[forced|resonance]]. A guitar string 0.650 m long with v = 190 m/s has f₁ = 146 Hz.

Sound is the most familiar mechanical [[wave]]. It travels through gases, liquids and solids as a longitudinal wave, so the results of Chapter 16 apply to it: its speed follows from the [[Bmod|bulk modulus]] and density of the medium, it carries energy, and it reflects and forms standing waves. This chapter adds what is particular to sound: the link between pressure and displacement in a sound wave, the decibel scale of intensity, the modes of air columns in musical instruments, beats, the Doppler effect of moving sources and observers, and the shock waves of supersonic flight.

A [[sound|sound wave]] is a longitudinal [[wave]]. A vibrating source pushes the neighbouring layer of air, which pushes the next, so *compressions*, where the molecules are crowded and the [[pres|pressure]] is slightly raised, alternate with *rarefactions*, where it is slightly lowered. Let s(x, t) = s_{max} cos(kx − ωt + φ) be the displacement of the air along the direction of travel. A layer whose displacement varies with x is compressed by the fractional amount −∂s/∂x, and the [[Bmod|bulk modulus]] B turns this into the pressure change Δp = −B ∂s/∂x = Δp_{max} sin(kx − ωt + φ), with Δp_{max} = Bks_{max}. The pressure wave is a quarter cycle out of phase with the displacement wave: the pressure change is greatest where the displacement is zero. *Hearing*, the perception of sound, belongs to physiology.

The [[vsound|speed of sound]] is a property of the medium. Apply [[n2|Newton's second law]] to a thin slab of fluid that a [[sound|sound wave]] pushes back and forth: the net pressure force on the slab, set by the [[Bmod|bulk modulus]] B, accelerates its mass, set by the [[rho|density]] ρ. The result is the wave equation with v = √(B/ρ), the square root of an *elastic property* over an *inertial property*. Because v = fλ and the source fixes the *frequency*, the *wavelength* in a medium is λ = v/f; a 343 Hz tone in air at 20 °C has λ = 1.00 m. All audible frequencies travel at the same speed in air, so the low notes of a *woofer* and the high notes of a *tweeter* reach a listener together.

In a thin solid rod the elastic property is [[Ymod|Young's modulus]] Y, and the [[vsound|speed of sound]] is v = √(Y/ρ), with ρ the [[rho|density]] of the rod. Steel, with Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa and ρ = 7.8 × 10³ kg/m³, carries sound at about 5.1 × 10³ m/s, some fifteen times faster than air. In a gas, the compressions of a sound wave are too quick for heat to flow between them, and for an ideal gas the bulk modulus is then γp, with γ the ratio of the gas's heat capacities, 1.40 for air. This gives v = √(γRT/M), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T the absolute temperature and M the molar mass: in air, 331 m/s at 0 °C and 343 m/s at 20 °C. *Seismic waves* in the Earth include longitudinal and transverse waves, which travel at different speeds.

The ear responds to sound [[Iint|intensities]] from about 10⁻¹² W/m² to above 1 W/m², twelve orders of magnitude, and perceives equal ratios of intensity roughly as equal steps. Sound is therefore described on a logarithmic scale. The [[beta|sound intensity level]] is β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀), in *decibels* (dB), with the reference intensity I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m², near the threshold of hearing at 1000 Hz. The decibel is a tenth of the bel, named after Alexander Graham Bell. Multiplying the intensity by 10 adds 10 dB, and doubling it adds 10 log₁₀ 2 ≈ 3.0 dB.
