The [[coul|Coulomb force]] points along the line from Q, so only the radial part of each displacement contributes to the work, and W = kqQ(1/r_A − 1/r_B), whatever the path. The force is therefore [[cons|conservative]], and the system has a [[U|potential energy]] whose change equals minus this work. With the zero at infinite separation, the [[Ue|electric potential energy]] of two point charges is U(r) = qQ/(4πε₀r). The calculation is the same as for gravitation, but the sign of U follows the sign of qQ. For like charges U is positive and decreases as they separate, so released charges fly apart. For unlike charges U is negative, and work must be supplied to pull them apart.

For several point charges the potential energy is a sum over pairs, U = k Σ q_{i}q_{j}/r_{ij}, with each pair counted once. It equals the work needed to bring the charges together from infinite separation. When only electric forces act, the [[Emech|mechanical energy]] K + U is conserved, as in mechanics. Two protons released from rest 2.00 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, a typical distance in a nucleus, start with [[Ue|potential energy]] ke²/r = 1.15 × 10⁻¹³ J. When they are far apart this energy has become kinetic energy, shared equally because their momenta are equal and opposite, so each proton has 5.77 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. Inside a nucleus a stronger attractive force holds the protons together against this repulsion.

The [[Ue|potential energy]] of a test charge q placed among fixed source charges is proportional to q. The ratio V = U/q therefore depends only on the sources and on the position of the test charge. It is the [[Vfield|electric potential]], a scalar field: a single number at each point, defined, like any potential energy, only up to an additive constant. For a point source Q, with the zero at infinity, V = Q/(4πε₀r). The unit of potential is the *volt*, 1 V = 1 J/C, named after Alessandro Volta. A [[q|charge]] q at a point where the potential is V has potential energy qV.

The potential can also be found from the [[Efield|field]] directly. On a small step dl⃗ the field does work E⃗·dl⃗ on a unit charge, a [[dot|scalar product]], and the potential falls by the same amount. Adding the steps in an [[integ|integral]] gives the difference in [[Vfield|potential]] between two points. The result does not depend on the path, because the electrostatic field is conservative. In a uniform field E, the potential falls by Ed over a distance d along the field, which is why the unit of field, N/C, can also be written V/m.

Only differences of potential have physical meaning, and the arbitrary constant cancels in them. The potential difference ΔV_{AB} = V_B − V_A between two points is also called the [[dV|voltage]]; it follows from the [[Vfield|potential]] and is measured with a voltmeter. A charge q that moves through a potential difference ΔV changes its potential energy by ΔU = qΔV. For particles a convenient energy unit is the *electron-volt*, the energy a particle of charge e gains in moving through a potential difference of 1 V: 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. An electron accelerated from rest through 1.00 kV gains 1.00 keV of kinetic energy. Its speed is then v = √(2K/mₑ) = 1.88 × 10⁷ m/s, about 6 % of the speed of light, so the nonrelativistic expression for K is adequate.

Potentials of point charges add like fields, but as scalars. For a [[pts|point-charge configuration]], the potential at P is the sum of the point-charge potentials, with r_i the distance from q_i to P and the constant 1/(4πε₀) set by the [[eps0|permittivity of vacuum]]. No directions enter, so this sum is easier than the vector sum for the field, and the field can be found from it afterward. The potential of an electric dipole is an example. At a distance r much larger than the separation d, the distances from P to the two charges differ by about d cos θ, and the two terms combine into V = kp⃗·r̂/r², where p⃗ is the [[pdip|electric dipole moment]] and θ the angle between p⃗ and r̂. This [[Vfield|potential]] falls off as 1/r², faster than that of a single charge, because the two charges nearly cancel.

For a [[chdist|continuous distribution]] the sum becomes an [[integ|integral]], V_P = k∫dq/r. On the axis of a ring of radius R carrying charge Q, every piece is at the same distance √(z² + R²) from the point, so V = kQ/√(z² + R²), with no vector components to track. Outside a uniformly charged sphere, or a charged spherical conductor, V = kQ/r, as for a point charge. A *Van de Graaff generator* uses a large hollow metal sphere of this kind to reach high potentials. The surrounding air sets the limit: at the surface E = V/R, and air begins to conduct at about 3 × 10⁶ V/m, so a sphere of radius 0.20 m can reach about 6 × 10⁵ V.

The integral of the field gives the potential; the reverse step is differentiation with respect to position. For a scalar field V(x, y, z), the partial derivative ∂V/∂x is the [[ddt|derivative]] with respect to x taken with y and z held fixed, and ∂V/∂y and ∂V/∂z are defined in the same way. The three partial derivatives, taken as [[comp|components]] along î, ĵ and k̂, form the [[grad|gradient]], ∇V = î ∂V/∂x + ĵ ∂V/∂y + k̂ ∂V/∂z. The gradient points in the direction in which V increases fastest, and its magnitude is that fastest rate of increase per unit length. Along any small step dl⃗, the change in V is dV = ∇V·dl⃗.

Along every small step dV = −E⃗·dl⃗ and also dV = ∇V·dl⃗, so the [[Efield|electric field]] is minus the [[grad|gradient]] of the [[Vfield|potential]]. In components, E_x = −∂V/∂x, E_y = −∂V/∂y and E_z = −∂V/∂z. The field points toward decreasing potential, as a ball rolls downhill. For a point charge, V = kQ/r depends only on r, and E_r = −dV/dr = kQ/r² recovers the Coulomb field. For V = (5.0 V/m²)x², the field is E_x = −(10 V/m²)x, which points toward x = 0 from both sides. The whole field thus follows from one scalar function. The relation holds for static charges; when magnetic fields change in time, the electric field gains a part that no potential describes.

Points at the same [[Vfield|potential]] form [[equipot|equipotential surfaces]]; in a plane drawing they appear as *equipotential lines*. Moving a charge along an equipotential takes no work, since ΔV = 0 there. For a step dl⃗ within the surface, dV = ∇V·dl⃗ = 0, so the [[grad|gradient]], and with it the [[Efield|electric field]] E⃗ = −∇V, is perpendicular to every equipotential. Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles and point from higher to lower potential. The picture resembles a topographic map: equipotentials are the contour lines of constant height, the field points down the steepest slope, and it is strongest where the contours are closest. For a point charge the equipotentials are concentric spheres; in a uniform field they are parallel planes.

A [[condeq|conductor in electrostatic equilibrium]] has zero field inside and a field perpendicular to its surface outside, so the whole conductor is at one potential. Connecting a conductor to the Earth, a very large conductor, brings it to the Earth's potential, usually chosen as zero; this is *grounding*. On an isolated conductor, charge gathers where the surface curves most sharply. Two distant spheres of radii R₁ and R₂ joined by a wire share one potential, kQ₁/R₁ = kQ₂/R₂. Their surface charge densities, and the fields σ/ε₀ just outside them, are then in the ratio R₂/R₁, so the smaller sphere has the stronger field. Near a sharp point the field can exceed the breakdown field of air, about 3 × 10⁶ V/m, and charge leaks away. A *lightning rod* is a pointed conductor connected to the ground, so that a strike reaches the ground through it, not through the building.

Many devices use the [[F|force]] F⃗ = qE⃗ on charged particles together with [[n2|Newton's second law]]. A *Van de Graaff generator* carries charge on a moving belt into a hollow metal sphere; the charge moves to the outer surface of the [[condeq|conductor]], so more can be added until the potential reaches millions of volts. *Xerography* charges a drum coated with a *photoconductor*, which is an [[insul|insulator]] in the dark and a [[cond|conductor]] when lit. Light from the original discharges the bright areas, charged toner sticks to the remaining charge, and the toner is transferred to paper and fused by heat. A *laser printer* writes the pattern with a laser. Continuous *ink jet printers* steer charged droplets between deflecting plates, and *electrostatic precipitators* charge smoke particles and collect them on plates.

Two conductors with equal and opposite charges store charge, and with it energy, in the field between them. Such a device, the capacitor, is in almost every circuit: it smooths voltages, stores the energy for a camera flash or a defibrillator, and tunes radios. This chapter defines capacitance from the [[condeq|equilibrium of conductors]] and the [[dV|voltage]] between them, combines capacitors in networks, finds the energy they store and assigns that energy to the [[Efield|electric field]]. It ends with the effect of an [[insul|insulator]] placed between the conductors, explained by the polarization of its molecules.

A [[capst|capacitor]] consists of two conductors, called plates whatever their shape, that carry charges +Q and −Q; usually a battery has moved the charge Q from one to the other. Each plate is a [[condeq|conductor in electrostatic equilibrium]] and therefore an equipotential, so a single potential difference ΔV exists between them. The field is concentrated in the space between the plates, which holds vacuum, air or an insulating *dielectric*. The standard example is the *parallel-plate capacitor*: two flat plates of area A a distance d apart, with d small compared with the size of the plates, so that the field between them is nearly uniform and the field outside nearly zero.

Doubling the charges on the plates doubles the field everywhere, by superposition, and therefore doubles the [[dV|potential difference]]. The ratio C = Q/ΔV is the [[Cap|capacitance]] of the [[capst|capacitor]], the charge stored per volt. It depends only on the shape, size and spacing of the conductors and on the material between them, not on Q. The SI unit is the *farad*, 1 F = 1 C/V, named after Michael Faraday. One farad is a large capacitance; capacitors in electronic circuits typically range from picofarads to millifarads. An *electrolytic capacitor* reaches a large capacitance in a small volume, because its dielectric is a very thin oxide film.

For a parallel-plate capacitor, the charge spreads over the inner faces with density σ = Q/A. By the [[symm|symmetry method]], each plate alone produces a field σ/(2ε₀); between the plates the two fields add to E = σ/ε₀, and outside they cancel. The potential difference is ΔV = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A), so the [[Cap|capacitance]] is C = ε₀A/d, set by the geometry and the [[eps0|permittivity of vacuum]]. Plates of area 1.0 m² that are 1.0 mm apart give only 8.9 nF; one farad at that spacing would need about 110 km² of plate. The same method gives C = 4πε₀R₁R₂/(R₂ − R₁) for concentric spheres and C = 2πε₀l/ln(R₂/R₁) for a length l of *coaxial cable*.

Practical capacitors vary these quantities. A *variable air capacitor*, used to tune radios, changes the overlap of two sets of interleaved plates as a shaft turns. Rolled capacitors wind two long strips of metal foil, separated by a thin insulating film, into a compact cylinder, which gives a large area with a small spacing. Living cells also act as capacitors. A *cell membrane*, an insulating layer a few nanometres thick, separates conducting fluids that carry opposite charges on its two sides. Its [[Cap|capacitance]] is about 1 μF per square centimetre, so a small transfer of ions sets up the potential difference of about 70 mV across it.

Capacitors are often connected in networks, and a network can be replaced by a single equivalent capacitor. In a *parallel combination*, every capacitor connects the same two conductors, so all share one [[dV|potential difference]] ΔV, and their charges add: Q = (C₁ + C₂ + ⋯)ΔV. In a *series combination*, the capacitors are joined end to end. The two plates connected between neighbouring capacitors form an isolated conductor that starts neutral, so by [[qcons|charge conservation]] it carries +Q on one plate and −Q on the other. Every capacitor in the series then holds the same charge Q, and the potential differences add: ΔV = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ + ⋯. With the definition of [[Cap|capacitance]], these give the rules for [[capnet|capacitors in series and parallel]].

A series combination has less capacitance than its smallest member, and a parallel combination more than its largest. Take C₁ = 2.00 μF and C₂ = 3.00 μF. In parallel they act as 5.00 μF. In series, 1/C_S = (1/2.00 + 1/3.00) μF⁻¹, so C_S = 1.20 μF. Connected in series to a 12.0 V battery, each capacitor holds Q = C_{S}ΔV = 14.4 μC. The potential differences are then Q/C₁ = 7.20 V and Q/C₂ = 4.80 V, which add up to the 12.0 V of the battery: the smaller capacitor takes the larger share. Larger networks are reduced step by step, one series or parallel group at a time, with the same [[capnet|combination rules]].

Charging a capacitor takes work, because each new bit of charge must be carried from the negative plate to the positive plate against the field between them. When the charge is q, the [[dV|potential difference]] is q/C, and moving a further dq takes [[W|work]] dW = (q/C) dq. Integrating from zero to the final charge Q, with the definition of [[Cap|capacitance]], gives the [[UC|energy stored in a capacitor]]. The factor ½ appears because the voltage rises from zero during charging. A *defibrillator* may, for example, charge a 150 μF capacitor to 2.0 kV, which stores ½(150 × 10⁻⁶ F)(2.0 × 10³ V)² = 300 J, and then send much of this energy through the patient's chest in a few milliseconds.

The energy can be located. In a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε₀A/d and V = Ed, so the [[UC|stored energy]] is U = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)² = ½ε₀E²(Ad). The product Ad is the volume between the plates, where the field is. The [[uE|energy density]], the energy per unit volume, is therefore u_E = ½ε₀E², fixed by the [[Eval|field]] and the [[eps0|permittivity of vacuum]] alone. Although derived here for a capacitor, the result holds for any electric field in vacuum, and it shows that energy can be assigned to the field itself, wherever the field is. In air at 3.0 × 10⁶ V/m, close to breakdown, u_E = 40 J/m³.

Charge a parallel-plate capacitor, disconnect it so that its charge Q stays fixed, and slide a slab of [[insul|insulating]] material into the gap until it fills the space. A voltmeter across the plates shows the potential difference falling from V₀ to V₀/κ. The number κ is the [[kappa|dielectric constant]] of the material. Since Q is unchanged, the [[Cap|capacitance]] rises from C₀ to C = κC₀, and the field between the plates, V/d, falls from E₀ to E₀/κ. Measured values are never below 1: κ = 1 for vacuum, 1.0006 for air at atmospheric pressure, between about 2 and 4 for common plastics and paper, and about 80 for water at room temperature. A parallel-plate capacitor filled with a dielectric has C = κε₀A/d.

The stored energy changes as well. With Q fixed, U = Q²/(2C) falls to U₀/κ: the field does work on the slab and pulls it into the gap. If the battery stays connected instead, the voltage stays fixed, the charge rises to κQ₀, and the [[UC|stored energy]] ½CV² grows by the factor κ, with the energy drawn from the battery. In practice a dielectric serves three purposes: it raises the capacitance, it holds the plates apart mechanically, and it withstands a larger field than air before conducting. The next section explains the value of the [[kappa|dielectric constant]] from the response of molecules.

A dielectric weakens the field because its molecules respond to it. In an applied field E⃗₀, nonpolar molecules acquire *induced electric-dipole moments* along the field, and polar molecules, which are permanent [[pdip|dipoles]], turn partly into line with it against the disorder of thermal motion. Inside the [[insul|insulator]], the positive end of each dipole sits next to the negative end of its neighbour, and these charges cancel on average. At the two faces next to the plates they do not: thin layers of *induced surface charges* ±σ_i remain, each opposite in sign to the charge on the nearby plate. The surface charges produce an *induced electrical field* of magnitude σ_i/ε₀ opposite to the applied one, so the net [[Efield|field]] inside is E = E₀ − σ_i/ε₀. This is the [[dielmod|molecular model of a dielectric]].

The [[dielmod|molecular model]] explains the [[kappa|dielectric constant]]. Write the induced field as a component E_i along E⃗₀, which is negative because the induced field opposes the applied one. The net field is E₀ + E_i, so κ = E₀/(E₀ + E_i). The induced field opposes the applied field but never reverses it, so κ > 1. Equivalently, the induced field is E⃗_i = (1/κ − 1)E⃗₀, and the induced surface charge density is σ_i = (1 − 1/κ)σ, where σ is the charge density on the plates. For weak fields the induced dipoles are proportional to the field, so κ is a constant of the material.

A strong enough field tears bound electrons from their molecules, and the [[insul|insulator]] suddenly conducts. This is *dielectric breakdown*. The largest [[Eval|field]] a material can withstand without breaking down is its [[Ebreak|dielectric strength]]. For dry air at atmospheric pressure it is about 3 × 10⁶ V/m, and good solid insulators withstand ten or more times as much. Breakdown sets the largest voltage a capacitor can hold, V_{max} = E_{max}d. An air-filled capacitor with a 1.0 mm gap sparks over at about 3 kV, which is one reason capacitors for high voltages use solid dielectrics.

Until now the charges have been at rest, and inside a [[condeq|conductor in equilibrium]] the [[Efield|field]] was zero. This chapter lets charge move. A battery keeps a [[dV|potential difference]] between the ends of a wire, so a field persists inside the metal and drives a steady flow of [[q|charge]], an electric current. The chapter describes current in terms of moving carriers, introduces resistivity and resistance, states Ohm's law and where it fails, finds the power delivered to circuit elements, and ends with superconductors, which carry current with no resistance at all.

An [[curr|electric current]] is a flow of charge. Choose a cross section of a wire and count the [[q|charge]] ΔQ that crosses it in a time Δt. The average current is I_{ave} = ΔQ/Δt, and the current at an instant is the [[ddt|time derivative]] I = dQ/dt. The SI unit is the *ampere*, 1 A = 1 C/s, named after André-Marie Ampère; it is one of the base units of the SI. A phone charger that delivers 2.0 A for one hour moves 7.2 × 10³ C, the charge of 4.5 × 10²² electrons. The direction of the *conventional current* is the direction in which positive charge would move. In metals the carriers are electrons, which move opposite to the conventional current, a consequence of Franklin's choice of signs.

A steady current needs a closed path. If a wire simply ended, charge would pile up at the end and its field would stop the flow. An [[circuit|electric circuit]] is a closed loop of [[cond|conductors]] through a source, such as a battery, and elements such as lamps, resistors and capacitors. In a single loop the [[curr|current]] is the same at every point once it is steady. Charge is not used up in a circuit: it circulates, while the source supplies energy and the elements take it. Circuits are drawn as a *schematic*, in which wires are lines and each element has a standard symbol. A car's *starter motor*, for example, appears as one element in a loop with the battery, a switch and heavy cables.

In a metal the [[cond|conduction electrons]] move in random directions at speeds near 10⁶ m/s, colliding constantly with the vibrating lattice. Random motion carries no net charge through a cross section. An applied field adds a small average velocity, the [[vd|drift velocity]] v⃗_d, which for electrons is opposite to the field. Suppose a wire of cross section A contains n carriers per unit volume, each with [[q|charge]] q. In a time Δt the carriers within a distance v_{d}Δt of a cross section pass through it, so ΔQ = nqAv_{d}Δt and the [[curr|current]] is I = nqAv_d. Copper has about one free electron per atom, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. For 1.0 A in a copper wire of cross section 1.0 mm², v_d = I/(neA) = 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, less than a tenth of a millimetre per second.

The [[Jcur|current density]] J⃗ = nqv⃗_d is the current per unit area at a point, built from the [[vd|drift velocity]] and the carrier [[q|charge]]. It points along the motion of positive carriers; for electrons q = −e and v⃗_d is opposite to the field, so J⃗ points along the field. The current is the flux of J⃗ through a cross section, I = ∫ J⃗·dA⃗, which reduces to I = JA for a uniform current. In the copper wire above, J = 1.0 × 10⁶ A/m². A switch lights a lamp at once, despite the slow drift, because the field that pushes the carriers is set up along the wire at a speed comparable to the speed of light, and electrons everywhere in the circuit start drifting together. In an incandescent lamp, a thin tungsten filament carries a large current density and is heated until it glows.

A field is needed to keep a current flowing, because collisions with the lattice continually take away the momentum that the carriers gain. In many materials the [[Jcur|current density]] is proportional to the [[Eval|field]]. The [[resist|resistivity]] ρ = E/J states how large a field a material needs per unit current density; its inverse σ = 1/ρ is the *electrical conductivity*. Here ρ and σ are properties of the material, not charge densities. The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm metre. Copper at 20 °C has ρ = 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, glass between about 10¹⁰ and 10¹⁴ Ω·m, and semiconductors lie in between. In metals ρ rises with [[temp|temperature]], because the lattice vibrates more and scatters the electrons more often; near room temperature ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)], with α = 3.9 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ for copper.

For a whole component, the [[Rres|resistance]] is the ratio of the [[dV|voltage]] across it to the [[curr|current]] through it, R ≡ ΔV/I. Its unit is the *ohm*, 1 Ω = 1 V/A, and a resistor is a component made to have a stated resistance. The definition applies to any element, whatever the relation between its current and voltage. For a uniform wire of length L and cross section A, the [[resist|resistivity]] fixes R: integrating E = ρJ along the wire gives ΔV = EL = ρ(I/A)L, so R = ρL/A. A copper wire 10 m long with a cross section of 1.0 mm² has R = 0.17 Ω. Because R is proportional to ρ, resistance also rises with temperature, as R = R₀(1 + αΔT), and a platinum wire whose resistance is measured serves as a precise thermometer.

For a metal wire kept at constant temperature, experiment shows that the current is proportional to the applied voltage over a wide range, so its [[Rres|resistance]] does not depend on V or I. This is [[ohm|Ohm's law]], published by Georg Simon Ohm in 1827. In local form it reads J⃗ = σE⃗, with a conductivity, and hence a [[resist|resistivity]], that does not depend on the field. Materials and devices that obey it are *ohmic*. Ohm's law is an empirical property of many materials, not a general law of nature, and the definition R ≡ ΔV/I does not imply it. Many devices are *nonohmic*: a *diode* conducts readily in one direction and hardly at all in the other, and the filament of a lamp heats up as the current rises, so its resistance grows.

In the form I = V/R, [[ohm|Ohm's law]] predicts the [[curr|current]] in an ohmic element: the source fixes the [[dV|voltage]] across it, the element fixes its [[Rres|resistance]], and the current follows. A 12.0 V battery across a 4.00 Ω resistor drives a current of 3.00 A, and doubling the voltage doubles the current. A graph of current against voltage for an ohmic element is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/R. For a diode it is a curve that stays near zero for one polarity and rises steeply for the other. The simple relation V = IR is the basis of the circuit analysis in the next chapter.

A charge dq that passes through an element with a [[dV|potential difference]] ΔV across it loses potential energy dq ΔV, which the element receives. Dividing by dt gives the rate of energy transfer, the [[P|power]] P = dW/dt = (dq/dt)ΔV. Since dq/dt is the [[curr|current]], the [[Pel|electric power]] delivered to the element is P = IV; one watt equals one ampere times one volt. In a resistor the energy becomes thermal energy, and with V = IR the power can be written P = I²R = V²/R. A 12.0 V headlamp that draws 5.00 A uses 60.0 W, and its hot filament has a resistance of 2.40 Ω.

Electrical energy is sold by the kilowatt-hour, 1 kW·h = (1000 W)(3600 s) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; a 1.5 kW heater running for 4.0 h uses 6.0 kW·h. The I²R loss explains how power is sent over long distances. To deliver a [[Pel|power]] P at voltage V, a line must carry the current I = P/V, and the line's [[Rres|resistance]] R dissipates I²R = P²R/V². Raising the voltage tenfold cuts the current to a tenth and the loss in the line to a hundredth, which is why long-distance lines operate at hundreds of kilovolts. Efficiency matters at the user's end too: a light-emitting diode gives the same light as an incandescent lamp for a small fraction of its power.

As a metal is cooled its [[resist|resistivity]] decreases, and classical conduction theory predicts a smooth approach to a small residual value set by impurities and defects. In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, cooling mercury with liquid helium, found instead that its resistance dropped abruptly to zero below about 4.2 K. This is *superconductivity*. Each superconducting material has a *critical temperature* T_c below which ρ = 0 within the precision of every measurement; a current started in a superconducting ring persists for years without a source. The [[supercond|superconducting state]] is reached by lowering the [[temp|temperature]] and is a distinct phase of matter. In 1933 the *Meissner effect* was found: a superconductor also expels magnetic fields from its interior, which zero resistance alone would not require.

The explanation requires quantum mechanics. In the *BCS theory* of John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer, published in 1957, an electron moving through the lattice slightly distorts it, and the distortion attracts a second electron. The two form a bound pair, and these *Cooper pairs* all occupy one collective quantum state. Scattering would have to disturb this whole state, which costs a finite energy, so at low temperature the pairs flow without loss; classical physics has no counterpart to the [[supercond|superconducting state]]. Materials with T_c above 77 K, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, have been known since 1987. Superconducting coils produce the strong magnetic fields of MRI scanners and particle accelerators. A *Josephson junction*, a thin barrier through which pairs tunnel, is the basis of the *SQUID*, a detector of extremely weak magnetic fields.

Charge flows steadily only around a closed [[circuit|circuit]] that contains a source. This chapter analyses circuits with steady, direct currents. It starts with the source itself, its electromotive force and internal resistance, and then reduces networks of [[Rres|resistors]] to single equivalent resistances. Kirchhoff's rules, which rest on [[qcons|charge conservation]] and on the [[Vfield|potential]], handle circuits that cannot be reduced in this way. The same rules show how meters measure current and voltage and, applied to a resistor together with a [[Cap|capacitor]], give currents that change exponentially in time. The chapter ends with household wiring and electrical safety.

A charge that goes once around a closed circuit returns to its starting [[Vfield|potential]], so the electrostatic field does no net work on it. Yet the charge loses energy steadily in the resistors. A source must therefore do nonelectrostatic work, chemical in a *battery* and mechanical in a generator, to carry charge inside it from the low-potential terminal to the high-potential one. The [[emf|electromotive force]] ε, or emf, is this [[W|work]] per unit [[q|charge]], ε = dW/dq, measured in volts. Despite its name, it is not a force. With no current, the [[dV|potential difference]] between the terminals equals ε. The first battery was Alessandro Volta's *voltaic pile* of 1800, a stack of zinc and copper disks separated by cloth soaked in salt water.

A real source has an *internal resistance* r, because the current must also pass through the materials inside it. When the source delivers a [[curr|current]] I, [[ohm|Ohm's law]] applied inside it gives a potential drop Ir, so the [[Vterm|terminal voltage]] is V = ε − Ir, lower than the [[emf|emf]]. A 9.0 V battery with r = 1.5 Ω connected to a 16.5 Ω load drives I = 9.0 V/18.0 Ω = 0.50 A, and its terminal voltage is 9.0 V − 0.75 V = 8.25 V. A *lead–acid battery* joins six cells of about 2 V each to give 12 V. During discharge, the negative electrode is the *anode*, where oxidation releases electrons into the external circuit, and the positive electrode is the *cathode*. Internal resistance grows as a battery ages, so *battery testers* measure the terminal voltage while drawing a current.

Several resistors can be replaced by a single *equivalent resistance* that draws the same current at the same voltage. In a *series circuit* the resistors are joined end to end, and the same current I passes through each, because in a steady state [[qcons|charge conservation]] does not let charge pile up between them. The [[dV|potential differences]] add, and with [[ohm|Ohm's law]] for each resistor V = IR₁ + IR₂ + ⋯, so the resistances of [[Req|resistors in series]] add. In a *parallel circuit* each resistor connects the same two points, so all have the same voltage V, and the currents add: I = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + ⋯. For resistors in parallel, the inverses of the resistances therefore add.

A series combination has more resistance than its largest member, a parallel combination less than its smallest. Consider 6.00 Ω and 3.00 Ω in parallel, equivalent to 2.00 Ω, in series with 4.00 Ω and a 12.0 V source. The total [[Req|equivalent resistance]] is 6.00 Ω, so the source supplies 2.00 A. The parallel pair has (2.00 A)(2.00 Ω) = 4.00 V across it, so 0.667 A flows through the 6.00 Ω resistor and 1.33 A through the 3.00 Ω resistor, together 2.00 A. Household appliances are connected in parallel, so each receives the full supply voltage and can be switched on its own. Switching on a *refrigerator* adds a branch and raises the total current drawn from the supply.

Some circuits, such as a *multi-loop circuit* with sources in more than one branch, cannot be reduced to series and parallel combinations. They are solved with [[kirch|Kirchhoff's rules]], formulated by Gustav Kirchhoff. The *junction rule* states that the total current into any junction equals the total current out; it is [[qcons|charge conservation]], since in a steady state no charge accumulates at a junction. The *loop rule* states that the potential differences around any closed loop add to zero; it holds because the [[Vfield|potential]] has a single value at each point, so a trip around a loop returns to the starting value. Applied to the junctions and loops of a [[circuit|circuit]], the two rules give linear equations for the unknown branch currents.
eqs: Σ I_{in} = Σ I_{out},   Σ ΔV = 0

paragraphs.text: To apply the rules, give each branch current a symbol and an assumed direction. Crossing a resistor in the assumed direction of its current is a potential drop, −IR, and crossing it the other way is +IR. Crossing a source from its negative to its positive terminal adds +ε, and crossing it the other way adds −ε. One junction equation fewer than the number of junctions, together with enough independent loops, gives as many equations as unknown currents. A negative result means that the current flows against the assumed direction. The same [[kirch|rules]] govern *solar cells* joined into panels: cells in series add their emfs, and rows of cells in parallel add their currents.

As an example, connect three branches between the same two junctions: a 10.0 V source in series with 2.00 Ω, a 4.00 V source in series with 2.00 Ω, both with their positive terminals toward the upper junction, and a 4.00 Ω resistor. Take the lower junction as zero potential and let V be the potential of the upper one. Each branch then carries (ε − V)/R toward the upper junction, and the junction rule gives (10.0 V − V)/2.00 Ω + (4.00 V − V)/2.00 Ω = V/4.00 Ω, so V = 5.60 V. The currents are 2.20 A up through the first source, 1.40 A down through the resistor and −0.800 A through the second source. The stronger source drives current backward through the weaker one and charges it, as the [[kirch|loop rule]] around the two sources confirms.

An *ammeter* measures the current in a branch, so the current must pass through it: it is connected in series, and its own resistance adds to that of the branch. A *voltmeter* measures the potential difference between two points and is connected in parallel with the element between them, so it draws some current itself. By the rules for [[Req|resistors in series and parallel]], an [[meters|ammeter or voltmeter]] disturbs the [[circuit|circuit]] little only if the ammeter's resistance is much smaller, and the voltmeter's much larger, than the resistances around it. A 10 MΩ voltmeter across a 10 kΩ resistor forms a parallel combination of 9.99 kΩ, a change of 0.1 %. A 1 kΩ voltmeter across the same resistor would form 0.91 kΩ and change the voltage it is meant to measure.

An *analog meter* is built around a galvanometer, a coil that turns in the field of a permanent magnet and deflects a needle in proportion to the current through it. A small resistance connected in parallel with the coil, a shunt, turns it into an ammeter for large currents; a large resistance in series turns it into a voltmeter. A *digital meter* converts a voltage into a number electronically and typically has an input resistance of about 10 MΩ on its voltage ranges. An *ohmmeter* passes a known current through a component and measures the voltage across it, giving its [[Rres|resistance]] as R = ΔV/I. The component must first be disconnected from its circuit, so that no other source or path affects the reading.

An [[rc|RC circuit]] contains a resistor and a capacitor in series. Connect an uncharged capacitor C and a resistor R to a source of emf ε by closing a switch at t = 0. The [[kirch|loop rule]] gives ε − IR − q/C = 0, where IR is the potential drop across the resistor from [[ohm|Ohm's law]] and q/C is the voltage across the [[Cap|capacitor]]. The current charges the capacitor, I = dq/dt, so the loop rule becomes a first-order differential equation for q(t). Its solution with q(0) = 0 is q(t) = Cε(1 − e^{−t/RC}). The current starts at ε/R, as if the capacitor were a plain wire, and decays as I = (ε/R)e^{−t/RC}. The product τ = RC, in seconds, is the *time constant*: after one τ the charge has reached 1 − 1/e = 63.2 % of its final value Cε.

A capacitor with initial charge Q that discharges through a resistor obeys q/C − IR = 0 with I = −dq/dt, so q(t) = Qe^{−t/RC}, and the current decays in the same way. With R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 μF, τ = 1.0 s, and after 3τ only e^{−3} ≈ 5 % of the charge remains. During charging the source supplies energy Qε = Cε², while the capacitor stores ½Cε²; the other half is dissipated in the resistor, whatever the value of R. [[rc|RC circuits]] set the timing of many devices. A *flash camera* charges its capacitor slowly from a battery and discharges it through the flash tube in about a millisecond, and an RC circuit can set the interval between the pulses of a *pacemaker*.

Household wiring carries alternating current, but its hazards follow from the same relations. A *thermal hazard* arises when a wire carries more [[curr|current]] than it is rated for: the [[Pel|power]] I²R heats it and can start a fire. A *short circuit*, a path of very low [[Rres|resistance]] around the load, makes the current very large; fuses and circuit breakers open the circuit. A *shock hazard* arises when current passes through the body: about 1 mA can be felt, and about 100 mA across the chest can disrupt the heartbeat. In the *three-wire system* a ground wire connects metal cases to the Earth, so a fault trips the breaker. A *ground fault circuit interrupter* opens the circuit when the currents in the live and neutral wires differ by a few milliamperes.

Chapters 5 to 10 described [[q|charges]] at rest, the [[Efield|electric field]] they produce and the steady [[curr|currents]] that flow in circuits. Moving charges show a second interaction, magnetism. A compass needle turns near a current, and two wires carrying currents pull on or push each other. This chapter defines the magnetic field through the force it exerts on a moving charge, follows charged particles through such a field, and finds the force and torque on wires and current loops. It ends with the Hall effect and with instruments that sort charged particles. The sources of magnetic fields are the subject of Chapter 12.

A magnetized needle that can turn freely, a *compass needle*, settles along a north–south line. The end that points north is its *north magnetic pole*, and the other end its *south magnetic pole*. When two magnets are brought together, the [[F|forces]] between their [[magnet|magnetic poles]] follow a simple rule: like poles repel and unlike poles attract, more strongly the closer the poles are. Poles differ from electric charges in one essential way: they always come in pairs. A bar magnet cut in two gives two shorter magnets, each with its own north and south pole. Earth also acts as a magnet. Its magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole is in fact a south pole, which is why it attracts the north end of a compass needle.

Magnetism and electricity were long treated as separate subjects. In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted found that a current in a wire deflects a nearby compass needle, so currents have magnetic effects. Soon afterwards Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart measured how this effect falls off with distance from a wire, André-Marie Ampère showed that two [[curr|currents]] exert [[F|forces]] on each other, and François Arago and Humphry Davy magnetized iron with a current. In 1831 Michael Faraday found the converse effect: a changing magnetic influence drives a current in a closed circuit. These results underlie motors, generators and transformers, and also modern devices such as the read heads of hard drives, which use *giant magnetoresistance*, a large change in the resistance of layered metal films in a magnetic field.

A charge at rest near a magnet feels no magnetic force, but a moving charge does. Experiments fix the properties of this [[lorentzF|magnetic force]]. It is proportional to the charge q and to the speed v. It vanishes for motion along the direction in which a compass needle would point, is largest for motion perpendicular to it, and always acts perpendicular both to the [[vvec|velocity]] and to that direction. The [[cross|vector product]] F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗ summarizes all of this, with the vector B⃗ describing the magnet's influence at the position of the charge. For a positive charge the direction follows *right-hand rule-1*: point the fingers of the right hand along v⃗ and curl them toward B⃗; the thumb gives F⃗. A negative charge feels the opposite force. Since F⃗ is perpendicular to v⃗, the magnetic force does no work: it changes the direction of motion, never the speed.

The vector B⃗ defines the [[Bfield|magnetic field]]. Around a [[magnet|magnet]] its direction is mapped with a small compass, whose needle lines up with B⃗ at each point. Its magnitude is defined, as the electric field was, by the [[F|force]] on a test charge, here a moving one: B⃗ is the field for which a charge q moving at v⃗ feels the [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] q v⃗ × B⃗. The SI unit is the *tesla*, 1 T = 1 N/(A·m); the older *gauss* is 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T. Earth's field at the surface is about 5 × 10⁻⁵ T. *Magnetic field lines* are drawn tangent to B⃗ and crowded where the field is strong. Outside a magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole, and inside they continue back, so every line closes on itself. Field lines never start or end, because no isolated poles, *magnetic monopoles*, have been found.

The [[Bval|value of the field]] at one point is found by sending a test charge through that point. If a charge q moving at speed v at angle θ to the [[Bfield|field]] feels a force of magnitude F, then B = F/(qv sin θ). Conversely, a [[q|charge]] in a known field feels a magnetic [[F|force]] of magnitude qvB sin θ, directed along the [[cross|vector product]] of its [[vvec|velocity]] with B⃗. This [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] enters [[n2|Newton's second law]] like any other force, and when an electric field is also present the total force is q(E⃗ + v⃗ × B⃗). A proton moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.50 T field, for example, feels F = (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(2.0 × 10⁶ m/s)(0.50 T) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N, about 10¹³ times its weight.
eqs: F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗,  F = qvB sin θ

paragraphs.text: In a uniform field, a charge moving perpendicular to B⃗ feels a [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] of constant size qvB, always perpendicular to its velocity. This is the condition for [[circ|uniform circular motion]], with the magnetic force acting as the [[Fc|centripetal force]]: qvB = mv²/r. The charge therefore moves on a [[helix|circular orbit]] of radius r = mv/(qB), with period T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB). The period does not depend on the speed: a faster particle moves on a larger circle and returns in the same time. An electron moving at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a field of 1.0 × 10⁻³ T has r = 5.7 mm and T = 3.6 × 10⁻⁸ s. A velocity component along B⃗ feels no force and stays constant, so in general the orbit is a helix wound around a field line, *helical motion*. These results assume speeds well below c.

Earth's magnetic field guides charged particles in the same way. Fast protons and electrons from the Sun, and *cosmic rays* from beyond the solar system, move along [[helix|helical paths]] around the field lines. Many are trapped in two doughnut-shaped regions around Earth, the *Van Allen radiation belts*, where they spiral back and forth between the polar regions. Near the poles the field lines bend down into the atmosphere, so particles that follow them reach low altitudes there. Their collisions with oxygen and nitrogen make the gases emit light, the *aurorae*. Particles that arrive across the field lines are deflected instead, so the [[Bfield|magnetic field]] also shields the surface from part of this radiation.

A current in a wire is a flow of charge carriers, so a wire in a magnetic field feels the sum of the forces on its carriers. Take a straight segment of length l and cross-sectional area A, with n carriers of charge q per unit volume moving at the [[vd|drift velocity]] v⃗_d. Each carrier feels the [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] q v⃗_d × B⃗, and the segment holds nAl carriers. Since the [[curr|current]] is I = nqAv_d, the total [[F|force]] is F⃗ = I l⃗ × B⃗, where l⃗ has the length of the segment and points along the current, and the direction follows from the [[cross|vector product]]. For a curved wire or a nonuniform field, the forces dF⃗ = I dl⃗ × B⃗ on the elements are summed along the wire. A 0.50 m wire carrying 2.0 A at right angles to a 0.30 T field feels a force of 0.30 N.

A closed current loop in a uniform field feels no net force, because the forces on opposite parts cancel: the sum of I dl⃗ × B⃗ around a closed path is zero. The loop can still turn. How strongly it turns is set by its [[mu|magnetic dipole moment]], defined for a flat coil of N turns, each carrying [[curr|current]] I around an area A, as μ⃗ = NIA n̂. The area follows from the coil's [[L|lengths]], for example A = ab for a rectangle with sides a and b. The unit normal n̂ points along the thumb of the right hand when the fingers curl with the current. A coil of 50 turns and radius 2.0 cm carrying 0.40 A has μ = 50 × 0.40 A × π(0.020 m)² = 2.5 × 10⁻² A·m². A current loop is a *magnetic dipole*: it acts like a small bar magnet whose north pole lies on the side n̂ points to.

Take a rectangular loop with sides a and b in a uniform field B⃗, free to turn about an axis parallel to the sides a and perpendicular to B⃗. Those two sides feel equal and opposite forces IaB, a couple. When n̂ makes angle θ with B⃗, their lines of action are b sin θ apart, so the [[tau|torque]] is IabB sin θ = μB sin θ; the forces on the other two sides lie along the axis. In vector form the torque is the [[cross|vector product]] of the [[mu|dipole moment]] with the [[Bval|field]], and it turns μ⃗ toward B⃗. The work done against this torque gives the loop a [[U|potential energy]] U = −μ⃗·B⃗, a [[dot|scalar product]] chosen to be zero at θ = 90°. It is lowest, −μB, when μ⃗ points along B⃗, and highest, +μB, when it points against it. Both results hold for a flat loop of any shape.

The [[tau|torque]] on a current loop drives the dc electric motor. A coil turns between the poles of a magnet, and the torque μB sin θ pulls its [[mu|dipole moment]] toward the field. Once μ⃗ passes the field direction, the torque would reverse and swing the coil back. A *commutator*, a split ring with sliding contacts, reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the torque keeps the same sense and the coil keeps turning. Practical *motors* use many turns and iron cores to raise μ and B. The coil described above, with μ = 2.5 × 10⁻² A·m², feels a maximum torque of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N·m in a 0.20 T field.

In 1879 Edwin Hall found that a current-carrying strip in a magnetic field develops a voltage across its width, the *Hall effect*. Let the strip have width l and cross-sectional area A, with the [[Bval|field]] B perpendicular to its face. Carriers moving at the [[vd|drift velocity]] v_d feel a sideways [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] qv_{d}B and collect on one edge. The charge separation sets up a transverse electric field E, which grows until qE = qv_{d}B. The [[VH|Hall voltage]] is then V = El = Blv_d, or V = IBl/(neA), since I = neAv_d. Its sign shows whether the carriers are positive or negative, and its size gives their density n. In copper (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) a strip 1.0 mm thick carrying 10 A in 1.0 T gives only 0.7 μV. Semiconductors have far fewer carriers and larger Hall voltages, so the Hall probes used to measure B are made from them.

The balance in the Hall effect is one case of a general arrangement. When a uniform [[Eval|electric field]] and a uniform magnetic field are perpendicular to each other and to the velocity of a charged particle, and oriented so that their forces oppose, the net force qE⃗ + qv⃗ × B⃗ vanishes at exactly one speed, v = E/B. Particles with that speed pass straight through. Faster ones are pushed aside by the larger [[lorentzF|magnetic force]], and slower ones by the electric force. The device is a [[vsel|velocity selector]], and the speed it passes depends on neither the charge nor the mass. Fields of 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m and 0.10 T, for instance, select particles moving at 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s.

Circular orbits in a magnetic field are the basis of two instruments. In a *mass spectrometer*, ions first pass a [[vsel|velocity selector]], so all have the speed v = E/B. They then enter a second uniform field B₀, travel on a semicircle of radius R = mv/(qB₀), and strike a detector. Ions with different charge-to-mass ratios land at different places, and q/m = E/(BB₀R). In a *cyclotron*, charged particles circle in a uniform field inside two hollow D-shaped electrodes, the *dees*. An alternating voltage across the gap between the dees accelerates the particles twice per turn. Because the period 2πm/(qB) of a [[helix|circular orbit]] does not depend on speed, a fixed frequency stays in step as the orbit grows. Particles leave at the rim radius R with speed v_{max} = qBR/m, valid while v is well below c.

Chapter 11 took the magnetic field as given and found its effect on moving charges and currents. This chapter asks where the field comes from. The answer is [[curr|currents]], and moving charges in general. Two laws give the field. The Biot–Savart law adds up the contributions of small current elements, much as [[coul|Coulomb's law]] adds up point charges. Ampère's law relates the field around a closed path to the current through it, much as [[gauss|Gauss's law]] relates the electric field to the enclosed charge. Applied to wires, loops, solenoids and toroids, they give the [[Bfield|magnetic field]] of each and the force between parallel wires, and lead finally to magnetism in matter.

The [[bs|Biot–Savart law]] gives the magnetic field of a steady current. Divide a wire into elements dl⃗ that point along the [[curr|current]] I. An element contributes, at a field point a distance r away in the direction of the unit vector r̂, the field dB⃗ = (μ₀/4π) I dl⃗ × r̂/r². Like Coulomb's law it falls as the inverse square of the distance. Unlike it, the contribution is perpendicular to both dl⃗ and r̂, as the [[cross|vector product]] requires, with magnitude (μ₀/4π) I dl sin θ/r², zero along the line of the element. The constant μ₀ is the [[mu0|permeability of free space]], 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A; since 2019 it is a measured constant, equal to this value within about one part in 10⁹. Because contributions add as vectors, the [[Bfield|magnetic field]] of a whole circuit is an [[integ|integral]] along it. The law summarizes measurements on many current shapes.

Apply the [[bs|Biot–Savart law]] to a long straight wire carrying [[curr|current]] I along the x-axis, at a point a perpendicular distance R from it. An element dx at position x is a distance r = √(x² + R²) from the point, and sin θ = R/r. All elements contribute in the same direction, so the magnitudes add: B = (μ₀I/4π) ∫ R dx/(x² + R²)^{3/2}. From −∞ to ∞ the integral equals 2/R, so the [[Bwire|field of a long straight wire]] is B = μ₀I/(2πR), with [[mu0|μ₀]] the permeability of free space. The field lines are circles centred on the wire. Their sense follows a *right-hand rule*: with the thumb along the current, the fingers curl in the direction of B⃗. A wire carrying 10 A produces 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T at 5.0 cm, comparable to Earth's field. A real wire fits the result when its length is much greater than R.

Two long parallel wires a distance r apart carry currents I₁ and I₂. Wire 1 produces at the position of wire 2 the [[Bwire|field]] B₁ = μ₀I₁/(2πr), perpendicular to wire 2. Adding the [[lorentzF|magnetic forces]] on the moving carriers of wire 2, as in Section 11.4, gives a force F = I₂lB₁ on a length l of it. The [[Fpar|force between parallel currents]] per unit length is therefore μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr). By [[n3|Newton's third law]], wire 1 feels an equal and opposite force. The right-hand rules show that [[curr|currents]] in the same direction attract and currents in opposite directions repel. Two wires 1.0 cm apart, each carrying 10 A, attract with 2.0 × 10⁻³ N per metre.

The same attraction acts between parallel streams of charge within one conductor. A large current through a plasma or a liquid metal is squeezed inward by it, the *pinch effect*. Because the [[Fpar|force]] depends only on currents and distance, it once served to define the *ampere*: 1 A was the steady current that, in two long, thin parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produced a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length. Since 2019 the ampere has been fixed instead by giving the elementary charge the exact value 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the *coulomb* is the [[q|charge]] carried by 1 A in 1 s.

The [[bs|Biot–Savart law]] also gives the field of a circular loop of radius R carrying [[curr|current]] I, at a point on its axis a distance z from the centre. Every element is perpendicular to the line to that point, at distance √(z² + R²). The components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs from opposite sides, and the axial components add to the result below. At the centre it is μ₀I/(2R). An arc of angle θ contributes the fraction θ/2π of this, μ₀Iθ/(4πR). Far along the axis, z ≫ R, the field approaches μ₀μ/(2πz³), with μ = IπR² the [[mu|magnetic dipole moment]]. This inverse-cube fall-off is that of a dipole, like the field on the axis of an [[pdip|electric dipole]].

[[ampere|Ampère's law]] states the field of steady currents in another form. For any closed path, the line integral of B⃗ around it equals μ₀ times the net current I_{enc} through any surface bounded by the path. A current counts as positive if it passes in the direction of the thumb when the fingers of the right hand curl along the path. The [[Bwire|field of a long wire]] shows how this works: on a circle of radius r centred on the wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr) is tangent and constant, so the [[integ|integral]] is (μ₀I/2πr)(2πr) = μ₀I for every radius. For a path that does not enclose the wire, the contributions cancel. The general statement follows from the [[bs|Biot–Savart law]] for any steady current. It holds for every path, but it yields B only when symmetry makes B constant along a suitable path. Chapter 16 adds a term needed when electric fields change in time.

With [[symm|symmetry]], [[ampere|Ampère's law]] gives fields quickly. Inside a long straight wire of radius a whose current I is spread uniformly over its cross section, a circular path of radius r < a encloses the current Ir²/a². Then B·2πr = μ₀Ir²/a², so B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²): the field grows linearly from zero at the axis to μ₀I/(2πa) at the surface, and falls as 1/r outside. In a *coaxial cable*, a central wire and a surrounding cylindrical conductor carry equal currents in opposite directions. A path outside the cable encloses zero net current, so the field there is zero, and the cable's field stays between its conductors.

A [[solen|solenoid]] is a long wire wound into a tight helical coil, with n turns per unit length. When it is long compared with its radius, the field inside is nearly uniform and along the axis, and the field outside is nearly zero. Choose a rectangular path with one side of length l inside along the axis and the opposite side outside. Only the inside side contributes to the line integral, and the path encloses nl turns, each carrying [[curr|current]] I. [[ampere|Ampère's law]] gives Bl = μ₀nlI, so B = μ₀nI anywhere inside. Adding the axial fields of the individual turns gives the same result. A *toroid* is a solenoid bent into a ring of N turns; by [[symm|symmetry]] its field lines are circles, and a circular path of radius r inside gives B = μ₀NI/(2πr), with zero field outside. *Magnetic resonance imaging* uses large solenoids with fields of 1.5 to 3 T.

Matter responds to a magnetic field because its atoms carry [[mu|magnetic dipole moments]], from the orbital motion and the spin of their [[atom|electrons]]. If a solenoid is filled with a material, the field inside becomes B = μnI, where μ = (1 + χ)μ₀ is the permeability of the material and χ its *magnetic susceptibility*. The sum of the atomic moments in a volume decides how [[magmat|magnetic materials]] behave. In a *paramagnetic material*, such as aluminium, the atoms have permanent moments that the [[Bfield|field]] partly aligns against thermal agitation; χ is small and positive, about 2 × 10⁻⁵ for aluminium, and decreases as the temperature rises. In a *diamagnetic material*, such as copper or water, the atoms have no net moment; the applied field induces weak moments that oppose it, so χ is small and negative, about −1 × 10⁻⁵ for copper. Both responses are linear in the applied field.

In a *ferromagnetic material*, such as iron, nickel or cobalt, neighbouring atomic moments line up with each other spontaneously over regions called *magnetic domains*. In an unmagnetized sample the domains point in random directions. An applied field makes the domains aligned with it grow, so the material adds a field hundreds or thousands of times larger than the applied one; in effect χ is very large and depends on the field. The response is nonlinear and depends on history. When the applied field is removed, much of the alignment remains, which is how permanent magnets are made. A plot of magnetization against applied field traces a loop, called *hysteresis*. Above a temperature characteristic of each [[magmat|ferromagnetic material]], 1043 K for iron, thermal agitation destroys the domains and the material becomes paramagnetic.

[[curr|Currents]] produce magnetic fields, as Chapter 12 showed. The reverse question is whether a [[Bfield|magnetic field]] can produce a current. A steady field cannot: a magnet resting beside a closed wire loop drives no current. A changing field does. This is electromagnetic induction, discovered by Faraday. This chapter defines magnetic flux, states Faraday's law for the induced [[emf|emf]] and Lenz's rule for its direction, and then treats the emf of moving conductors, the electric field created by a changing magnetic field, eddy currents in bulk metal and the electric generator, the source of nearly all electric power.

Induction depends on how much field passes through a circuit. The [[PhiB|magnetic flux]] through a surface S is the [[integ|integral]] over S of the normal component of the [[Bfield|magnetic field]], Φ_m = ∫_S B⃗·n̂ dA, a sum of [[dot|scalar products]] of B⃗ with the unit normal n̂ of each area element. For a flat area A in a uniform field it reduces to Φ_m = BA cos θ, with θ the angle between B⃗ and n̂. The SI unit is the *weber*, 1 Wb = 1 T·m². The sign of the flux depends on which way n̂ is chosen. A field of 0.40 T crossing a 0.010 m² loop at 60° to its normal gives a flux of 2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb. Magnetic flux is defined like the [[PhiE|electric flux]] of Chapter 6, but through a closed surface it is always zero, since magnetic field lines close on themselves.

Faraday found in 1831 that a current appears in a closed coil while a magnet moves near it, or while the current in a nearby coil is switched on or off, but not while everything is steady. What matters is a change of flux. [[faraday|Faraday's law]] states that the *induced emf* in a circuit equals minus the [[ddt|rate of change]] of the [[PhiB|magnetic flux]] through it; for a coil of N turns, each with flux Φ_m, ε = −N dΦ_m/dt. The flux may change because B changes, because the area changes or because the circuit turns. The induced [[emf|emf]] drives a current as the emf of a battery does, but no battery is present. A 200-turn coil of area 0.010 m², in a perpendicular field that falls steadily from 0.50 T to zero in 0.10 s, has |ε| = 200 × (0.50 T × 0.010 m²)/(0.10 s) = 10 V. The minus sign gives the direction of the emf.

The direction of the induced emf is given by [[lenz|Lenz's law]]: the induced current flows so that its own magnetic field opposes the change in flux that produces it. Push the north pole of a magnet toward a loop, and the flux through the loop, directed away from the magnet, grows. The induced current makes a field toward the magnet, so the near face of the loop acts as a north pole and repels the magnet; pulling the magnet away reverses the current. This rule is the minus sign in [[faraday|Faraday's law]], and conservation of energy, as in the [[flaw|first law of thermodynamics]], requires it. If the induced current aided the change, the magnet would be drawn in faster, the current would grow further, and energy would grow without limit. Instead, the work done against the repulsion becomes electrical energy dissipated in the loop. For a loop or a solenoid, *right-hand rule 2* then gives the current: with the thumb along the induced field, the fingers curl along the current.

When a conductor moves through a magnetic field, the field acts on the charges it carries along. A metal rod of length l slides at [[speed|speed]] v along two rails, perpendicular to a uniform [[Bval|field]] B. Each carrier in the rod moves with it and feels a [[lorentzF|magnetic force]] qvB along the rod. The force per unit charge, vB, acts along the whole rod, so the work per unit charge from one end to the other is Blv. This is the [[emfmot|motional emf]], ε = Blv. If the rails are joined through a resistor R, a current ε/R flows. A rod 0.20 m long moving at 4.0 m/s in a 0.50 T field has ε = 0.40 V; with R = 2.0 Ω the current is 0.20 A.

The same result follows from [[faraday|Faraday's law]]. The rod and rails form a circuit whose area lx grows at the rate lv, so the [[PhiB|magnetic flux]] changes at dΦ_m/dt = Bl dx/dt = Blv, and the [[emfmot|motional emf]] is again Blv. By [[lenz|Lenz's law]] the current makes the field push back on the rod with a force IlB that opposes the motion. Keeping the rod at constant speed takes a force IlB = B²l²v/R, and the mechanical power supplied, B²l²v²/R, equals the electrical power ε²/R dissipated in the resistor; in the example above both are 0.080 W. A *rail gun* reverses the process: a large current through the rails and a sliding conductor produces a force IlB that accelerates the conductor. A conducting tether several kilometres long, orbiting with a satellite at about 7.7 km/s through Earth's field, develops a motional emf of the order of a kilovolt.

A loop at rest in a changing magnetic field also has an induced emf, yet no magnetic force acts on charges at rest. The force on them must be electric: a changing magnetic field creates an [[Eind|induced electric field]]. Since emf is work per unit charge around the loop, [[faraday|Faraday's law]] becomes a statement about the line [[integ|integral]] of E⃗ around any closed path, shown below. The field exists whether or not a wire is present. It is an [[Efield|electric field]] in every respect, but its circulation is not zero: its lines close on themselves, it is not conservative, and no electric potential can describe it. Inside a long solenoid of radius R whose field changes at the rate dB/dt, symmetry gives E·2πr = πr² dB/dt in magnitude at radius r < R, so E = (r/2) dB/dt. With dB/dt = 0.050 T/s, E = 1.0 × 10⁻³ V/m at r = 4.0 cm.

Faraday's law applies inside bulk metal as well as in wires. When a [[cond|conductor]] moves through a nonuniform field, or sits in a changing one, the flux through closed paths inside it changes and drives loops of current, [[eddy|eddy currents]]. By [[lenz|Lenz's law]] their fields oppose the change, so they oppose the motion that causes them. A metal plate swinging between the poles of a magnet stops within a few swings, while a plate with slots cut across it, which break the current loops, swings almost freely. This *magnetic damping* turns kinetic energy into heat in the resistance of the metal, as [[faraday|Faraday's law]] and [[ohm|Ohm's law]] together imply.

Eddy currents are useful in some devices and wasteful in others. *Braking systems* on some trains and amusement rides use them: magnets near a moving metal rail or fin produce a drag force that grows with speed and needs no contact. *Metal detectors* send an alternating or pulsed field into the ground or through a doorway; [[eddy|eddy currents]] induced in a metal object produce their own field, which a receiving coil detects. Induction cooktops heat a pan by eddy currents in its base. In transformers and motors, eddy currents waste energy as heat, so their iron cores are made of thin insulated sheets that interrupt the current loops.

An *electric generator* turns mechanical work into emf by rotating a coil in a magnetic field. Let a coil of N turns and area A turn with constant [[angvel|angular velocity]] ω in a uniform field B, about an axis perpendicular to B⃗. If its normal points along B⃗ at t = 0, the angle between them is ωt and the [[PhiB|flux]] through each turn is Φ_m = BA cos ωt. [[faraday|Faraday's law]] then gives the emf of the [[gen|generator]], ε = NBAω sin ωt, a sinusoid with *peak emf* ε₀ = NBAω. The emf is largest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where the flux is zero but changes fastest. A coil of 100 turns and area 0.020 m², turning 60 times per second in a 0.20 T field, has ω = 377 rad/s and a peak emf of 151 V. Power stations apply the same principle with turbines driven by steam, water or wind.

A motor is a generator run in reverse, and its rotating coil also produces an emf. By [[lenz|Lenz's law]] this emf opposes the applied voltage that drives the current, so it is called *back emf*. With applied voltage V, back emf ε_b and coil resistance R, the current is I = (V − ε_b)/R. When a motor starts, the coil is at rest, ε_b = 0, and the current is large. As the motor speeds up, the back emf grows in proportion to ω, and the current falls to the value needed to drive the load. A jammed or overloaded motor draws a large current and can overheat. The [[gen|generator]] and the motor are thus one device, converting energy in opposite directions.

Induction is at work in many everyday devices. In *hard drives*, a small coil in the write head magnetizes tiny regions of the spinning disk; older read heads detected the [[faraday|induced emf]] as these regions passed, while modern ones sense their field through giant magnetoresistance. Graphics tablets and some *tablet computers* locate a pen that contains a coil through induction between that coil and a grid of wires. Swiping a *credit card* moves its magnetic stripe past a pickup coil and induces a signal. *Hybrid vehicles* and electric cars brake by running their motors as [[gen|generators]], which returns energy to the battery. In *transcranial magnetic stimulation* (TMS), a brief, strong current pulse in a coil held near the head creates an [[Eind|induced electric field]] that drives currents in brain tissue and excites neurons.

Chapter 13 showed that a changing [[PhiB|magnetic flux]] induces an [[emf|emf]]. When that flux comes from a current in a circuit, a changing current induces an emf in a nearby circuit or in the circuit itself. This chapter measures the effect by inductance, finds the energy stored in a magnetic field, and adds coils to circuits with [[Rres|resistors]] and [[Cap|capacitors]]. The currents then grow and decay exponentially, as in the [[rc|RC circuit]], or oscillate like a mass on a spring. Wireless charging of a *smartphone* is one example: an alternating current in a coil in the charging pad induces an emf in a coil inside the phone.

Two coils placed near each other are coupled by their fields. A [[curr|current]] I₁ in coil 1 sends a [[PhiB|magnetic flux]] Φ₂₁ through each of the N₂ turns of coil 2, and without iron nearby this flux is proportional to I₁. The ratio M = N₂Φ₂₁/I₁ is the [[Mind|mutual inductance]] of the pair. When I₁ changes, [[faraday|Faraday's law]] gives an emf in coil 2, ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ₂₁/dt = −M dI₁/dt. The same M gives the emf in coil 1 when the current in coil 2 changes. M depends on the sizes, shapes, positions and turns of the coils, and on any magnetic material nearby. Its SI unit is the *henry*, named after Joseph Henry: 1 H = 1 Wb/A = 1 V·s/A. Coils with M = 5.0 mH and a current changing at 200 A/s have an induced emf of 1.0 V. Mutual *inductance* is used in transformers and chargers, and is a nuisance between neighbouring wires in fast electronics, such as *digital signal processing* circuits.

A coil's own field also passes through its turns. If N turns each carry flux Φ_m when the current is I, the [[Lind|self-inductance]] L is defined by NΦ_m = LI. Since the [[PhiB|flux]] changes with the [[curr|current]], [[faraday|Faraday's law]] gives an emf in the coil itself, ε = −L dI/dt. By [[lenz|Lenz's law]] this emf opposes the change: it acts against a rising current and keeps a falling one going. An *inductor* is a coil built to have a large L, and it resists sudden changes of current. If the current through a 50 mH inductor falls from 2.0 A to zero in 1.0 ms, the induced emf is 0.050 H × 2000 A/s = 100 V. This is why opening a switch in a circuit with a large inductance can draw a spark.

For a long [[solen|solenoid]] of N turns, length l and cross-sectional area A, the field B = μ₀nI with n = N/l gives a flux μ₀NIA/l through each turn. Then NΦ_m = μ₀N²AI/l, so the [[Lind|self-inductance]] is L = μ₀N²A/l, with end effects neglected. It depends only on geometry and grows as the square of the number of turns. A coil of 500 turns, 0.25 m long, with A = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m², has L = 1.26 mH; an iron core raises this greatly. Inductors have many uses. Wire loops under a road change their inductance when a car stops above them, which triggers *traffic signals*; *metal detectors* sense the change of a coil's inductance near metal; and *camera flashes* use inductors in the circuits that raise a battery's voltage.

Building up a current in an inductor takes work, because the source must push charge against the induced emf. When the [[curr|current]] is I and changes at the rate dI/dt, the source does [[W|work]] on the inductor at the rate LI dI/dt. Integrating from zero to the final current gives the [[UL|energy stored in an inductor]], U = ∫₀^{I} LI′ dI′ = ½LI², with L the [[Lind|self-inductance]]. The energy is returned when the current falls. A 0.50 H inductor carrying 4.0 A stores 4.0 J. A capacitor's energy is tied to a separation of charge; this energy is stored in the magnetic field of the current, as the next calculation shows.

Apply this to a long [[solen|solenoid]] with n turns per unit length, length l and area A. Its inductance is L = μ₀n²Al, and its field is B = μ₀nI. The stored [[UL|energy]] is then ½μ₀n²AlI² = (B²/2μ₀)Al. Dividing by the volume Al gives the [[uB|magnetic energy density]] below, with [[mu0|μ₀]] the permeability of free space. The result holds for any magnetic field in vacuum, just as the [[uE|electric energy density]] ε₀E²/2 holds for any electric field. A field of 1.0 T stores 4.0 × 10⁵ J/m³. Integrating u_B over a volume gives the energy, and through U = ½LI² the inductance. For a *coaxial cable* with inner radius R₁, outer radius R₂ and length l, the field μ₀I/(2πr) between the conductors gives U = (μ₀I²l/4π) ln(R₂/R₁), so L = (μ₀l/2π) ln(R₂/R₁).

An [[rl|RL circuit]] is a resistor R and an inductor L in series with a source of emf ε. When the switch is closed at t = 0, [[kirch|Kirchhoff's loop rule]] gives ε − IR − L dI/dt = 0, where the drop across the resistor follows [[ohm|Ohm's law]] and the [[Lind|inductor]] contributes L dI/dt. This first-order equation, with I(0) = 0, has the solution below. The current cannot jump, so it starts at zero and rises toward ε/R. The *inductive time constant* τ_L = L/R is the time to reach 1 − 1/e ≈ 63 % of the final current. If the source is then removed and the circuit closed through R alone, the current decays as I = I₀e^{−t/τ_L}. With L = 0.30 H, R = 15 Ω and ε = 12 V, τ_L = 20 ms and the final current is 0.80 A. The behaviour mirrors the [[rc|RC circuit]].

Connect a charged capacitor to an inductor, with negligible resistance. The capacitor discharges through the inductor, but the inductor keeps the current going after the capacitor is empty, so the capacitor charges again with the opposite sign, and the process repeats. [[kirch|Kirchhoff's loop rule]] for the [[Lind|inductor]] and the [[Cap|capacitance]] C gives L dI/dt + q/C = 0, and with I = dq/dt this is the equation below. Its solution is q = q₀ cos(ωt + φ) with ω = 1/√(LC), and the current is i = −ωq₀ sin(ωt + φ). This is the [[lc|LC circuit]]. Its energy q²/(2C) + Li²/2 stays equal to q₀²/(2C) and passes back and forth between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the inductor twice each period. With L = 10 mH and C = 1.0 μF, ω = 1.0 × 10⁴ rad/s and f = 1.59 kHz.

The [[lc|LC circuit]] obeys the same equation as a mass on a spring, m d²x/dt² + kx = 0, the [[sho|simple harmonic oscillator]]. The correspondence is L ↔ m, 1/C ↔ k, q ↔ x and i ↔ v. The inductor plays the role of inertia, opposing changes of current as mass opposes changes of velocity, and the capacitor plays the role of the spring. The magnetic energy Li²/2 corresponds to the kinetic energy mv²/2, the electric energy q²/(2C) to the elastic energy kx²/2, and ω = 1/√(LC) to ω = √(k/m). Every result for the mechanical oscillator carries over.

Every real circuit has resistance, which removes energy as heat. With a resistor R added in series to the [[lc|LC circuit]], [[kirch|Kirchhoff's loop rule]] gives L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = 0, where dots denote time derivatives and the [[Rres|resistance]] contributes the drop IR. For small resistance, R² < 4L/C, the charge still oscillates but with decaying amplitude, q = q₀e^{−Rt/2L} cos(ω′t + φ), with ω′ = √(1/LC − (R/2L)²) a little below the LC frequency. This is the underdamped [[rlc|RLC circuit]]. At R² = 4L/C the circuit is critically damped and returns to zero charge fastest without oscillating. For R² > 4L/C it is overdamped, and the charge decays more slowly, again without oscillation.

The comparison with mechanics extends to damping. A [[damp|damped oscillator]], m ẍ + bẋ + kx = 0, has the same form as the [[rlc|RLC circuit]], with the resistance R in the place of the damping coefficient b. Both amplitudes decay as e^{−t/τ}, with τ = 2m/b in one case and τ = 2L/R in the other, and both show the same three damping regimes. Take L = 10 mH, C = 1.0 μF and R = 20 Ω. Then R/2L = 1.0 × 10³ s⁻¹, so ω′ = √(1.0 × 10⁸ − 1.0 × 10⁶) s⁻¹ = 9.95 × 10³ rad/s, only 0.5 % below 1/√(LC). Critical damping would need R = √(4L/C) = 200 Ω.

A rotating coil gives a sinusoidal emf, as the [[gen|generator]] showed, and nearly all electric power is generated and distributed in this form. This chapter studies circuits driven by such sources. Resistors, capacitors and inductors respond differently to a sinusoidal voltage: capacitors and inductors shift the current in time relative to the voltage and oppose it by amounts that depend on frequency. Rotating vectors handle these shifts. The [[rlc|RLC circuit]] of Chapter 14, now driven, shows resonance like a [[forced|driven oscillator]]. The chapter ends with power in ac circuits and with transformers, which make long-distance transmission practical.

A battery drives *direct current* (dc), which flows in one direction only. A generator produces a voltage v = V₀ sin ωt that reverses its sign periodically; V₀ is the peak voltage, or amplitude, and ω = 2πf is the [[omega|angular frequency]] for the [[freq|frequency]] f. Power grids use f = 50 Hz in most of the world and 60 Hz in North America. The sinusoid comes directly from the [[gen|generator]], whose coil turns at constant ω, and such a source is an [[acsrc|alternating source]]. Connected across a resistor R, this *ac voltage* drives an *ac current* i = I₀ sin ωt with I₀ = V₀/R. In a resistor, current and voltage reach their peaks together: they are in phase. A current whose direction reverses periodically is called *alternating current* (ac).

Sinusoids of one frequency are handled with [[phasor|phasors]]. A phasor is a vector of length A that rotates counterclockwise at angular frequency ω; its projection on the vertical axis is A sin(ωt + φ), where φ is its angle at t = 0. This is the reference circle that related simple harmonic motion to [[circ|uniform circular motion]]. Two sinusoids of the same frequency keep a fixed angle between their phasors, and their sum is the projection of the [[vadd|vector sum]] of the phasors. Adding voltages that differ in phase thus becomes vector addition in a *phasor diagram*. For a [[Rres|resistor]], the current and voltage phasors point in the same direction: they are in phase, and V₀ = I₀R.

For a capacitor C across the source v = V₀ sin ωt, the charge is q = Cv, so the current is i = dq/dt = ωCV₀ cos ωt = I₀ sin(ωt + π/2). The current leads the voltage by 90°: it peaks a quarter cycle earlier, when the capacitor is uncharged and charging fastest. The ratio of peak voltage to peak current is the [[XC|capacitive reactance]], X_C = V₀/I₀ = 1/(ωC), measured in ohms. It depends on the frequency of the [[acsrc|ac source]] and on the [[Cap|capacitance]]: a capacitor blocks dc (X_C → ∞ as ω → 0) and passes high frequencies easily. A 10 μF capacitor at 60 Hz has X_C = 265 Ω.

Meters for alternating current read root-mean-square values. The power dissipated in a resistor is i²R = I₀²R sin²ωt, and since sin²ωt averages to ½ over a cycle, the average power is ½I₀²R. A steady current I_{rms} = I₀/√2 would deliver the same power; this is the *rms current*. In the same way the *rms voltage* of an [[acsrc|ac source]] is V_{rms} = V₀/√2, the square root of the mean of v². With these [[rms|rms values]], the average power in a resistor is I_{rms}²R = V_{rms}²/R, of the same form as the dc [[Pel|electric power]]. Mains voltage is quoted as an rms value: 230 V rms has a peak of 325 V.

For an [[Lind|inductor]] L across the [[acsrc|ac source]], the voltage is v = L di/dt. With v = V₀ sin ωt, integration gives i = −(V₀/ωL) cos ωt = I₀ sin(ωt − π/2). The current lags the voltage by 90°: it peaks a quarter cycle later, because the emf of the inductor opposes each change of current. The ratio of peak voltage to peak current is the [[XL|inductive reactance]], X_L = V₀/I₀ = ωL, also in ohms. It grows with frequency, so an inductor passes dc and low frequencies and opposes high ones. A 0.10 H inductor at 60 Hz has X_L = 37.7 Ω. Reactances relate peak values only; since current and voltage are out of phase, they do not relate v and i at each instant as a resistance does.

In an *RLC series circuit* driven by v = V₀ sin ωt, the same current i = I₀ sin(ωt − φ) flows through the resistor, the inductor and the capacitor. The voltage across the [[Rres|resistance]] has amplitude I₀R and is in phase with i. The voltage across the inductor has amplitude I₀X_L, set by the [[XL|inductive reactance]], and leads i by 90°; the voltage across the capacitor has amplitude I₀X_C, set by the [[XC|capacitive reactance]], and lags i by 90°. These voltages add as [[phasor|phasors]]. The inductor and capacitor phasors point in opposite directions and combine to I₀(X_L − X_C), at right angles to I₀R. The source amplitude is therefore V₀ = I₀√(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) = I₀Z, which defines the [[Zimp|impedance]] Z. The *phase angle* φ by which the current lags the source voltage satisfies tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.

The relation I₀ = V₀/Z is the ac form of Ohm's law; it holds for peak values and equally for rms values. Take R = 40 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω. Then Z = √(40² + 30²) Ω = 50 Ω and φ = tan⁻¹(30/40) = 36.9°. A source of amplitude 100 V drives a current of amplitude 2.0 A that lags the voltage by 36.9°. When X_L > X_C the circuit is mainly inductive and φ is positive; when X_C > X_L it is mainly capacitive, φ is negative, and the current leads. Because the reactances depend on ω, the [[Zimp|impedance]] and the phase angle change with the source frequency.

The instantaneous power delivered by the source is p = iv = I₀V₀ sin(ωt − φ) sin ωt. Expanding sin(ωt − φ) = sin ωt cos φ − cos ωt sin φ and averaging over a cycle, the term in sin²ωt gives ½ and the term in sin ωt cos ωt gives zero. The [[Pac|average power]] is therefore ½I₀V₀ cos φ, or I_{rms} V_{rms} cos φ in [[rms|rms values]]. The factor cos φ is the *power factor*. From the phasor diagram of the [[Zimp|impedance]], cos φ = R/Z, so the average power equals I_{rms}²R, the [[Pel|electric power]] dissipated in the resistor alone. The inductor and capacitor store energy during part of each cycle and return it to the source during another. For the circuit above, cos φ = 0.80 and the average power is 80 W.
