A low power factor means a larger current, and larger losses in supply lines, for the same power delivered.

Since I_{rms} = V_{rms}/Z, the current in a driven [[rlc|RLC circuit]] is largest when the [[Zimp|impedance]] is smallest. Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) has its minimum, R, when X_L = X_C, that is, when ωL = 1/(ωC). This defines the *resonant frequency* ω₀ = 1/√(LC), the frequency at which the undamped [[lc|LC circuit]] oscillates on its own. At [[acres|resonance]] the reactances cancel, the circuit behaves as a pure resistance, the current is in phase with the voltage, and the average power reaches its maximum, V_{rms}²/R. Tuning a radio means adjusting a capacitor until ω₀ matches the frequency of the wanted station.

A plot of average power against ω has a peak at ω₀. Its *bandwidth* Δω is the full width of the peak at half the maximum power, and the *quality factor* Q = ω₀/Δω measures its sharpness. For a series circuit Δω = R/L, so Q = ω₀L/R: a small resistance gives a tall, narrow peak. With L = 10 mH, C = 1.0 μF and R = 20 Ω, ω₀ = 1.0 × 10⁴ rad/s, Q = 5.0 and Δω = 2.0 × 10³ rad/s. The same curve describes a [[forced|driven oscillator]] with damping. The circuit equation L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = V₀ sin ωt has the form of m ẍ + bẋ + kx = F₀ sin ωt, so electrical and mechanical [[acres|resonance]] are one phenomenon.

A [[transf|transformer]] changes the amplitude of an alternating voltage. Two coils, a primary of N_P turns and a secondary of N_S turns, are wound on a common iron core that guides nearly all the flux of one coil through the other, so their [[Mind|mutual inductance]] is large. An [[acsrc|alternating current]] in the primary produces a changing flux Φ in the core, and by [[faraday|Faraday's law]] every turn of either coil has the same emf, −dΦ/dt. Hence V_P = −N_P dΦ/dt and V_S = −N_S dΦ/dt, which gives the *transformer equation* below. In an ideal transformer, without resistance or flux leakage, the power taken by the primary equals the power delivered by the secondary, so I_S/I_P = N_P/N_S. A *step-up transformer* has N_S > N_P and raises the voltage; a *step-down transformer* lowers it. A steady current gives no changing flux, so transformers work only with ac.

Transformers make long-distance power transmission efficient. To deliver power P at voltage V, *transmission lines* must carry the current I = P/V, and they lose I²R_{line} = P²R_{line}/V² as heat. Raising V by a factor of 20 reduces the loss by a factor of 400. Delivering 10 MW through lines of total resistance 5.0 Ω at 10 kV would need 1000 A and lose 5.0 MW, half the [[Pel|power]]. At 200 kV the current is 50 A and the loss is 12.5 kW, about 0.1 %. Power stations therefore use step-up [[transf|transformers]] to raise the voltage to hundreds of kilovolts, and step-down transformers near the users reduce it to the mains voltage.

The field laws so far are [[gauss|Gauss's law]] for the electric field, [[faraday|Faraday's law]] and [[ampere|Ampère's law]]. Ampère's law, however, fails when electric fields change in time. This chapter presents the correction made by James Clerk Maxwell, which completes the laws of electromagnetism. The completed laws predict [[wave|waves]] of electric and magnetic field that travel through empty space at the [[c|speed of light]], and light is such a wave. These waves carry energy and momentum, and their momentum exerts a pressure; it pushes the dust tails of comets, such as Comet McNaught in 2007, away from the Sun. The chapter ends with the full spectrum of electromagnetic waves.

[[ampere|Ampère's law]] relates the field around a closed path to the current through any surface bounded by the path. Apply it to a path around the wire leading to a charging capacitor. A flat surface is crossed by the wire and gives μ₀I. A surface that bulges between the plates is crossed by no conduction current and gives zero, although the path is the same. Between the plates, however, the [[PhiE|electric flux]] Φ_E = q/ε₀ grows, and the [[eps0|permittivity of free space]] ε₀ times its [[ddt|rate of change]] equals dq/dt = I. Maxwell therefore added the [[Id|displacement current]] I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt to the conduction current in Ampère's law. With this term every surface gives the same answer, in agreement with [[qcons|conservation of charge]]. A changing electric field now produces a magnetic field, as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. The corrected law completes [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]].

With this correction the field laws take their complete form. [[gauss|Gauss's law]] states that the electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀. Gauss's law for magnetism states that the flux of the [[Bfield|magnetic field]] through any closed surface is zero, because field lines close and there are no monopoles. [[faraday|Faraday's law]] relates the circulation of E⃗ to the changing magnetic flux. The Ampère–Maxwell law relates the circulation of B⃗ to the current plus the [[Id|displacement current]], correcting [[ampere|Ampère's law]]. These four laws are [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]]. Together with the *Lorentz force* F⃗ = q(E⃗ + v⃗ × B⃗), which the fields exert on charges, they contain all of classical electromagnetism.

Maxwell's equations treat the electric and magnetic fields as one system, the [[EB|electromagnetic field]]. Its state at a given time is the pair of fields E⃗ and B⃗ at every point, and [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]] give how that state evolves: a changing [[Bfield|magnetic field]] produces a circulating [[Efield|electric field]], and a changing electric field produces a circulating magnetic field. The static fields of earlier chapters are special cases in which nothing changes and the two fields separate. Maxwell saw that this mutual production allows a self-sustaining disturbance to travel through empty space. Thomas Young's interference experiments had already shown light to be a wave. In the late 1880s Heinrich Hertz produced electromagnetic waves with spark circuits, detected them across a room, and showed that they reflect, refract and interfere like light.

Consider empty space, with no charges or currents, and look for fields that depend only on x and t. Gauss's laws then require any field component along x to be uniform, so it carries no wave: the wave is transverse. Take E⃗ along y and B⃗ along z. Faraday's law applied to a thin rectangle in the xy-plane gives ∂E_y/∂x = −∂B_z/∂t, and the Ampère–Maxwell law applied to a rectangle in the xz-plane gives −∂B_z/∂x = ε₀μ₀ ∂E_y/∂t. Differentiating the first with respect to x and using the second yields the [[waveeq|linear wave equation]] below, so [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]] let the [[EB|electromagnetic field]] carry waves. The [[emwave|plane electromagnetic wave]] E_y = E₀ sin(kx − ωt), B_z = B₀ sin(kx − ωt) solves both equations if B₀ = E₀/c. The fields are in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, and E⃗ × B⃗ points along that direction.

Comparing this equation with the wave equation for a string, ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t², gives the speed of the [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] in terms of two constants measured in electric and magnetic experiments, [[eps0|ε₀]] and [[mu0|μ₀]]: c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). With ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²) and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, this is 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, the measured [[c|speed of light]]. Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. At every point and time the fields of the wave satisfy E = cB. Such waves are produced by accelerated charges, for instance by an oscillating current in a *dipole antenna*, two straight conductors fed at the centre. A *half-wave antenna*, of total length λ/2, resonates at the wavelength λ. A receiving antenna works in reverse: the electric field of the wave drives currents along a rod parallel to it.

An electromagnetic wave carries energy in its fields. The *energy density* is the sum of the [[uE|electric energy density]] ε₀E²/2 and the [[uB|magnetic energy density]] B²/(2μ₀). In the [[emwave|wave]], B = E/c and c² = 1/(ε₀μ₀), so B²/(2μ₀) = ε₀E²/2: the two parts are equal and the total is u = ε₀E². This energy moves at the speed c. In a time dt, the energy in a box of cross-section A and length c dt crosses A, so the *energy flux*, the power per unit area, is S = cu = cε₀E² = EB/μ₀. Its direction is that of propagation, given by the [[cross|vector product]] E⃗ × B⃗, so the flux is the [[Spoynt|Poynting vector]] S⃗ = E⃗ × B⃗/μ₀, measured in W/m². It oscillates in time with the fields.

The fields oscillate far too fast for an instrument to follow, so what is measured is the [[Iint|intensity]], the time average of the magnitude of the [[Spoynt|Poynting vector]]. Since the average of sin² is ½, I = S_{avg} = cε₀E₀²/2 = cB₀²/(2μ₀) = E₀B₀/(2μ₀). Sunlight above the atmosphere has an intensity of about 1.36 kW/m², which corresponds to E₀ = √(2I/(cε₀)) = 1.01 × 10³ V/m and B₀ = E₀/c = 3.37 × 10⁻⁶ T. In this wave picture the energy depends on the field amplitude and not on the frequency. Volume 3 shows that light is also absorbed in quanta whose energy is proportional to the frequency, which the wave picture does not explain.

Electromagnetic waves also carry momentum. When a wave falls on an absorber, its electric field sets charges moving along E⃗, and the magnetic force qv⃗ × B⃗ on these moving charges points along the direction of propagation. Maxwell's theory shows that absorbed energy U brings [[p|momentum]] U/c. Momentum delivered per unit area per unit time is a pressure, so with the energy flux given by the [[Spoynt|Poynting vector]], the [[prad|radiation pressure]] on a full absorber is p = I/c, where c is the [[c|speed of light]]. A perfect reflector reverses the momentum and feels twice this, 2I/c. For sunlight at Earth, I/c = (1360 W/m²)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ Pa. This is small, but in space it acts continuously: it pushes the dust of *comets* into tails pointing away from the Sun, and it can propel a *light sail*. A perfectly reflecting sail of 1.0 × 10⁴ m² facing the Sun near Earth feels a force of 0.091 N.

[[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]] place no limit on the frequency of a wave. [[emwave|Electromagnetic waves]] of every frequency travel in vacuum at the [[c|speed of light]], and the relation v = fλ between [[vwave|wave speed]], frequency and wavelength gives λ = c/f. The [[spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]] is the whole range of these waves, divided into named bands that differ in how the waves are produced and detected, not in their nature. *Radio waves*, with wavelengths from about a metre up to kilometres, are emitted by oscillating currents in antennas and carry radio and *television* broadcasts; FM radio at 100 MHz has λ = 3.00 m. *Microwaves*, from about 1 mm to 1 m, come from electronic oscillators. They carry *cell phone*, *WiFi* and *Bluetooth* signals and are used in *radar* and in microwave ovens, which work at 2.45 GHz with λ = 12.2 cm.

Shorter wavelengths give the bands most familiar from heat and light. *Infrared radiation*, from about 760 nm to 1 mm, is emitted through the *thermal agitation* of molecules; every object emits it, and a body near room [[temp|temperature]] emits most strongly near 10 μm. *Visible light*, from about 380 nm (violet) to 760 nm (red), is emitted by hot objects such as the Sun and by electrons changing their state in atoms, and is the narrow band the eye detects. *Ultraviolet radiation*, from about 10 nm to 380 nm, causes sunburn and is largely absorbed by ozone in the upper atmosphere. *X-rays*, roughly 0.01 nm to 10 nm, are produced when fast electrons strike a target and are used in medical imaging. *Gamma rays* (γ rays), the shortest, come from nuclear processes. All of these bands make up one continuous [[spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]].

Volume 2 ended with light as an [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] that travels through vacuum at the speed [[c|c]]. This chapter follows light as it meets matter. In a uniform material light travels more slowly and in straight lines, so for most purposes it can be traced as rays. At a boundary a ray is partly reflected and partly refracted, and both effects obey simple rules for the angles. The same rules explain total internal reflection and the separation of colours by a prism. The chapter closes with two properties that rays cannot describe: the wave construction of Huygens, and polarization, the direction in which the electric field of light oscillates.

Light needs no medium. In vacuum all electromagnetic radiation travels at the [[c|speed of light]], c = 2.997 924 58 × 10⁸ m/s, a value now fixed exactly by the definition of the metre. Ole Roemer first estimated it in 1676 from the timing of eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io. Fizeau in 1849 and later Foucault measured it on Earth with a toothed wheel and a rotating mirror, and Michelson refined the rotating-mirror method. In matter light is slower. The [[nidx|index of refraction]] of a medium compares the two speeds, n = c/v, where v is the [[vwave|wave speed]] of light in the medium. Since v ≤ c, n ≥ 1: n = 1.000 293 for air at standard conditions, 1.33 for water and about 1.5 for glass. In water, v = c/1.33 = 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s.

Light reaches a point from its source in three ways: directly through vacuum or air, through a transparent medium such as glass, or after reflection from a surface. In each case, as long as the medium is uniform, the energy travels along straight lines called rays. The [[raymod|ray model of light]] describes light by these paths alone, which bend or split only at boundaries; it is the basis of geometric optics. It approximates the [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] and holds when mirrors, lenses and openings are much larger than the [[lam|wavelength]], about 0.5 µm for visible light. When an opening is comparable to the wavelength, light spreads beyond the straight-line shadow and the ray picture fails; Chapters 3 and 4 treat those cases.

Angles at a surface are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it. The [[reflect|law of reflection]] states that a ray leaves a smooth surface at the same angle to the normal as it arrives, θ_r = θ_i, and that the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in one plane. Within the [[raymod|ray model]] this is an empirical rule, tested with mirrors and polished metals. A rough surface obeys the same law at each small patch, but the patches face in many directions, so a parallel beam leaves in all directions as *diffused light*; that is why a printed page can be read from any angle. Three mutually perpendicular mirrors form a *corner reflector*, which returns any ray parallel to its incoming direction; such reflectors are used on bicycles and were placed on the Moon for laser ranging.

A ray that crosses the boundary between two media changes direction. This is refraction. The [[snell|law of refraction]], or Snell’s law after Willebrord Snell, relates the angles θ₁ and θ₂ of the incident and refracted rays, both measured from the normal, to the [[nidx|indices of refraction]] of the two media: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Like the law of reflection, it is an empirical rule of the [[raymod|ray model]], and it holds for either direction of travel. A ray entering a medium of higher index bends toward the normal; a ray entering a medium of lower index bends away from it. Light passing from air (n = 1.00) into water (n = 1.33) at θ₁ = 45.0° has sin θ₂ = 0.707/1.33 = 0.532, so θ₂ = 32.1°. At normal incidence the ray goes straight through.

When light passes into a medium of lower index, n₁ > n₂, the refracted ray bends away from the normal, and θ₂ reaches 90° before θ₁ does. Setting θ₂ = 90° in the [[snell|law of refraction]] gives the [[thetac|critical angle]], sin θ_c = n₂/n₁. For θ₁ > θ_c no refracted ray exists and all the light returns into the first medium. This is total internal reflection. For glass (n = 1.50) in air θ_c = 41.8°, and for diamond (n = 2.42) θ_c = 24.4°, so light inside cut *diamonds* is reflected many times before it escapes, which makes them sparkle. In *fiber optics*, light travels along a thin glass core surrounded by a *cladding* of slightly lower index and stays inside by repeated total internal reflection. Bundles of fibres carry images in an *endoscope*, and single fibres carry signals of *high bandwidth* over long distances with little loss.

The [[nidx|index of refraction]] of a material is not a single number: it depends on the [[lam|wavelength]] of the light. This [[dispn|dispersion]], n = n(λ), is a measured property of each material. In glass and water n decreases slowly with wavelength across the visible range, so violet light is refracted more than red; in a typical glass n is about one percent larger at 400 nm than at 700 nm. A prism therefore spreads white light into its colours. A *rainbow* forms in the same way in raindrops. Sunlight is refracted on entering a drop, reflected from its back surface and refracted again on leaving, and each colour emerges most strongly at its own angle from the direction opposite the Sun: about 42° for red and about 40° for violet, so red lies on the outside of the bow. Dispersion is useful in spectrometers but harmful in lenses and optical fibres, where it blurs images and spreads pulses.

Rays describe where light goes but not why. The wave description, called wave optics, rests on [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]]: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread forward at the local [[vwave|wave speed]] v, and the wavefront a time Δt later is the surface tangent to all the wavelets, their envelope. The principle applies to any [[wave|wave]]. It follows from the [[superp|superposition principle]]: the disturbance at a later time is the sum of the wavelets, and they reinforce one another only along the envelope. At the edge of an obstacle or opening there are no neighbouring wavelets to cancel the sideways spread, so the wave bends into the geometric shadow. This bending is diffraction, and it is noticeable only when the opening is not much larger than the wavelength.

Huygens’s construction recovers both laws of geometric optics. In reflection, the incident and reflected wavelets travel in the same medium at the same speed, so in a time Δt the edge of the incoming wavefront and the first reflected wavelet cover the same distance vΔt. The two right triangles built on the mirror are congruent, which gives the [[reflect|law of reflection]], θ_r = θ_i. In refraction, the wavelets in the second medium travel at v₂ while the incoming front advances at v₁. Over a length w of the boundary, sin θ₁ = v₁Δt/w and sin θ₂ = v₂Δt/w, so sin θ₁/v₁ = sin θ₂/v₂. With v = c/n this is the [[snell|law of refraction]]. The wavefront turns because the [[vwave|wave speed]] changes, so [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]] explains why the index of refraction sets the bending.

An [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] is transverse: its electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel. The [[pol|polarization]] of light is the direction of its electric field within that perpendicular plane, called the direction of polarization. Only transverse waves can be polarized in this sense; a longitudinal wave such as sound has only one direction of oscillation. Light whose field stays along one line is polarized, for example vertically polarized or horizontally polarized relative to the ground. Light from the Sun or a lamp is unpolarized: it comes from many independent atoms, and its direction of polarization changes randomly in time. Sunlight scattered by air molecules is partly polarized, most strongly at 90° from the Sun, because the oscillating molecular dipoles do not radiate along their own axis.

A polarizing filter transmits only the component of the electric field along its axis. If polarized light with field amplitude E₀ meets a filter whose axis makes an angle θ with the [[pol|direction of polarization]], the transmitted amplitude is E = E₀ cos θ. The [[Iint|intensity]] is proportional to the square of the field amplitude, so the transmitted intensity is I = I₀ cos²θ. This is [[malus|Malus’s law]]. Unpolarized light averages cos²θ over all directions and loses half its intensity in the first filter. Two filters with axes 60.0° apart therefore pass (1/2)(cos 60.0°)² = 1/8 of the incident unpolarized intensity, and crossed filters pass none. *Liquid crystal displays (LCDs)* use this effect: between crossed filters, a liquid crystal layer rotates the direction of polarization and lets light through, unless a voltage across the layer stops the rotation.

Reflection also polarizes light. At one angle of incidence the reflected light is completely polarized parallel to the surface. This [[brewster|Brewster’s angle]] θ_b is reached when the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, θ_b + θ₂ = 90°. Then sin θ₂ = cos θ_b, and the [[snell|law of refraction]] n₁ sin θ_b = n₂ cos θ_b gives Brewster’s law, tan θ_b = n₂/n₁. The cause is that the dipoles in the second medium oscillate along the refracted field; for [[pol|polarization]] in the plane of incidence they would point along the reflected ray, and a dipole does not radiate along its axis. For reflection from water, θ_b = tan⁻¹ 1.33 = 53.1°. Some materials are *optically active* and rotate the direction of polarization; others are *birefringent*, with an index that depends on polarization. *Optical stress analysis* places a transparent model between crossed filters, where stress-induced birefringence shows as coloured fringes.

Chapter 1 gave the rules for a single ray at a surface. This chapter applies them to many rays at once to explain how mirrors and lenses form images. Rays leaving one point of an object are followed through each [[reflect|reflection]] or [[snell|refraction]]; the point where they meet again, or from which they appear to diverge, is the image of that point. For rays close to the axis the geometry reduces to one equation that locates the image and one that gives its size. The same two equations then describe the eye, the camera, the magnifier, the microscope and the telescope.

An optical [[image|image]] of a point is the point where rays from it meet after reflection or refraction, or the point from which they appear to come. If the rays actually converge there, it is a real image and can be caught on a screen. If they only appear to diverge from it, it is a virtual image, which can be seen but not projected. A plane mirror forms a virtual image. By the [[reflect|law of reflection]], each ray from an object point leaves the mirror as if from a point the same distance behind it on the same normal, and tracing the reflected rays back in the [[raymod|ray model]] shows that all of them pass through that point. With the object distance d_o positive in front of the mirror and the image distance d_i negative behind it, d_i = −d_o. The image is upright, the same size as the object, and reversed front to back.

A curved mirror is usually part of a sphere of radius R. It is a concave mirror if it reflects on the inside of the sphere and a convex mirror if it reflects on the outside. The optical axis is the line through the centre of curvature and the centre of the mirror, its vertex. Rays parallel to the axis are reflected through the focal point, or appear to come from it, at a focal length f = R/2 from the vertex. This holds only for rays close to the axis, where the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ is valid. Applying the [[reflect|law of reflection]] at the spherical surface within that approximation shows that all rays from one object point meet at one [[image|image]] point, located by the [[mirroreq|mirror equation]]. By convention f > 0 for concave and f < 0 for convex mirrors, and d_o > 0 for a real object and d_i > 0 for a real image.

Images are also located by ray tracing with a few principal rays from the top of the object: a ray parallel to the axis is reflected through the focal point, a ray through the focal point is reflected parallel to the axis, and a ray that strikes the vertex is reflected symmetrically about the axis. That last ray forms two similar triangles, one with the object height h_o and one with the image height h_i, and gives the linear [[mag|magnification]] m = h_i/h_o = −d_i/d_o. Together with the [[mirroreq|mirror equation]] it fixes the size and orientation of the [[image|image]]: m < 0 means inverted, and |m| > 1 means enlarged. For a concave mirror with f = 10.0 cm and an object 30.0 cm away, 1/d_i = 1/(10.0 cm) − 1/(30.0 cm), so d_i = 15.0 cm and m = −0.500: a real, inverted image half the size of the object.

The [[mirroreq|mirror equation]] is exact only for rays very close to the axis. Rays that strike a spherical mirror far from the axis violate sin θ ≈ θ and cross the axis slightly closer to the mirror than the focal point, so the image of a point becomes a small blur. Such departures from ideal imaging are called [[aberr|aberrations]]. This one is spherical aberration. Coma is the comet-shaped blur of points away from the axis, and there are others. Aberrations are reduced by a stop that blocks the rays far from the axis, at the cost of light, or by surfaces that are not spherical: a parabolic mirror brings all rays parallel to its axis to a single focus.

A single spherical boundary between media of indices n₁, on the object side, and n₂ also forms images. Applying the [[snell|law of refraction]] at the surface in its small-angle form, n₁θ₁ ≈ n₂θ₂, with the same geometry as for the mirror, sends every paraxial ray from an object point through one [[image|image]] point. The result for [[refrsurf|refraction at a curved surface]] is n₁/d_o + n₂/d_i = (n₂ − n₁)/R, with R > 0 when the centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side. The surface has two foci: the first focus, or object focus, at d_o = n₁R/(n₂ − n₁), and the second focus, or image focus, at d_i = n₂R/(n₂ − n₁). For a flat surface R → ∞ and d_i = −(n₂/n₁)d_o, a virtual image at the apparent depth. A stone 1.00 m deep in water (n₁ = 1.33), seen from above in air, appears 1.00 m/1.33 = 0.752 m deep.

A lens is a piece of glass or plastic with two refracting surfaces. A lens thicker at the centre, convex in shape, bends parallel rays together and is a converging lens; a lens thinner at the centre, concave in shape, spreads them apart and is a diverging lens. Thin lenses are those whose thickness is small compared with the radii and with the object and image distances; this is the thin-lens approximation. The result for [[refrsurf|refraction at a curved surface]] is then applied twice: the image formed by the first surface is the object of the second, and the two equations add. The outcome is the [[thinlens|thin-lens]] equation, of the same form as the mirror equation, with the focal length given by the lens maker’s equation for a lens of index n₂ in a medium of index n₁.

The sign conventions follow those of the mirror: f > 0 for a converging and f < 0 for a diverging lens, d_i > 0 for a real image on the far side of the lens, and m = −d_i/d_o. Parallel rays meet in the focal plane, a distance f from the lens. In ray tracing, a ray parallel to the axis leaves through the far focal point of a converging lens, or as if from the near focal point of a diverging lens; a ray through the centre goes straight on. A glass [[thinlens|thin lens]] (n₂ = 1.50) in air with R₁ = 20.0 cm and R₂ = −20.0 cm has 1/f = 0.50 × 2/(20.0 cm), so f = 20.0 cm. An object 60.0 cm away then gives d_i = 30.0 cm and m = −0.500. Because of [[dispn|dispersion]], a single lens focuses different colours at slightly different points; these are chromatic aberrations.

Light enters the eye through the cornea, which does most of the bending, and then passes through the lens to the retina, where receptor cells record the image. The distance from lens to retina is fixed, about 2.0 cm, so [[eye|the eye]] focuses on objects at different distances by changing the shape, and with it the focal length, of its lens. This is accommodation. The far point is the greatest distance at which an object is seen sharply, normally infinity; the near point is the closest, normally about 25 cm in young adults and farther with age. In nearsightedness, or myopia, the eye converges light too strongly, so the far point is at a finite distance. In farsightedness, or hyperopia, it converges light too weakly, so the near point is too far away. Both are corrected by a lens in front of the eye.

The strength of a lens is expressed by its [[Popt|optical power]] P = 1/f, measured in diopters, 1 D = 1 m⁻¹. For [[thinlens|thin lenses]] in contact the powers add, P_{total} = P₁ + P₂ + …, because each lens acts on the image formed by the one before. The [[eye|eye]] is then a thin lens of variable power with the image distance fixed at the retina, 1/d_o + 1/d_{retina} = P_{eye}. With d_{retina} = 2.00 cm, a distant object needs P_{eye} = 50.0 D and an object at 25.0 cm needs 54.0 D, so normal accommodation spans about 4 D. A myopic eye with far point 0.500 m is corrected by a diverging lens of −2.0 D, which forms virtual images of distant objects at 0.500 m. A hyperopic eye with near point 1.00 m needs +3.0 D, which places the image of an object at 25 cm at 1.00 m. Both values neglect the distance between lens and eye.

Cameras form a real, inverted, reduced image of a scene on a light-sensitive surface. The lens system acts as a converging [[thinlens|thin lens]], and for a distant object the [[image|image]] lies almost in the focal plane. To focus on nearer objects the lens is moved away from the sensor: a lens of focal length 50.0 mm focused on an object 2.00 m away needs d_i = 51.3 mm, 1.3 mm more than for an object at infinity. An adjustable aperture sets how much light reaches the sensor. In a digital camera the sensor is a charge-coupled device (CCD) or a similar chip, an array of millions of pixels in which absorbed light frees electric charge that is read out pixel by pixel.

How large an object looks depends on the angle it subtends at the eye. Without help, the largest useful angle comes from holding the object at the near point of the [[eye|eye]], 25 cm. A simple magnifier, or magnifying glass, is a converging [[thinlens|thin lens]] with the object inside its focal length; it forms an enlarged virtual image that the eye can focus on. Its [[Mang|angular magnification]] is M = θ_{image}/θ_{object}, where θ_{object} is the angle the object subtends at 25 cm. For small angles, a lens of focal length f held a distance ℓ from the eye, with the image a distance L from the eye, gives M = (25 cm/L)(1 + (L − ℓ)/f). With the lens at the eye and the image at the near point, M = 1 + 25 cm/f, the largest value; with the image at infinity, M = 25 cm/f. A lens with f = 5.00 cm gives M from 5.0 to 6.0.

A [[instr|compound microscope]] uses two converging lenses. The objective, of short focal length, forms a real, enlarged image of a nearby object; the eyepiece, used as a simple magnifier, views that image. The image of the objective is the object of the eyepiece, so with each lens treated as a [[thinlens|thin lens]] the net magnification is the product of the objective's linear [[mag|magnification]] and the eyepiece's [[Mang|angular magnification]], M_{net} = m^{obj} M^{eye}. For the final image at the near point, and with the object just outside the objective's focal point so that d_o^{obj} ≈ f^{obj}, this gives M_{net} ≈ −d_i^{obj}(f^{eye} + 25 cm)/(f^{obj} f^{eye}). An objective with f^{obj} = 0.400 cm that forms its image 16.0 cm away, used with an eyepiece of f^{eye} = 2.50 cm, gives M_{net} ≈ −(16.0)(27.5)/(0.400 × 2.50) = −440. A refracting telescope also has two lenses, but its objective forms a real image of a distant object near its focal plane, and the angular magnification is −f^{obj}/f^{eye}.

Telescopes gather light from distant objects. Galileo turned a two-lens telescope to the sky in 1609 and soon found moons orbiting Jupiter. Large lenses sag and suffer chromatic aberrations, so most large telescopes use a concave mirror as the objective; Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope. In the Newtonian design a small flat mirror sends the light out through the side of the tube to the eyepiece. In the Cassegrain design a small convex mirror sends it back through a hole in the primary mirror. A larger mirror collects more light and, as Chapter 4 shows, resolves finer detail. Each Keck telescope in Hawaii has a 10 m primary mirror made of 36 hexagonal segments, and the Hubble telescope, in orbit above the blurring atmosphere since 1990, has a 2.4 m mirror.

Geometric optics treats light as rays and ignores its wavelength, which is valid only when every opening is much larger than λ. When two or more light waves overlap, the [[superp|superposition principle]] adds their fields, and bright and dark bands appear where the waves arrive in or out of step. This chapter studies such [[interf|interference]] of light: from two slits, from many slits, from the two surfaces of a thin film, and in an interferometer that measures lengths in fractions of a wavelength. These effects belong to wave optics, the description of light based on [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]].

Two light waves give a steady interference pattern only if their relative phase stays fixed. Waves with a constant phase difference are [[coh|coherent waves]]; waves whose phase difference changes randomly are incoherent. Two separate lamps are incoherent: each emits short, independent wave trains from many atoms, so the phase difference of their [[emwave|electromagnetic waves]] wanders rapidly, the interference averages out, and the intensities simply add. Coherent sources are made by splitting the light of one source into two parts, or by using a laser. The light should also be monochromatic, of a single wavelength, so that patterns of different colours do not overlap and wash out. Where coherent waves arrive in phase, *constructive interference* gives brightness; where they arrive half a cycle apart, *destructive interference* gives darkness.

In Thomas Young's experiment of the early nineteenth century, light from one source passes through two narrow parallel slits a distance d apart. By [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]] each slit acts as a source of wavelets, and the two sources are [[coh|coherent]] because the same wavefront feeds both. On a distant screen the two waves show [[interf|interference]] and form bright and dark interference fringes. In a direction at angle θ from the central axis, the wave from one slit travels an extra distance Δl = d sin θ, provided the screen is far away compared with d so that the two paths are nearly parallel. This [[dslit|double-slit interference]] gives brightness where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, d sin θ = mλ, and darkness halfway between, d sin θ = (m + ½)λ, with m = 0, ±1, ±2, …. Young's fringes were early evidence that light is a wave.

The integer m in the [[dslit|double-slit]] conditions is the order of a bright fringe. The central fringe, m = 0, lies where the two paths are equal; the first-order fringes on either side have a path difference of one [[lam|wavelength]]. On a screen at distance D, a fringe at angle θ lies at y = D tan θ from the centre. For small angles tan θ ≈ sin θ = mλ/d, so the bright fringes lie at y_m = mλD/d and are equally spaced. With slits 0.100 mm apart, light of 600 nm and a screen 2.00 m away, the spacing is (600 × 10⁻⁹ m)(2.00 m)/(1.00 × 10⁻⁴ m) = 12.0 mm. Measuring the fringes thus gives the wavelength of light. Since |sin θ| ≤ 1, the order cannot exceed d/λ.

With N equally spaced slits, adjacent slits still differ in path by d sin θ, so wherever d sin θ = mλ all N waves arrive in phase. These principal maxima lie at the same angles as the [[dslit|double-slit]] fringes but are brighter and narrower. By the [[superp|superposition principle]], the field on the screen is the sum of N waves of equal amplitude with a phase step φ = 2πd sin θ/λ between neighbours. Drawn as [[phasor|phasors]], they form a chain of N arrows, each turned by φ from the last. At a principal maximum the chain is straight: the amplitude is N times that of one slit and the intensity N² times. Between adjacent principal maxima the chain closes, giving zero, at N − 1 angles, and between these zeros lie N − 2 weak secondary maxima. This is [[multislit|multiple-slit interference]]. For three slits the single secondary maximum, at φ = π, has 1/9 of the principal intensity.

[[thinfilm|Thin-film interference]] occurs when light reflected from the top of a thin film overlaps light reflected from its bottom. Near normal incidence, the second wave travels an extra distance 2t through a film of thickness t, where its wavelength is λ/n, with n the film's [[nidx|index of refraction]]. [[reflect|Reflection]] from a medium of higher index shifts the phase by π, half a wavelength, while reflection from a lower index does not. Their [[interf|interference]] thus depends on t, n and these shifts. In a soap bubble in air only the top reflection is shifted, so reflection is strongest where 2nt = (m + ½)λ, and regions of different thickness show different colours. Nonreflective coatings use the opposite case: on glass (n = 1.50), a magnesium fluoride layer (n = 1.38) has both reflections shifted and cancels 550 nm light when t = 550 nm/(4 × 1.38) = 99.6 nm. Newton’s rings are the circular fringes of the air film between a curved lens and a flat plate.

An interferometer uses interference to measure lengths or changes of optical path. In the [[michint|Michelson interferometer]], devised by Albert Michelson, a half-silvered mirror splits a beam into two [[coh|coherent]] parts that travel along perpendicular arms, reflect from mirrors at their ends and recombine. Their [[interf|interference]] depends on the difference between the two round-trip paths. Moving one end mirror by Δd changes that difference by 2Δd, so the pattern shifts by one fringe each time the mirror moves λ₀/2, where λ₀ is the vacuum wavelength: Δd = mλ₀/2 after m fringes pass. Counting 1000 fringes of 633 nm light thus measures a displacement of 0.3165 mm. A change of medium in one arm also shifts the fringes: a gas cell of length L and index n adds 2(n − 1)L to the optical path, which moves the pattern by 2(n − 1)L/λ₀ fringes as the cell fills.

Chapter 3 combined waves from a few separate sources. Light passing an edge or a single opening also interferes with itself, because by [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]] every part of the opening sends out wavelets. The result is diffraction: light spreads into the geometric shadow and forms fringes. A famous test came from Fresnel's wave theory of diffraction. Poisson argued that the theory predicted a bright spot at the centre of the shadow of a small disk, which seemed absurd; Arago then observed the spot, now called Poisson’s spot. This chapter treats single slits, gratings, circular apertures, X-rays in crystals and holograms.

Diffraction through a slit of width a is analysed by applying [[huygens|Huygens’s principle]] inside the opening. Each point across the slit emits wavelets, [[coh|coherent]] because one incident wavefront feeds them, and by the [[superp|superposition principle]] the wave on a distant screen is their sum. Straight ahead they all add, giving a broad central maximum. At an angle θ, pair each wavelet from the top half of the slit with the one a/2 below it. If their path difference (a/2) sin θ is half a wavelength, every pair cancels and the screen is dark. Dividing the slit into 4, 6, … parts gives further dark directions. This is [[sslit|single-slit diffraction]], and the minima of the single-slit diffraction pattern follow the condition for destructive interference for a single slit: a sin θ = mλ, with m = ±1, ±2, … but not 0. For a = 2.00 µm and λ = 550 nm, the first minimum lies at sin θ = 0.275, θ = 16.0°.

The intensity across the [[sslit|single-slit]] pattern follows from a phasor diagram. Divide the slit into N strips, each contributing a small [[phasor|phasor]] ΔE₀. Between the two edges of the slit the phase difference is φ = 2πa sin θ/λ, so the chain of phasors bends steadily through the total angle φ. As N becomes large the chain becomes an arc of a circle of length E₀ = NΔE₀, the amplitude straight ahead, and the resultant is the chord of that arc, E = E₀ sin β/β with β = φ/2. Squaring gives the [[Isslit|single-slit intensity]]. It vanishes at β = mπ, that is a sin θ = mλ, as found before. The secondary maxima lie near β ≈ ±1.43π, ±2.46π, …, and the first has only 4.7 % of the central intensity. The width of the central peak, between the minima at sin θ = ±λ/a, grows as the slit narrows.
eqs: I = I₀ (sin β/β)²,   β = πa sin θ/λ

paragraphs.text: Real double slits have a finite width a as well as a separation d. Each slit diffracts with the [[Isslit|single-slit intensity]], and the two diffracted waves then interfere as in [[dslit|double-slit interference]]. The intensity is the product of the two patterns: the interference factor cos²(φ/2), with φ = 2πd sin θ/λ, under the diffraction envelope (sin β/β)². This is the [[dsdiff|two-slit diffraction pattern]]. Since d > a, the fringes are narrower than the envelope, and several fit under its central peak. An interference maximum that falls exactly on a diffraction minimum is absent, a missing order. This happens when d sin θ = mλ and a sin θ = m′λ hold together, that is at m = (d/a)m′. If d = 3a, the orders ±3, ±6, … are missing, and the central peak of the envelope holds 5 bright fringes, m = 0, ±1, ±2.

A [[grating|diffraction grating]] is a [[multislit|multiple-slit]] array with a very large number of equally spaced lines, often hundreds per millimetre, ruled or etched on glass or on a reflecting surface. Its principal maxima still lie at d sin θ = mλ, but as the number of lines N grows their angular width shrinks in proportion to 1/N and the secondary maxima become negligible. Each wavelength is therefore sent into sharp lines at its own angles. This spectroscopic dispersion makes the grating the main tool for measuring wavelengths. A grating with 600 lines per millimetre has d = 1.667 µm, so light of 500 nm appears in first order at sin θ = 0.500 µm/1.667 µm = 0.300, θ = 17.5°. Natural periodic structures, such as the tracks of a compact disc or the scales of some butterfly wings, act as gratings and produce iridescence.

Light passing a circular aperture of diameter D, such as a lens or a telescope mirror, also diffracts. The calculation for a round opening follows the same steps as for the [[sslit|single slit]] and gives a bright central disk whose first dark ring lies at sin θ = 1.22λ/D; the factor 1.22 comes from the round shape. The image of a point source is therefore never a point. By the [[rayl|Rayleigh criterion]], two point sources are just resolved when the centre of one pattern falls on the first minimum of the other, θ_{min} = 1.22λ/D for small angles. This diffraction limit bounds the resolution of every optical instrument and favours large apertures and short wavelengths. For the Hubble Space Telescope, D = 2.4 m and λ = 550 nm give θ_{min} = 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ rad. A laser beam leaving an aperture of diameter D likewise spreads at an angle of about 1.22λ/D.

A grating works best when its spacing is not much larger than the wavelength. Neighbouring atoms in a crystal are about 0.1 nm apart, comparable to the wavelengths of X-rays in the [[spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]], so a crystal acts as a three-dimensional [[grating|grating]] for X-rays. Max von Laue showed this in 1912, founding X-ray diffraction. William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg treated it as reflection from parallel planes of atoms, the Bragg planes. Waves reflected from adjacent planes a distance d apart differ in path by 2d sin θ, with θ measured from the planes rather than from the normal. Their [[interf|interference]] is constructive when this difference is a whole number of wavelengths, which is [[bragg|Bragg’s law]]. In rock salt d = 0.282 nm, so X-rays of 0.154 nm reflect strongly in first order at sin θ = 0.154/0.564 = 0.273, θ = 15.8°. X-ray diffraction images of DNA were key evidence for its double helix in 1953.

A photograph records only the intensity of light, so the phase, which carries information about depth, is lost. A hologram records both. [[coh|Coherent]] light from a laser is split: one part illuminates the object, and the other, the reference beam, goes directly to the recording plate. The [[interf|interference]] of the object light with the reference beam produces fine fringes whose spacing and contrast encode the phase and amplitude of the object wave at each point. After development the recorded fringes act as a complex [[grating|diffraction grating]]. Illuminated by the reference beam alone, the hologram diffracts it into a copy of the original object wave, and an observer sees a three-dimensional image that changes with the viewing angle. This is [[holo|holography]]. Dennis Gabor proposed it in the late 1940s, but bright holograms became practical only with lasers.

Newtonian mechanics assumes one universal time, combines velocities by the rules of [[galrel|relative motion]], and has the same laws in every [[inframe|inertial frame]]. Maxwell's equations, completed in the 1860s, predict electromagnetic waves that travel at one speed, [[c|c]], without saying relative to what. If velocities combine in the Galilean way, the two theories cannot both hold in every inertial frame. In 1905 Albert Einstein resolved the conflict by keeping the equivalence of inertial frames and making the speed of light the same in all of them. This chapter derives the consequences for time, length, velocity, momentum and energy.

In Newtonian mechanics the laws of motion have the same form in every [[inframe|inertial frame of reference]], so no mechanical experiment inside a closed cabin moving at constant velocity reveals that motion. This is [[galrel|Galilean relativity]], and with it velocities measured in two frames differ by the frame velocity, u = u′ + v. [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]], however, contain one speed, the [[c|speed of light]], with no reference to any frame. Nineteenth-century physicists concluded that light moves at c only relative to a medium, the ether, that is, only in the ether's rest frame; in any other frame its speed would follow from Galilean addition. Electromagnetism would then single out one frame. The [[SR|special theory of relativity]] removes this conflict. It rests on two postulates and reduces to Newtonian mechanics when all speeds are much less than c.

The [[sr1|first postulate]] of special relativity extends [[galrel|Galilean relativity]] from mechanics to all of physics: the laws of physics, including [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]], have the same form in every [[inframe|inertial frame]]. No experiment of any kind, mechanical, electrical or optical, can then detect uniform motion, and there is no preferred frame, in particular no ether frame in which light is special. The postulate is a generalisation: the principle was established for mechanics and is asserted for electromagnetism as well. Its consequence is sharp. If Maxwell's equations hold unchanged in every inertial frame, so does the speed of the waves they predict, and that contradicts Galilean velocity addition. Experiment had to decide.

The ether hypothesis was tested with the [[michint|Michelson interferometer]]. In 1887 Michelson and Morley mounted one on a stone slab floating on mercury, folded each arm with mirrors to an effective length of about 11 m, and watched the fringes while the whole apparatus slowly rotated. Any difference between the [[c|speed of light]] along and across Earth's motion would change the travel times in the two arms as they exchanged directions, and so move the fringes. The fringes did not move beyond the small scatter of the readings, and later repetitions at other times of year, when Earth moves in a different direction, agreed. This null [[mmnull|Michelson–Morley result]] of the Michelson-Morley experiment shows that light travels at the same speed in every direction relative to the moving Earth.

Galilean physics predicted a clear shift. Suppose Earth moves through the ether at its orbital speed, v ≈ 3.0 × 10⁴ m/s. By [[galrel|Galilean velocity addition]], light in an arm of length L along the motion travels at c − v one way and c + v back, taking (2L/c)/(1 − v²/c²); in the perpendicular arm it takes (2L/c)/√(1 − v²/c²). The times differ by about (L/c)(v²/c²), and turning the [[michint|interferometer]] through 90° exchanges the arms, so the fringes should shift by ΔN below. With L = 11 m, λ = 550 nm and v²/c² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸, ΔN ≈ 0.40 fringe; the observed shift was less than a twentieth of this. The [[c|speed]] of light does not change with the motion of the apparatus, and [[mmnull|the null result]] forced a choice: give up the relativity principle for light, or give up Galilean velocity addition and the absolute time on which it rests.

Einstein took the second option in 1905 with the [[sr2|second postulate of special relativity]]: light in vacuum travels at the same [[c|speed]] c in every inertial frame, whatever the motion of its source or of the observer. Theory and experiment agree on this. [[maxwell|Maxwell's equations]] give c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀), built from two constants that contain no reference to a frame, and the [[mmnull|Michelson–Morley result]] shows no dependence of c on the motion of the apparatus. Together with the [[sr1|first postulate]], the second postulate is the whole basis of [[SR|special relativity]]; everything in the rest of this chapter follows from the two. Galilean velocity addition must therefore be replaced by a rule that reduces to the familiar one for speeds much less than c.

The second postulate makes simultaneity depend on the frame. Consider a thought experiment: a lamp at the midpoint of a railway carriage flashes, and the light travels to detectors at the front and back ends. In the carriage frame both flashes cover equal distances at c and arrive at the same time. Seen from the platform, the carriage moves forward at v while the light travels, and by the [[sr2|second postulate]] the light still moves at c in both directions in this frame, not at c ± v. The back wall moves toward its flash and the front wall away from its flash, so the back detector is reached first. Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving along the line joining them. This [[simul|relativity of simultaneity]] is a basic result of [[SR|special relativity]]: there is no absolute time.

A light clock shows the effect of the second postulate on time. A pulse of light bounces between two mirrors a distance d apart, and each round trip is one tick. In the frame where the clock is at rest, the two events that bound a tick, departure from and return to the lower mirror, occur at the same place, and the time between them, Δτ = 2d/c, is the proper time. In a frame where the clock moves sideways at speed v, the pulse follows a longer zigzag path but still travels at c, so the tick lasts longer. A moving clock runs slow compared with the clocks of the observer's frame. This is [[dtdil|time dilation]]. The proper time, measured by one clock present at both events, is the shortest time between them in any inertial frame.

The size of the effect follows from Pythagoras. During half a tick, Δt/2 in the observer's frame, the clock moves sideways by vΔt/2 while the light covers the hypotenuse cΔt/2 at the [[c|speed of light]], so (cΔt/2)² = d² + (vΔt/2)². With d = cΔτ/2 this gives Δt²(1 − v²/c²) = Δτ². The ratio Δt/Δτ is the [[gamma|Lorentz factor]] γ, which depends only on the [[speed|speed]] v of the clock relative to the observer. The argument uses nothing but the postulates of [[SR|special relativity]]. The factor equals 1 at rest, stays extremely close to 1 at everyday speeds, and grows without bound as v approaches c: γ = 1.25 at v = 0.600c and γ = 10.0 at v = 0.995c.

In [[SR|special relativity]] time dilation therefore reads Δt = γΔτ, with the [[gamma|Lorentz factor]] γ. The dilated interval Δt is read from two clocks of the observer's frame, at the two places where the tick begins and ends, synchronized in that frame. By the [[simul|relativity of simultaneity]] the clock's own frame disagrees with that synchronization, so each observer finds the other's clocks slow without contradiction. Muons test the effect. Their mean lifetime at rest is 2.20 µs, so at 0.995c they would travel only 657 m on average, yet many made high in the atmosphere reach sea level: in Earth's frame they live 22.0 µs and travel about 6.6 km. In the twin paradox the travelling twin ages less, and the twins are not symmetric, since only the traveller changes inertial frame. For v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 + v²/(2c²), [[dtdil|time dilation]] becomes negligible, and the [[dtm|elapsed time]] is the same in every frame, as Newton assumed.

Lengths depend on the frame as well. The proper length L₀ of an object is its length in its own [[inframe|rest frame]]. Measuring a moving object means locating both ends at the same time, and simultaneity is relative. Take a muon and a stretch of atmosphere at rest relative to Earth; both frames agree on their relative speed v. In Earth's frame the stretch has its proper length L₀ and the muon crosses it in the dilated time Δt, so L₀ = vΔt. In the muon's frame the atmosphere moves past, the crossing takes the proper time Δτ, and the length is L = vΔτ. By [[dtdil|time dilation]] Δt = γΔτ, so L = L₀/γ with the [[gamma|Lorentz factor]] γ. This is [[Lcon|length contraction]]: a moving body is shorter along its motion, while its dimensions across the motion are unchanged. At 0.995c, 6.6 km of atmosphere is only about 660 m long in the muon's frame.

An event happens at one place at one instant and has coordinates (x, y, z, t) in a frame S. Let a frame S′ move at velocity v along the x-axis of S, with the origins together at t = t′ = 0. The Galilean transformation of classical mechanics, x′ = x − vt, y′ = y, z′ = z, t′ = t, gives a light pulse the speed c − v in S′ and so violates the [[sr2|second postulate]]. Its replacement must be linear, so that uniform motion stays uniform in every frame as the [[sr1|first postulate]] requires, and it must keep x² − c²t² unchanged, so that a pulse with x = ct has x′ = ct′. The only such map is the [[lorentzT|Lorentz transformation]], with y′ = y, z′ = z and the [[gamma|Lorentz factor]] γ. For v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and vx/c² is negligible at ordinary distances, so it reduces to the Galilean form: classical [[galrel|relative motion]] is the slow limit.
eqs: x′ = γ(x − vt),   t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)

paragraphs.text: The [[lorentzT|Lorentz transformation]] mixes space and time, but one combination is the same in every [[frame|reference frame]]: the interval (Δs)² between two events. Space and time therefore form one four-dimensional geometry, [[spacetime|space-time]], in which an event is a point and the history of a particle is a curve, its world line. Light leaving an event spreads along its light cone, where (Δs)² = 0. Events inside the cone, with (Δs)² < 0, can be linked by signals slower than light, have the same time order in all frames, and are separated by the proper time Δτ = √(−(Δs)²)/c. Events outside the cone have no frame-independent order; this is the [[simul|relativity of simultaneity]] in geometric form. The twin paradox becomes geometry: between departure and return, the bent world line of the travelling twin has less proper time than the straight one of the twin at home.

Velocities transform as ratios of transformed displacements. A body moving along x at velocity u′ in S′ covers dx′ = u′dt′ in a time dt′. The inverse [[lorentzT|Lorentz transformation]] gives dx = γ(dx′ + v dt′) and dt = γ(dt′ + v dx′/c²) in S, and the velocity in S is the [[ddt|time derivative]] u = dx/dt. Dividing gives [[reladd|relativistic velocity addition]]. A spacecraft moving at 0.600c relative to Earth fires a probe forward at 0.800c relative to itself; observers on Earth measure the probe's speed as (0.800 + 0.600)c/(1 + 0.480) = 0.946c, not 1.400c. Combining c with any v gives c again, as the second postulate requires, and speeds below c never combine to reach c. For u′ and v both much less than c the denominator is close to 1, and the rule reduces to classical (Galilean) velocity addition, u = u′ + v.

Light from a moving source is shifted in [[freq|frequency]], as sound is, but for a different reason. The Doppler shift of sound depends on the speeds of source and observer relative to the air; light needs no medium, so only their relative velocity can matter. Let a source recede at speed v and emit wave crests with the period T_s = 1/f_s of its own frame. By [[dtdil|time dilation]] the observer finds the crests emitted at intervals γT_s, during which the source moves a further vγT_s away. Each crest travels to the observer at c by the [[sr2|second postulate]], so it arrives later by vγT_s/c, and the observed period is γT_s(1 + v/c). This gives the [[relDop|relativistic Doppler effect]]. A receding source shows a lower frequency, a red shift; for an approaching source v is replaced by −v and the frequency rises. At v = 0.600c the received frequency is f_s√(0.400/1.600) = 0.500f_s.

In Newtonian mechanics the total [[p|momentum]] mu⃗ of an isolated system is conserved in every inertial frame related by Galilean transformations. Under the Lorentz transformation, however, a collision that conserves the total mu⃗ in one frame does not conserve it in another. To keep [[pcons|conservation of momentum]] valid in all inertial frames, momentum is redefined as the [[prel|relativistic momentum]], with the [[gamma|Lorentz factor]] γ taken at the speed u of the body. Here m is the rest mass, measured with the body at rest, and is the same in every frame. For u ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and the classical momentum p⃗ = mu⃗ returns. An electron at 0.600c, where γ = 1.25, has p = 1.25 × (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)(0.600)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) = 2.05 × 10⁻²² kg·m/s. As u approaches c, p grows without bound, so a finite force acting for a finite time cannot bring a massive body to c.

The [[wet|work–energy theorem]] still holds: the kinetic energy of a body equals the work done to bring it from rest to its speed. With the force F = dp/dt along the motion, the work is ∫F dx = ∫(dp/dt) dx = ∫u dp. Using the [[prel|relativistic momentum]] p = γmu and integrating by parts from rest to speed u gives the [[Krel|relativistic kinetic energy]]. As u approaches c, γ and with it K grow without bound, so no finite amount of work brings a massive body to the [[c|speed of light]]. For u ≪ c the expansion γ = 1 + u²/(2c²) + … gives K ≈ ½mu², the Newtonian [[K|kinetic energy]]. The difference matters at high speed: at u = 0.600c, K = 0.250mc², while ½mu² = 0.180mc².

The [[Krel|relativistic kinetic energy]] is the difference of two terms, K = γmc² − mc². The second term does not depend on speed and is itself an energy: the rest energy E₀ = mc² that a body has in its rest frame. The [[Erel|total energy]] is then E = K + mc² = γmc², and mass is a form of energy. One kilogram of matter has a rest energy of (1.00 kg)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ J; in nuclear reactions a measurable fraction of the rest mass becomes kinetic energy. Combining E = γmc² with the [[prel|relativistic momentum]] p = γmu eliminates the speed: E² − (pc)² = γ²m²c⁴(1 − u²/c²) = (mc²)², the same in every frame. The relation also holds for a particle of zero mass, which has E = pc and must travel at c.

The classical physics of the earlier chapters treats light as a continuous [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] and matter as particles moving on definite paths. Between the 1880s and the 1920s, measurements of thermal radiation, of electrons ejected from metals by light, of X-rays scattered by electrons and of atomic spectra gave results that these theories could not reproduce. This chapter takes each failure in turn: the classical argument, what was observed, and the quantum idea that replaced it. The new ideas are energy exchanged in steps of hf, light carried by photons, atoms with discrete energy levels, and matter with a wavelength h/p. It ends with wave–particle duality and the uncertainty principle.

Every body at a [[temp|temperature]] T emits electromagnetic radiation and absorbs part of what falls on it, and a good *absorber* is also a good *emitter*. A *blackbody* absorbs all incident radiation. A small hole in the wall of a cavity held at temperature T is a close approximation, and the radiation leaving it is [[bbrad|blackbody radiation]]. Spreading this radiation into a [[spectrum|spectrum]] measures its *power intensity* I(λ, T), the power emitted per unit area per unit wavelength interval. The measured curves depend on T alone, not on the material of the walls. Each has a single maximum, at a wavelength that decreases as T rises according to *Wien's displacement law*, λ_{max} T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. Skin at 310 K radiates most strongly near 9.3 μm, in the infrared, and the bluish star Rigel is hotter than the reddish star Betelgeuse.

The area under a curve is the total power emitted per unit area. It grows as the fourth power of the temperature: a blackbody of area A radiates P = σAT⁴, which is [[sbl|Stefan's law]], with the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴). Classical physics predicts a different curve. The radiation in the cavity is a set of standing [[emwave|electromagnetic waves]], with 8π/λ⁴ modes per unit volume per unit wavelength interval, so ever more modes fit at short wavelengths. In equilibrium the [[equip|equipartition theorem]] gives each mode an average energy k_{B}T, where k_B is [[kB|Boltzmann's constant]]. The result is the *Rayleigh–Jeans law*, I(λ, T) = 2πck_{B}T/λ⁴. It matches the measured [[bbrad|blackbody spectrum]] at long wavelengths but grows without limit as λ → 0, so the predicted total power is infinite: the *ultraviolet catastrophe*. The measured curves instead fall to zero at short wavelengths.

In 1900 Planck found a formula that fits the measured curves at all wavelengths and then justified it with a new assumption. He modelled the walls as charged oscillators exchanging energy with the radiation, and allowed an oscillator of [[freq|frequency]] f, otherwise an ordinary [[sho|harmonic oscillator]], only the *quantized energies* E_n = nhf, where the *quantum number* n = 0, 1, 2, … labels the *quantum state of a Planck oscillator*. This is [[planck|Planck's hypothesis of energy quanta]]: energy is absorbed and emitted in whole steps of hf. The constant h, [[hbar|Planck's constant]], was fixed by fitting the data; its value is h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s = 4.136 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s. Because h is so small, the steps are far too fine to notice for a pendulum or a mass on a spring. They matter when hf is comparable with the thermal energy k_{B}T.

With energies nhf occupied with Boltzmann probabilities proportional to exp(−nhf/k_{B}T), the average energy of an oscillator is hf/[exp(hf/k_{B}T) − 1] instead of k_{B}T. Using this average for each cavity mode, with f = c/λ and the [[c|speed of light]] c, turns [[planck|Planck's hypothesis]] into his radiation law for [[bbrad|blackbody radiation]], shown below. When hf ≪ k_{B}T the exponential is close to 1 + hf/k_{B}T, the average energy returns to k_{B}T, and the law reduces to the Rayleigh–Jeans form; this is the classical limit. When hf ≫ k_{B}T the average energy falls as exp(−hf/k_{B}T), so short-wavelength modes are hardly excited and the total power is finite. Integrating over all wavelengths gives [[sbl|Stefan's law]] with σ = 2π⁵k_{B}⁴/(15c²h³), built from [[kB|Boltzmann's constant]], c and h, which reproduces the measured 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴).

Light of high enough frequency falling on a clean metal surface ejects electrons. This is the *photoelectric effect*, and the ejected electrons are *photoelectrons*. In the usual apparatus the illuminated metal, the *photoelectrode*, faces a collecting electrode in an evacuated tube, and the electrons that arrive form a *photocurrent*. Making the collector negative repels the electrons. At the *stopping potential*, a [[dV|voltage]] ΔV_s, even the fastest electrons are turned back and the current stops, so their kinetic energy equals the potential energy their [[q|charge]] e gains across ΔV_s: the [[Kmax|maximum kinetic energy]] is K_{max} = eΔV_s. Repeating the measurement with light of different [[freq|frequency]] f reveals a [[fc|cut-off frequency]] f_c, which depends on the metal: below it no electrons leave at all, however intense the light. Equivalently, light longer than the *cut-off wavelength* c/f_c ejects none.

Classical wave theory makes three predictions here. An [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] delivers energy at a rate set by its [[Iint|intensity]], spread evenly over the wavefront, and an electron absorbs this energy continuously. Brighter light should therefore give faster electrons; light of any frequency should eject electrons if it is intense enough; and in dim light an electron should need time to gather enough energy. For 0.01 W/m² falling on an area of atomic size, 10⁻²⁰ m², collecting 2 eV (3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) would take about 3 × 10³ s. The observations contradict all three. The [[Kmax|maximum kinetic energy]] does not depend on the intensity, which changes only the number of electrons; it increases linearly with frequency; there is a sharp cut-off frequency; and emission begins without measurable delay, even in very dim light.

Einstein proposed in 1905 that light itself consists of quanta. A [[photon|photon]] of light of [[freq|frequency]] f carries the *energy of a photon* E_f = hf, with [[hbar|Planck's constant]] h, and is absorbed or emitted whole. An [[emwave|electromagnetic wave]] is the collective behaviour of very many photons, and at a given frequency its intensity measures how many arrive per unit area per second. The photoelectric effect is thus a *quantum phenomenon*: it shows that the energy of light is granular. A photon has zero rest mass, so the relation E² = p²c² + m₀²c⁴ between [[Erel|total energy]] and momentum reduces to E = pc. Its momentum has magnitude p = E/c = h/λ and points along the *propagation vector* k⃗, of magnitude 2π/λ, so that p⃗ = ħk⃗ with ħ = h/2π.

An electron is bound in the metal, and the least energy needed to free one from the surface is the [[phiw|work function]] ϕ, a property of the metal and its surface. In Einstein's picture one [[photon|photon]] gives all its energy to one electron, which spends at least ϕ to escape, so the fastest electrons leave with the [[Kmax|kinetic energy]] given below. A photon with hf < ϕ cannot free an electron at all, which explains the [[fc|cut-off frequency]] f_c = ϕ/h, with [[hbar|Planck's constant]] h. Brighter light brings more photons, hence more electrons but not faster ones, and each absorption is immediate. A plot of K_{max} against [[freq|frequency]] is a straight line of slope h for every metal; it crosses the frequency axis at f_c, and its extension meets the energy axis at −ϕ. For ϕ = 2.30 eV, f_c = 5.56 × 10¹⁴ Hz, and 400 nm light, with 3.10 eV per photon, gives K_{max} = 0.80 eV.

X-rays scattered by a block of graphite contain, besides the incident wavelength λ, a longer wavelength λ′. This [[compton|Compton shift]], measured by Compton in 1923, grows with the *scattering angle* θ and does not depend on the material. A classical wave would make each electron oscillate and re-radiate at the incident frequency, with no shift. Compton treated the X-ray as a [[photon|photon]] with momentum p⃗ = ħk⃗, where ħ = h/2π is the [[hbar|reduced Planck's constant]] and k = 2π/λ the [[kwave|wave number]], striking a free electron at rest. Applying [[pcons|conservation of momentum]] and of energy, with the electron's [[prel|relativistic momentum]] and [[Erel|total energy]], and eliminating the electron's recoil gives the shift below. Its scale is the *Compton wavelength* of the electron, λ_c = h/(m₀c) = 0.00243 nm. The photon loses energy, so this is *inelastic scattering*. The shift never exceeds 2λ_c, about 0.005 nm, so it is noticeable only for short wavelengths such as those of X-rays.
eqs: Δλ = λ′ − λ = λ_c(1 − cos θ)

paragraphs.text: Hydrogen made to glow by an electric discharge emits a [[spectrum|spectrum]] of sharp lines only, its *emission spectrum*. Cool hydrogen in front of a continuous source absorbs at the same wavelengths and leaves dark lines, its *absorption spectrum*; dark lines of this kind in sunlight are the *Fraunhofer lines*. In 1885 Balmer fitted the visible hydrogen lines with the *Balmer formula*. The measured [[lam|wavelengths]] of the whole [[Hspec|hydrogen line spectrum]] obey its generalization, the *Rydberg formula* below, with integers n_{i} > n_{f} and the *Rydberg constant for hydrogen* R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Each n_{f} gives a series: the *Lyman series* (n_{f} = 1) in the ultraviolet, the *Balmer series* (n_{f} = 2) in the visible and near ultraviolet, and the *Paschen*, *Brackett*, *Pfund* and *Humphreys series* (n_{f} = 3 to 6) in the infrared. For n_{i} = 3 and n_{f} = 2 the formula gives 656 nm, the red Balmer line.

Thomson had found that atoms contain light, negatively charged electrons, but how the positive and negative [[atom|charge carriers]] of an atom are arranged was unknown; Thomson pictured the positive charge spread through the whole atom. Some radioactive substances emit α-rays, β-rays and γ-rays, and α-rays are streams of fast, positively charged α particles. In the *Rutherford gold foil experiment*, α particles were sent through a thin gold foil. Most passed with small deflections, but a few were turned through large angles, some almost straight back. Positive charge spread over 10⁻¹⁰ m cannot exert a force strong enough for that. Treating each deflection as an elastic [[coll|collision]] with a point charge under [[coul|Coulomb's law]], Rutherford showed in 1911 that the measured angular distribution requires a tiny, massive, positive nucleus. This is the [[nucatom|nuclear model of the atom]]: a nucleus of radius about 10⁻¹⁵ m holding nearly all the mass, with electrons near 10⁻¹⁰ m. In 1932 Chadwick found the uncharged neutron in the nucleus.

The nuclear atom resembles a small planetary system, with Coulomb attraction in place of gravity, but classical physics makes it unstable. An electron on a circular orbit has a [[ac|centripetal acceleration]] v²/r, and an accelerated charge radiates [[emwave|electromagnetic waves]]. The electron should therefore lose energy continuously and spiral inward, its orbital frequency, and with it the radiated frequency, rising all the way; for hydrogen the collapse would take about 10⁻¹¹ s. The [[nucatom|nuclear atom]] of classical physics thus predicts a continuous spectrum and no stable atoms. Real atoms are stable, have a definite size near 10⁻¹⁰ m, and emit the discrete [[Hspec|hydrogen line spectrum]]. Classical electrodynamics cannot hold inside the atom without change.

In 1913 Bohr kept the [[nucatom|nuclear atom]] and [[coul|Coulomb's law]] but added two postulates for hydrogen. First, the electron moves only on circular orbits whose [[Lang|angular momentum]] is a whole multiple of ħ, L_n = nħ with quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, …, and on these stationary orbits it does not radiate, contrary to classical electrodynamics. Second, when the electron jumps from one orbit to another it emits or absorbs a single [[photon|photon]] whose energy equals the energy difference, hf = |E_n − E_m|, with [[hbar|Planck's constant]] h. These *postulates of Bohr's model* define [[bohr|Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom]]. They were not derived from earlier physics; they were justified by their results, and the angular-momentum condition was explained later by matter waves.

The allowed orbits follow from Newton's second law. The Coulomb force supplies the [[Fc|centripetal force]], m_e v²/r = ke²/r², while [[bohr|Bohr's first postulate]] requires m_e v r = nħ. Eliminating v gives the radii r_n = a₀n², where a₀ = 4πε₀ħ²/(m_e e²) = 0.529 Å is the *Bohr radius of hydrogen*. Since [[coul|Coulomb's law]] gives the potential energy −ke²/r and the kinetic energy is half its magnitude, the total energy is E_n = −ke²/(2r_n) = −E₀/n², with E₀ = m_e e⁴/(8ε₀²h²) = 13.6 eV. These [[bohrlev|hydrogen energy levels]] form the *energy spectrum of hydrogen*: the ground state at −13.6 eV, and excited states, n ≥ 2, that crowd towards the *ionization limit* E = 0. The *ionization energy* from the ground state is therefore 13.6 eV. A *hydrogen-like ion*, with one electron and nuclear charge Ze, has r_n = a₀n²/Z and E_n = −Z²E₀/n²; for He⁺ the ground state lies at −54.4 eV.

Bohr's second postulate now yields the spectrum. When the electron drops from level n_{i} to a lower level n_{f}, it emits a [[photon|photon]] of energy hc/λ equal to the difference of the two [[bohrlev|energy levels]], E₀(1/n_{f}² − 1/n_{i}²). Dividing by hc gives exactly the Rydberg formula of the [[Hspec|hydrogen line spectrum]], with R_H = E₀/(hc) = m_e e⁴/(8ε₀²h³c). With the measured e, m_e, h and ε₀ this equals 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the value fitted to the lines. Absorption is the reverse jump; at room temperature nearly all atoms are in the ground state, so cool hydrogen absorbs mainly the Lyman lines. The model obtained the size and spectrum of hydrogen from fundamental constants. It fails, however, for atoms with more than one electron, does not give the relative brightness of lines, and its definite orbits have no place in the quantum mechanics that replaced it.

In 1924 de Broglie reversed the reasoning that had led to the [[photon|photon]]: if light waves have particle properties, particles may have wave properties. He proposed that a particle of [[p|momentum]] p and energy E has an associated *de Broglie wave* with λ = h/p and f = E/h, the relations already found for photons. This is [[debrog|de Broglie's hypothesis of matter waves]], the starting point of *wave quantum mechanics*. The wavelength matters only at atomic scales. An electron accelerated through 100 V has p = √(2m_{e}K) = 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s and λ = 0.123 nm, comparable with the spacing of atoms in a crystal, while a 0.145 kg ball at 40 m/s has λ ≈ 1 × 10⁻³⁴ m. A wave of one wavelength fills all space, so a localized particle corresponds to a group of waves. The group moves at the *group velocity* dω/dk = dE/dp, which equals the particle's velocity.

Matter waves explain Bohr's quantization rule. An electron wave running around a circular orbit returns to its starting point, and unless a whole number of wavelengths fits the circumference, successive turns interfere destructively. An allowed orbit therefore carries a [[standw|standing wave]], like a string closed on itself: 2πr_n = nλ. With the [[debrog|de Broglie wavelength]] λ = h/p this becomes p r_n = nh/2π, that is, L = nħ, which is the first postulate of [[bohr|Bohr's model]]. Quantization appears as a condition on waves, not as an extra rule for particles.

The hypothesis was confirmed by electron diffraction. Davisson and Germer directed electrons of kinetic energy 54 eV at a nickel crystal and found a strong reflected beam at a scattering angle of 50°, a maximum that no particle picture predicts. The planes of atoms in the crystal act on the electrons as they do on X-rays, so [[bragg|Bragg's law]] mλ = 2d sin θ applies with the [[debrog|de Broglie wavelength]]. The wavelength obtained from the measured angle, 0.165 nm, agreed with h/p = 0.167 nm for 54 eV electrons. This *Davisson–Germer experiment*, reported in 1927, established [[DG|electron diffraction]]. Diffraction of electrons, neutrons and whole atoms has since been observed many times, always with λ = h/p.

Light and matter therefore both behave as waves and as particles. The clearest test is the *double-slit interference experiment* run at such low intensity that one quantum at a time passes through the apparatus. Each [[photon|photon]] or electron is recorded at a single point on the screen, as a particle would be. The points fall at random, but as thousands accumulate they build up the fringes of [[dslit|double-slit interference]], as a wave would. The electron version, with electrons whose wavelength is given by the [[debrog|de Broglie relation]], was carried out by Pozzi and colleagues and later by Tonomura's group. Closing one slit removes the fringes, and so does any arrangement that records which slit each quantum passed. This is [[duality|wave–particle duality]]: each detection is particle-like, while the probability of where detections occur follows a wave. Neither picture alone describes the experiment.

Duality limits how sharply the state of a particle can be specified. A wave with a single wave number k extends over all space. A wave confined to a region of width Δx must combine wave numbers with a spread Δk ≥ 1/(2Δx); this is a property of all waves and follows from Fourier analysis. For a matter wave p = ħk by the [[debrog|de Broglie relation]], so multiplying by ħ gives the [[uncert|Heisenberg uncertainty principle]] below, where Δx and Δp are the standard deviations of position and momentum over many identically prepared particles. The limit is not a defect of instruments; it follows from the wave side of [[duality|wave–particle duality]]. Because ħ is so small, it is irrelevant for everyday bodies but decisive inside atoms. Heisenberg, Schrödinger and Dirac turned these ideas into a complete theory in the mid-1920s, the subject of the next chapter.

Short de Broglie wavelengths make *electron microscopy* possible. Diffraction limits the detail a microscope can resolve to roughly the wavelength used, as the [[rayl|Rayleigh criterion]] expresses, so visible light cannot resolve structures much smaller than 200 nm. Electrons accelerated through 100 kV have a wavelength of 0.0037 nm, found with the relativistic momentum, and magnetic lenses focus them. In a *transmission electron microscope (TEM)* the beam passes through a very thin specimen and forms an image of it. In a *scanning electron microscope (SEM)* a fine beam is scanned across a surface, and the electrons it knocks out are counted point by point to form an image. Lens aberrations, not the wavelength, set the practical limit, of order 0.1 nm in the best instruments. Ruska built the first electron microscope in the early 1930s.

Chapter 6 established [[duality|wave–particle duality]] for light and matter and collected rules, such as [[bohr|Bohr's quantization condition]], that fit particular cases. This chapter presents the theory that replaces those rules. The state of a particle is a wave function whose squared magnitude gives probabilities, and the wave function obeys the Schrödinger equation. Applied to a particle in a box, a harmonic oscillator and a potential barrier, the equation produces quantized energies, a nonzero lowest energy and tunneling through barriers. In each case it also recovers classical mechanics in the limit of large quantum numbers.

The *two-slit interference* of single electrons shows that the behaviour of a particle is governed by a wave. Quantum mechanics takes that wave as the complete description of the particle's state and calls it the [[psi|wave function]] Ψ(x, t). Its model is the [[debrog|de Broglie wave]] of a free particle, written as a [[trav|traveling wave]] in complex form, Ψ(x, t) = A e^{i(kx − ωt)} = A[cos(kx − ωt) + i sin(kx − ωt)], with p = ħk and E = ħω. In general Ψ is a *complex function*, involving i = √−1.
