The complex form is needed: a real cosine wave has nodes that move through space, whereas a particle of sharp momentum has no preferred position, and the complex wave has |Ψ|² = |A|² everywhere. Ψ itself is not measured; only quantities built from it are.

Born proposed in 1926 that Ψ determines probabilities. In the *Born interpretation*, the probability of finding the particle between x and x + dx at time t is |Ψ(x, t)|² dx = Ψ^{∗}Ψ dx, so |Ψ|² is a *probability density*, with unit m⁻¹ in one dimension. This [[born|Born rule]] is tested by repeating an experiment on many identically prepared particles and recording the distribution of outcomes, as in the build-up of two-slit fringes. Since the particle is certainly somewhere, the probabilities over all x add to one, which is the *normalization condition* below; a wave function is normalized by choosing its amplitude to satisfy it. Multiplying Ψ by a constant phase factor e^{iα} leaves |Ψ|² unchanged everywhere, so such a global phase has no observable effect.

A measurement of position gives one definite result, not a spread, and an immediate repeat of the measurement gives the same result. The description must therefore change abruptly: the [[psi|wave function]] that supplied the probabilities through the [[born|Born rule]] is replaced by one concentrated at the outcome. This *state reduction*, or *wave function collapse*, is the [[collapse|measurement postulate]] of quantum mechanics. In the *Copenhagen interpretation*, associated with Bohr and Heisenberg, it is part of the rules, and the wave function encodes what can be predicted about outcomes. Whether collapse is a physical process is still debated. *Schrödinger's cat*, whose survival in a closed box depends on a single radioactive decay, dramatizes the question. A *qubit*, a two-state quantum system used to store information, can be in a superposition of both states until it is measured, and quantum computing depends on this.

The [[expval|expectation value]] ⟨x⟩ is the average of many position measurements on identically prepared systems. Each x is weighted by its probability density from the [[born|Born rule]], which gives the first formula below. Other quantities are averaged by letting an operator act on the [[psi|wave function]]: the *position operator* multiplies by x, the *momentum operator* is −iħ ∂/∂x, and the kinetic energy follows from ⟨p²⟩/2m. If Ψ is an *even function* of x, or an *odd function*, also called an *anti-symmetric function*, then |Ψ|² is even and ⟨x⟩ = 0. Bohr's [[corresp|correspondence principle]] requires quantum predictions to agree with classical mechanics in the limit of large quantum numbers. In hydrogen, for example, the frequency of light emitted in a jump from n to n − 1 approaches the classical orbital frequency of the electron as n grows. Each model in this chapter can be checked against this limit.

A particle with sharp momentum is described by a single plane wave, which has the same |Ψ|² everywhere. A localized particle is described by a [[wpack|wave packet]]. By the [[superp|superposition principle]], plane waves e^{i(kx − ωt)} with amplitudes A(k), spread over a range of [[kwave|wave numbers]], add to a [[psi|wave function]] that is large only in a region of width Δx. Fourier analysis shows that Δx Δk ≥ ½, with equality for a Gaussian packet: the narrower the packet, the more wave numbers it needs. With p = ħk this is [[uncert|Heisenberg's uncertainty principle]], Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2. An electron confined to Δx = 0.10 nm, the size of an atom, has Δp ≥ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s, a velocity spread of at least 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s, so it cannot follow a definite orbit.
eqs: Ψ(x, t) = ∫ A(k) e^{i(kx − ωt)} dk

paragraphs.text: The same Fourier relation holds between time and angular frequency: a wave train lasting a time Δt contains angular frequencies spread over Δω ≥ 1/(2Δt). For a [[photon|photon]], and for any quantum state, E = ħω, so multiplying by ħ gives the [[uncertE|energy–time uncertainty principle]] below. Here Δt is not the spread of a measured time but the time over which the state changes appreciably, such as the lifetime of an excited atom. A state with lifetime 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ s has an energy spread of at least ħ/(2Δt) = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ eV, so the photons it emits are not exactly monochromatic; this sets the natural width of spectral lines, and short-lived states give broad lines. Like the [[uncert|position–momentum uncertainty principle]], it is a property of waves, not of instruments.

The wave function changes in time according to an equation proposed by Schrödinger in 1926. It cannot be derived from classical physics, but it can be built to reproduce the free [[debrog|de Broglie wave]]. For Ψ = A e^{i(kx − ωt)}, the operation iħ ∂/∂t multiplies the [[psi|wave function]] by ħω = E, and −iħ ∂/∂x multiplies it by ħk = p. Writing the [[Emech|mechanical energy]] E = p²/2m + U with these operators acting on Ψ gives *Schrödinger's time-dependent equation*, the [[tdse|Schrödinger equation]] below, for a particle of mass m with potential energy U(x, t). It is linear, so superpositions of solutions are solutions. It is first order in time, so Ψ at one instant fixes Ψ at all later instants. It contains the *imaginary number* i, so its solutions are complex. For real U it keeps a normalized Ψ normalized.

When the potential energy depends on x only, the equation has solutions in which space and time separate. Substituting Ψ(x, t) = ψ(x)φ(t) into the [[tdse|time-dependent equation]] and dividing by ψφ leaves a function of t alone on one side and a function of x alone on the other, so both equal one constant, the energy E. The time part is φ = e^{−iEt/ħ} = e^{−iωt}, the *time-modulation factor*, and ψ(x) satisfies *Schrödinger's time-independent equation*, the [[tise|time-independent Schrödinger equation]] below. It is an eigenvalue problem. For a bound particle, solutions that are finite, continuous and normalizable exist only for particular values of E, and these are the allowed energies. For a free particle, with U = 0, ψ = e^{ikx} is a solution for any E = ħ²k²/2m ≥ 0.

The simplest bound system, the [[pib|particle in a box]], is a particle of mass m between rigid walls at x = 0 and x = L: an *infinite square well*, with U = 0 inside and U = ∞ outside. The wave function vanishes outside, so the [[bc|boundary conditions]] are ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0. Inside, the [[tise|time-independent equation]] gives ψ = A sin kx + B cos kx with k² = 2mE/ħ². The condition at x = 0 requires B = 0, and the one at x = L allows only kL = nπ, the [[standw|standing waves]] of a string fixed at both ends; normalization gives A = √(2/L). The *energy quantum number* n = 1, 2, 3, …, also called the *principal quantum number*, labels the *energy levels* below. Since n = 0 would make ψ vanish, the *ground state energy* E₁ is not zero: for an electron in a box 0.50 nm wide, E₁ = 1.50 eV and E₂ = 6.02 eV.

Each solution of the [[tise|time-independent equation]], multiplied by its time-modulation factor, is a [[stat|stationary state]] Ψ_n = ψ_n exp(−iE_{n}t/ħ). Because this factor has magnitude one, the probability density |Ψ_n|² = |ψ_n|² does not change in time, and neither does any expectation value. In the [[pib|particle in a box]] these are *standing wave states*. A state that changes in time is a superposition of stationary states with different energies. For large n, the density (2/L) sin²(nπx/L) has n closely spaced peaks, and its average over any small interval approaches the uniform value 1/L. A classical particle bouncing between the walls at constant speed spends equal times in equal intervals, so its [[xt|motion on a line]] gives exactly that uniform density. The relative spacing of the levels, (E_{n+1} − E_n)/E_n = (2n + 1)/n², also goes to zero, and the energy appears continuous, as the [[corresp|correspondence principle]] requires.

Near the bottom of almost any potential well the potential energy is close to quadratic, so the quantum oscillator describes vibrations of molecules and of atoms in solids. Putting the potential energy U = ½mω²x² of the classical [[sho|simple harmonic oscillator]] into the [[tise|time-independent equation]] gives the [[qho|quantum harmonic oscillator]]. Its normalizable solutions are ψ_n = N_n e^{−β²x²/2} H_n(βx), with β = √(mω/ħ), a normalization constant N_n, and a *Hermite polynomial* H_n of degree n. The energies are equally spaced by ħω, the spacing of [[planck|Planck's hypothesis]], but the lowest one is the zero-point energy ħω/2, not zero: a particle at rest at the bottom would have Δx = 0 and Δp = 0, which the [[uncert|uncertainty principle]] forbids. The wave functions also extend beyond the classical turning points, into regions where E < U; in the ground state the particle is found there with probability about 16 %.

The classical and quantum oscillators differ most in their lowest states. A classical particle in [[shm|harmonic oscillation]] with amplitude A moves fastest at the centre and slowest near the turning points ±A, so it is most likely to be found near the ends; its probability density is 1/(π√(A² − x²)) for |x| < A. The quantum ground state instead has its greatest density at the centre. As n increases, |ψ_n|² of the [[qho|quantum oscillator]] develops n + 1 peaks, the largest near the classical turning points, and its average over neighbouring peaks follows the classical curve. Meanwhile ħω becomes a small fraction of E_n, so the steps in energy are no longer noticeable. Both trends illustrate the [[corresp|correspondence principle]]. A mass on a spring with f = 1 Hz and energy 1 J has n ≈ 1.5 × 10³³.

A *potential barrier* is a region where the potential energy exceeds the energy of an approaching particle. Take U = U₀ for 0 ≤ x ≤ L, U = 0 elsewhere, and a particle in a [[stat|stationary state]] of energy E < U₀. Inside the barrier the [[tise|time-independent equation]] gives ψ″ = β²ψ with β² = 2m(U₀ − E)/ħ², so ψ is a combination of e^{−βx} and e^{βx}, not an oscillation. Matching ψ and ψ′ at both edges to the incident, reflected and transmitted waves leaves a transmitted wave of nonzero amplitude: the particle crosses by *quantum tunneling*. The ratio |ψ_{tra}|²/|ψ_{in}|² is the *transmission probability*, or [[Ttun|tunneling probability]] T; for βL ≫ 1 it is approximately the expression below. For an electron with E = 3.0 eV and U₀ = 4.0 eV, β = 5.12 × 10⁹ m⁻¹; a 1.0 nm barrier gives T ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁴, and a 2.0 nm barrier about 4 × 10⁻⁹.

Classical mechanics forbids this. On a [[pediag|potential-energy diagram]], a particle with E < U₀ reaches a turning point at the edge of the barrier, where its kinetic energy E − U falls to zero; inside, the kinetic energy would be negative. It is reflected with certainty, T = 0, however thin the barrier. Observation disagrees. Hund used tunneling to explain features of molecular spectra, and in 1928 Gamow explained how heavy nuclei emit α particles of a few MeV through a Coulomb barrier several times higher; the exponential sensitivity of T accounts for α-decay half-lives that range from below a microsecond to billions of years. Strong electric fields pull electrons out of cold metals through the surface barrier, which is *field emission*. In each case the [[Ttun|tunneling probability]] of the wave description replaces the classical certainty of reflection.

Tunneling is the working principle of several devices. In the *scanning tunneling microscope (STM)*, a sharp metal tip is held a fraction of a nanometre above a conducting surface, and a small voltage drives a tunneling current across the gap. The current changes by roughly a factor of ten for each 0.1 nm change in the gap, so scanning the tip while keeping the current constant maps the surface with atomic resolution. A *tunnel diode* passes current through a very thin junction by tunneling. In *resonant tunneling*, two thin barriers enclose a narrow well whose levels act like those of a box, and electrons whose energy matches a level cross both barriers with high probability; the *resonant-tunneling diode* uses this to switch very fast. A *quantum dot*, a tiny region that confines electrons in all three directions, has discrete levels of the same kind. Such devices belong to *nanotechnology*.

[[bohr|Bohr's model]] gave the energy levels of hydrogen but not a consistent theory of atoms. This chapter applies the [[tdse|Schrödinger equation]] of Chapter 7 to atoms. For hydrogen it yields the energy levels, the shapes of the electron's probability distributions and the quantization of angular momentum. Magnetic effects then reveal the electron's orbital magnetic moment and its intrinsic spin. Together with the exclusion principle, the same quantum numbers explain the periodic table, and transitions between atomic levels account for spectra, X-rays and lasers.

In the hydrogen atom the electron moves in the potential energy U(r) = −ke²/r of the proton, given by [[coul|Coulomb's law]]. The [[tise|time-independent Schrödinger equation]] in three dimensions separates in spherical coordinates, and its normalizable solutions ψ_{nlm}(r, θ, φ), the *atomic orbitals*, are labelled by three integers: the *principal quantum number* n = 1, 2, 3, …, the *angular momentum orbital quantum number* l = 0, 1, …, n − 1, and the *angular momentum projection quantum number* m = −l, …, l. The energies depend on n alone and equal Bohr's [[bohrlev|hydrogen energy levels]], E_n = −13.6 eV/n², now obtained without postulated orbits. The [[hatom|hydrogen atom]] of quantum mechanics gives probabilities, not paths. For states that do not depend on angle, the *radial probability density function* P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² is the probability per unit distance of finding the electron at radius r. For the normalized ground state below, P(r) peaks at r = a₀, the Bohr radius.

The angular part of ψ_{nlm} fixes the orbital [[Lang|angular momentum]] L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗. Applying the operator for L⃗ to the [[hatom|hydrogen wave functions]] shows that its magnitude and its component along one chosen axis, called z, take only the discrete values below; this is [[Lq|quantized angular momentum]]. In *spectroscopic notation* l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are written s, p, d, f, so the *ground state* is 1s, with L = 0 rather than the ħ of Bohr's first orbit. Because L_z = mħ is smaller than L for every l ≥ 1, L⃗ never points exactly along z: for l = 2 and m = 2, cos θ = 2/√6 and the angle to the axis is 35.3°. The components L_x and L_y then remain uncertain. For each n there are n values of l and 2l + 1 values of m, so each energy level holds n² orbitals.

A charge moving on a closed path forms a current loop and so has a [[mu|magnetic dipole moment]]. Classically, an electron on a circle of radius r at speed v passes each point once per period 2πr/v, which is a [[curr|current]] I = ev/(2πr); with area A = πr² the moment is μ = IA = evr/2. Since L = m_e v r, μ = (e/2m_e)L, and because the electron is negative the moment points opposite to L⃗. The relation carries over to quantum mechanics with the [[Lq|quantized angular momentum]]: the [[muorb|orbital magnetic dipole moment]] has z-component μ_z = −mμ_B, where m is here called the *magnetic orbital quantum number* and μ_B = eħ/(2m_e) = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ J/T = 5.79 × 10⁻⁵ eV/T is the *Bohr magneton*.

In an external magnetic field B⃗ along z, a magnetic dipole has [[U|potential energy]] U = −μ⃗·B⃗ = −μ_z B. With the [[muorb|orbital moment]], each level therefore shifts by U = mμ_B B. A level with orbital quantum number l splits into 2l + 1 equally spaced sublevels, μ_B B apart: 5.79 × 10⁻⁵ eV for a [[Bval|field strength]] of 1.00 T. Spectral lines from transitions between such levels split into several closely spaced components. This is the [[zeeman|Zeeman effect]]. It measures magnetic fields where no probe can go; a *magnetogram* of the Sun maps the field across its surface from the Zeeman splitting of lines in sunlight. The electron's spin, treated next, makes most observed splittings more complicated than this simple pattern.

In 1922 Stern and Gerlach sent a beam of silver atoms through a nonuniform [[Bfield|magnetic field]]. An atom with [[mu|magnetic moment]] component μ_z feels a force μ_z ∂B_z/∂z, so the beam spreads according to the values of μ_z. A classical moment with random orientation would give a continuous smear, and an orbital moment would give 2l + 1 beams, an odd number; the outer electron of silver, moreover, has l = 0. In this *Stern–Gerlach experiment* the beam split into two. The electron must therefore carry an intrinsic [[Lang|angular momentum]], [[spin|electron spin]], with *spin quantum number* s = ½, magnitude S = √(s(s + 1)) ħ = (√3/2)ħ, and component S_z = m_s ħ with *spin projection quantum number* m_s = ±½. Its magnetic moment is μ⃗_s = −(e/m_e)S⃗, twice the orbital value per unit angular momentum, so μ_z = ∓μ_B. An electron in hydrogen is thus described by five quantum numbers: n, l, m, s and m_s.

Spin also couples to fields inside the atom. In the electron's rest frame the proton circles the electron, a current loop like the one behind the [[muorb|orbital magnetic moment]], and produces a magnetic field proportional to the [[Lq|orbital angular momentum]]. The energy of the [[spin|spin]] magnetic moment in this field is U = −μ⃗_s·B⃗ ∝ S⃗·L⃗, the [[soc|spin-orbit coupling]]. It splits each level with l ≥ 1 into two, according to whether S⃗ is roughly parallel or antiparallel to L⃗, and so produces the *fine structure* of spectral lines; the yellow sodium line, for example, is a pair at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm. The electron's moment also interacts with the magnetic moment of the nucleus, hundreds of times smaller, giving the *hyperfine structure*. In the ground state of hydrogen, *spin-flip transitions* between the two hyperfine levels emit photons of 5.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV, the 21 cm line that radio astronomers use to map hydrogen in space.

In an atom with many electrons, each electron moves in the field of the nucleus and of the other electrons, and its states can still be labelled by n, l, m and m_s. How the electrons occupy these states is fixed by the [[pauli|Pauli exclusion principle]], stated in 1925: no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, m_s). The principle holds for all particles of half-integer spin. States with the same n form a *shell*, and states with the same n and l form a *subshell*. A subshell has 2l + 1 values of m and two values of m_s, so it holds at most 4l + 2 electrons: 2 in an s subshell, 6 in p, 10 in d and 14 in f. A shell holds 2n². Without the principle, all electrons would settle into the 1s state and every atom would behave alike chemically.

In its ground state an atom's Z electrons occupy the lowest-energy states available, one per state. The states carry the labels of the [[hatom|hydrogen atom]] plus [[spin|spin]], and the [[pauli|exclusion principle]] limits each subshell, so the ground state is given by an [[econf|electron configuration]]: sodium (Z = 11) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Inner electrons screen the nuclear charge, and s electrons penetrate closest to the nucleus, so the energy depends on l as well as n. Subshells fill in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, …; iron (Z = 26) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶. The *valence electrons* in the outermost shell set the chemistry. Elements with the same valence configuration form a *chemical group* of the *periodic table*, such as the alkali metals with one s electron, and the *transition metals* are those filling a d subshell. Transfer or sharing of valence electrons produces ionic and covalent bonds.

An atom emits or absorbs a [[photon|photon]] when an electron moves between levels, with hf equal to the energy difference. Not every pair of levels is connected. The photon carries one unit ħ of angular momentum, so by [[Lcons|conservation of angular momentum]] the orbital quantum number of the atom must change by one. These are the [[selrule|selection rules]] for electric dipole transitions, Δl = ±1 and Δm = 0, ±1, stated in terms of the [[Lq|quantized angular momentum]]. In hydrogen the transition 2p → 1s is allowed and gives the Lyman α line at 121.6 nm, while 2s → 1s is forbidden, so the 2s state lives far longer. An atom excited to a high level often returns in several smaller steps. In *fluorescence*, ultraviolet light absorbed by a material is re-emitted this way as visible light of lower frequency.

X-rays come from the inner electrons of heavy atoms. In an X-ray tube, electrons accelerated through a voltage V strike a metal target, and their deceleration produces *braking radiation*, a continuous spectrum that ends at λ = hc/(eV). Sharp characteristic lines, the [[xray|atomic X-rays]], stand out above it. They appear when a 1s electron of a target atom is knocked out and an electron from the n = 2 shell falls into the vacancy, emitting a Kα [[photon|photon]]. In the [[econf|electron configuration]] one 1s electron remains and screens one unit of nuclear charge, so the falling electron sees about (Z − 1)e. The [[bohrlev|hydrogen-like energy levels]] then give the frequency below, which is *Moseley's law*: √f is proportional to Z − 1. For copper (Z = 29) it gives 8.0 keV, close to the measured line. A *Moseley plot* of √f against Z is a straight line; Moseley used it to order the elements by atomic number.

An atom in an excited level can emit a photon spontaneously, at a random time and in a random direction. Einstein showed in 1917 that a [[photon|photon]] whose energy matches the gap between two [[bohrlev|energy levels]] can also trigger the emission. In this *stimulated emission* the new photon has the same frequency, phase, polarization and direction as the one that triggered it. The same photon is equally likely to be absorbed by an atom in the lower level, so light is amplified only when the upper level holds more atoms than the lower one. In thermal equilibrium the opposite holds; for a gap of 2.0 eV at 300 K the ratio is about 2.5 × 10⁻³⁴. A *population inversion* is created by pumping atoms to a higher level, from which they drop quickly into a long-lived *metastable state*. Mirrors send the light back and forth through the medium. The output of such a [[laser|laser]] is intense, [[coh|coherent]] and highly *monochromatic*.

Lasers are used to read optical discs. A CD, DVD or *Blu-Ray player* focuses a [[laser|laser]] beam to a small spot on a spiral track of pits and flat regions and detects the reflected light. The pits are about a quarter wavelength deep in the plastic of the disc, so light reflected from a pit bottom and from the surrounding surface differs in path by half a wavelength and interferes destructively; the edges of pits therefore show up as changes in reflected intensity, which encode the data. This works because laser light is [[coh|coherent]]. The smallest spot is limited by diffraction, as in the [[rayl|Rayleigh criterion]], and scales with the wavelength. CD players use 780 nm infrared light, DVD players 650 nm red light and Blu-ray players 405 nm violet light, so the shortest wavelength packs the most data onto a disc of the same size.

Chapter 8 built the electron structure of a single atom from the [[tise|Schrödinger equation]] and the [[pauli|exclusion principle]]. This chapter brings atoms together. Two atoms can lower their energy by transferring or sharing electrons, and the molecules they form rotate and vibrate with quantized energies. In a solid, about 10²³ atoms per cubic centimetre bind into a regular array, and their outer electrons occupy bands of allowed energies. How these bands are filled explains why metals conduct and insulators do not, how small amounts of impurity control a semiconductor, and why some metals lose all electrical resistance at low temperature.

A [[bonds|molecular bond]] holds atoms together when their total energy is lower together than apart. Bonds are of three main kinds: ionic, covalent and van der Waals. In an *ionic bond* one atom gives an electron to the other. The [[econf|electron configurations]] of sodium and chlorine show why this can pay. Removing sodium's single 3s electron costs its ionization energy, 5.14 eV, while chlorine, one electron short of a filled 3p shell, releases 3.61 eV, its *electron affinity*, when it gains one. The transfer therefore costs E_{transfer} = 1.53 eV. The two ions then attract by [[coul|Coulomb's law]]. At short range their filled shells overlap, and the [[pauli|exclusion principle]] pushes electrons into higher states, which adds a steep repulsion U_{ex} = A/rⁿ. The total energy is lowest at the *equilibrium separation distance* r₀, or *bond length*, and the depth of this minimum is the *dissociation energy*.

For a sodium chloride molecule r₀ = 0.236 nm, so U_{coul} = −(1.44 eV·nm)/(0.236 nm) = −6.10 eV and E_{transfer} + U_{coul} = −4.57 eV. The measured dissociation energy is about 4.3 eV; the remaining 0.3 eV is the repulsion U_{ex} at r₀. In a *covalent bond* two atoms share a pair of electrons instead. The wave function of two electrons must change sign when they are exchanged, a requirement called *exchange symmetry*. If the spin part is antisymmetric, with the two spins opposite, the spatial part is symmetric and piles charge up between the nuclei, where it attracts both. This is how two hydrogen atoms bind into H₂, with r₀ = 0.074 nm and a dissociation energy of about 4.5 eV. Parallel spins would force an antisymmetric spatial part with little charge between the nuclei, and no bond forms.

In a *polyatomic molecule* the bonds point in definite directions. In methane, CH₄, the 2s orbital and the three 2p orbitals of carbon combine into four equivalent orbitals aimed at the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart; this mixing is called *hybridization*. Atoms with filled shells still attract one another weakly. A momentary dipole in one atom induces a dipole in its neighbour, and the two dipoles attract. This *van der Waals bond* has energies of order 0.01 eV, enough to hold noble gases together as solids at low temperature.

A diatomic molecule can rotate about its centre of mass and vibrate along its bond; the quantized motions give the [[molspec|molecular energy levels]]. As a rigid rotor it has the [[I|moment of inertia]] I = μr₀², where μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂) is the reduced mass. Its [[Lq|angular momentum]] is quantized, L² = l(l + 1)ħ², so the *rotational energy levels* are E_r = l(l + 1)E_{0r}, with E_{0r} = ħ²/(2I). Near r₀ the [[bonds|bond]] energy is parabolic, so the vibration is a [[qho|quantum harmonic oscillator]] with *vibrational energy levels* (n + ½)ħω. *Electric dipole transitions*, the main way light is absorbed, obey the *selection rules* Δn = ±1 and Δl = ±1. The infrared spectrum is therefore a band of lines spaced by 2E_{0r} on both sides of ħω, with no line at ħω itself. For HCl, μ ≈ 0.98 u and r₀ = 0.127 nm give E_{0r} ≈ 1.3 meV, against ħω ≈ 0.36 eV. The spacing thus measures I and r₀.

The same levels explain why the heat capacity of a gas departs from classical [[equip|equipartition]]. A mode takes up energy only if k_{B}T, with k_{B} the [[kB|Boltzmann constant]], is comparable with its level spacing. When the spacing is much larger, nearly all molecules stay in the lowest level and the mode is frozen. For H₂ the [[molspec|molecular energy levels]] have E_{0r} ≈ 7.5 meV and ħω ≈ 0.55 eV, while k_{B}T ≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K. Rotation is active and vibration is frozen, so the [[CV|molar heat capacity at constant volume]] is close to (5/2)R rather than (7/2)R. Rotation freezes in turn as the temperature falls below about 100 K, and near 50 K C_V is close to (3/2)R, the value for translation alone.

In a crystalline solid, atoms or ions sit on a [[lattice|crystal lattice]], a pattern repeated in three dimensions. Three cubic patterns are common: *simple cubic*, with an atom at each corner of a cube; *body-centred cubic* (BCC), with one more at the centre of the cube; and *face-centred cubic* (FCC), with one more at the centre of each face. The pattern and its spacing d are measured by X-ray diffraction through [[bragg|Bragg's law]], 2d sin θ = mλ. In an ionic crystal each ion feels the [[bonds|ionic bonding]] of all the others. The Coulomb energy per ion pair is −αke²/r, where the *Madelung constant* α sums the attractions and repulsions over the whole lattice; α = 1.748 for sodium chloride. Adding a repulsion A/rⁿ, whose exponent n is called the *repulsion constant*, and setting dU/dr = 0 at r = r₀ gives the energy needed to separate the crystal into ions, per ion pair.

For sodium chloride, r₀ = 0.282 nm, so αke²/r₀ = 1.748 × (1.44 eV·nm)/(0.282 nm) = 8.93 eV. With n ≈ 9 the dissociation energy is 8.93 eV × 8/9 ≈ 7.9 eV per ion pair, within a few percent of the measured value. The repulsion lowers the result by only the fraction 1/n because it rises so steeply. Each ion has six nearest neighbours of opposite charge, and α > 1 expresses the extra binding this gives compared with a single ion pair. In metals the outer electrons leave their atoms and are shared by the whole lattice; this *metallic bonding* holds together iron, which is BCC at room temperature, and copper, which is FCC. Glass and many plastics lack long-range order. Such *amorphous solids* have no lattice, although each atom still has a well-defined set of near neighbours.

In the *free electron model* of a metal, the valence electrons move freely through the [[cond|conductor]] and are held in only at its surfaces. Classically they form an ideal gas; their *electron number density* N/V is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ in copper, one per atom. Quantum mechanically the metal is a cubic [[pib|particle in a box]] of side L, with energies E = (π²ħ²/(2mₑL²))(n₁² + n₂² + n₃²) for positive integers n₁, n₂, n₃. The [[pauli|exclusion principle]] allows two electrons, with opposite spins, in each spatial state. At T = 0 the electrons therefore fill the lowest states up to the *Fermi energy* E_F. Counting the states inside one octant of a sphere in the space of (n₁, n₂, n₃) gives E_F in terms of the density alone. This filled set of states is the [[fermigas|free electron gas]].

For copper the formula gives E_F = 7.0 eV. The *Fermi temperature* T_F = E_F/k_{B} is then 8.2 × 10⁴ K, while k_{B}T is only 0.026 eV at 300 K. Only electrons within a few k_{B}T of E_F can move to empty states when the metal is heated, which is why conduction electrons add almost nothing to its heat capacity, contrary to the classical gas model. The number of states per unit energy, the *density of states*, grows as g(E) ∝ E^{1/2}. At temperature T a state of energy E is occupied with the probability given by the *Fermi factor*, f(E) = 1/[exp((E − E_F)/k_{B}T) + 1]. It equals ½ at E_F and drops from nearly 1 to nearly 0 over a few k_{B}T around it.

The free electron model ignores the ions. In a crystal the electrons move in the periodic potential of the [[lattice|lattice]], and two approaches give their allowed energies. One starts from isolated atoms. When two atoms form a [[bonds|bond]], each atomic level splits into two; when N atoms are brought together and their wave functions overlap, each level splits into N closely spaced levels. With N near 10²³ these form an *energy band*. The other approach starts from the [[fermigas|free electron gas]] and adds a weak periodic potential. Electron waves whose wavelength satisfies the Bragg condition for the lattice are reflected, and standing waves at those wavelengths take two different energies. Both approaches give [[bands|energy bands]] separated by *energy gaps*, intervals of energy with no allowed states.

Conduction depends on how the bands are filled. In sodium the band formed from the 3s levels can hold 2N electrons but receives only N, so it is half full. A small electric field can move electrons into nearby empty states of the same band at almost no energy cost, so the metal is a [[cond|conductor]]. In an insulator or a semiconductor at T = 0, the highest filled band, the *valence band*, is full, and the empty band above it is the *conduction band*. A full band carries no current. When the gap is wide, 5.5 eV in diamond, thermal energy k_{B}T ≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K almost never lifts an electron across it, and the crystal is an [[insul|insulator]]. A *semiconductor* has a narrower gap, 1.1 eV in silicon, so a small number of electrons are thermally excited into the conduction band. Its conductivity rises with temperature, unlike that of a metal. Both behaviours follow from the [[bands|band]] structure.

An electron excited into the conduction band of a semiconductor leaves an empty state in the valence band, a *hole*. A neighbouring electron can move into the hole, so the hole moves through the crystal like a positive charge +e. Adding a small fraction of *impurity atoms*, called *doping*, controls which carrier dominates. Silicon uses all four valence electrons of its [[econf|electron configuration]] in bonds to its neighbours. A phosphorus atom, from group V, brings a fifth electron, bound by only about 0.05 eV in a *donor impurity* level just below the conduction band. At room temperature most of these electrons are freed, and the material is an *n-type semiconductor*. A boron atom, from group III, brings only three; its empty *acceptor impurity* level just above the valence band captures an electron from that band and leaves a hole, giving a *p-type semiconductor*. At high doping these levels broaden into an *impurity band*. A [[doping|doped semiconductor]] is thus the [[bands|band structure]] plus impurity levels in the gap.

The sign of the carriers is found with the Hall effect. A current I flows along a strip of width w and thickness t in a perpendicular magnetic field B. The carriers move with [[vd|drift velocity]] v_d, the magnetic force pushes them toward one edge, and charge builds up there until its electric force balances the magnetic one. The [[VH|Hall voltage]] across the strip is then V_H = v_{d}Bw. Positive and negative carriers carrying the same current move in opposite directions and are pushed toward the same edge, so V_H has opposite signs for the two. Measurements on a [[doping|doped semiconductor]] give negative carriers in n-type samples and positive carriers in p-type samples, so holes act as positive charges. The more numerous carriers are the *majority carriers*, the others the *minority carriers*. The Hall voltage also gives the majority-carrier density, n = IB/(|q|V_{H}t).

Where p-type and n-type material meet, at a *p–n junction*, electrons diffuse into the p side and holes into the n side, and they recombine. This leaves a *depletion layer* without mobile carriers, holding the fixed charges of ionized donors on the n side and ionized acceptors on the p side. Their field drives a drift current that cancels the diffusion current at equilibrium. An applied [[dV|voltage]] V_b shifts the barrier. In the *forward bias configuration*, p side positive, the barrier falls by eV_b, and by the Boltzmann factor, with k_{B} the [[kB|Boltzmann constant]], the number of majority carriers able to cross grows as exp(eV_{b}/k_{B}T). In the *reverse bias configuration* the barrier rises and only a small minority-carrier current I₀ flows. The [[pn|p–n junction]] of two [[doping|doped semiconductors]] thus rectifies. At 300 K, k_{B}T/e ≈ 26 mV, so the forward current grows tenfold every 60 mV. Beyond the *breakdown voltage*, a large reverse bias, the current rises abruptly.

A *junction transistor* combines two junctions back to back. In an npn transistor a thin p-type base separates an n-type emitter from an n-type collector. The emitter–base [[pn|p–n junction]] is forward biased and injects electrons into the base, while the base–collector junction is reverse biased. The base is so thin that most injected electrons cross it before they recombine, and the field of the reverse-biased junction sweeps them into the collector. Only a small *base current* I_B flows, while the *collector current* I_C is far larger: I_C = βI_B, with the current gain β typically about 100. A small signal at the base thus controls a large current, and the [[transistor|junction transistor]] works as an *amplifier*. Driven fully on or fully off, it works as a switch, the basic element of digital circuits.

Below its *critical temperature* T_c, a material in the [[supercond|superconducting state]] has zero resistance and expels magnetic field from its interior. A strong enough [[Bval|magnetic field]] destroys the state. The [[Bc|critical magnetic field]] B_c, measured by raising the applied field at fixed [[temp|temperature]] until resistance returns, closely follows the parabola below and falls to zero at T_c. For lead, T_c = 7.2 K and B_c(0) = 0.080 T, so at 3.6 K, where T/T_c = ½, B_c = 0.75 × 0.080 T = 0.060 T. A current I produces the [[Bwire|field of a long straight wire]], μ₀I/(2πR) at the surface of a wire of radius R, so B_c also limits the current a superconducting wire can carry. A *type I superconductor*, such as lead, loses superconductivity abruptly at B_c. A *type II superconductor* passes through a mixed state in which the field enters along thin tubes; niobium–titanium alloy stays superconducting up to about 10 T at 4 K and is used in MRI magnets.

The explanation came in 1957 from John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer and is called [[bcs|BCS theory]]. An electron moving through the [[lattice|lattice]] pulls nearby positive ions slightly toward its path, leaving a region of excess positive charge that attracts a second electron. Through this effective attraction, two electrons of the [[fermigas|free electron gas]] with energies near E_F, opposite momenta and opposite spins form a *Cooper pair*. Pairs have integer spin, are not limited by the exclusion principle, and condense into a single quantum state. Breaking a pair costs an energy gap of order k_{B}T_c. Below T_c, scattering that would change the motion of one electron must break a pair, and too little thermal energy is available, so the condensate flows without loss: [[supercond|superconductivity]] follows. Heavier isotopes of a metal have lower T_c, as expected if lattice vibrations cause the pairing. Copper oxides that superconduct above 77 K are not explained by this simple form of the theory.

The [[nucatom|nuclear model of the atom]] placed almost all of an atom's mass in a nucleus only a few femtometres (10⁻¹⁵ m) across, tens of thousands of times smaller than the atom. This chapter turns to the nucleus itself. It is made of protons and neutrons, held together by a force much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion between the protons. Nuclear energies are millions of electronvolts, large enough that the change in [[Erel|rest energy]], Δmc², is a measurable fraction of the mass. The same ideas explain radioactive decay, the energy of fission and fusion, the dating of old materials, and the medical uses and hazards of radiation.

The [[nucatom|nuclear model of the atom]] left open what the nucleus is made of. The *atomic nucleus* contains Z *protons*, each of charge +e, and N *neutrons*, which are uncharged and slightly heavier; together they are *nucleons*. The *atomic number* Z fixes the nuclear charge, hence the number of electrons in the neutral atom and its chemistry; electrons and protons are the [[atom|charge carriers]] of ordinary matter. The *neutron number* N adds mass without charge, and the *mass number* A = Z + N counts the nucleons. A [[nuclide|nuclide]] is a nucleus with given Z and N, written ᴬ_{Z}X; ²³⁸₉₂U, for example, has 146 neutrons. *Isotopes* have the same Z but different N, as do ordinary hydrogen ¹H, *deuterium* ²H and *tritium* ³H.

Two protons 1 fm apart repel each other, by [[coul|Coulomb's law]], with a force of about 230 N. Nuclei hold together because of the [[strong|strong nuclear force]], an attraction between any two nucleons that is much stronger than the Coulomb force at about 1 fm but falls to almost nothing beyond a few femtometres. It acts equally between protons and neutrons, and it saturates: each nucleon attracts only its nearest neighbours, while the Coulomb repulsion acts between every pair of protons. Light stable nuclei therefore have N ≈ Z, but heavy ones need extra neutrons, which add attraction without repulsion; lead-208 has Z = 82 and N = 126. On the *chart of the nuclides*, which plots N against Z, the stable [[nuclide|nuclides]] form a narrow band that bends away from the line N = Z toward more neutrons.

Nuclear sizes are measured by scattering high-energy electrons from nuclei. The *radius of a nucleus* follows r = r₀A^{1/3} with r₀ ≈ 1.2 fm, so ²³⁸U has r ≈ 1.2 fm × 6.20 = 7.4 fm. The volume is proportional to A, so all nuclei have about the same density, 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³. Masses are given in *atomic mass units*: 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, one-twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom. The proton has 1.007 276 u and the neutron 1.008 665 u. The *atomic mass* of an element is the average over its isotopes, weighted by abundance. Chlorine, 75.8 % ³⁵Cl at 34.969 u and 24.2 % ³⁷Cl at 36.966 u, has atomic mass 0.758 × 34.969 u + 0.242 × 36.966 u = 35.45 u.

A nucleus has less mass than its separated nucleons. The *mass defect* Δm = Zm_p + Nm_n − m_{nuc} measures the difference, and by the equivalence of mass and [[Erel|rest energy]] the [[BE|binding energy]] E_b = Δmc² is the energy needed to pull the [[nuclide|nuclide]] apart into free nucleons. With atomic masses, Zm(¹H) replaces Zm_p so that the electron masses cancel. For helium-4, Δm = 2(1.007 825 u) + 2(1.008 665 u) − 4.002 603 u = 0.030 377 u. Since 1 u corresponds to 931.5 MeV, E_b = 28.3 MeV, or 7.07 MeV per nucleon. The *binding energy per nucleon* (BEN), E_b/A, rises steeply among light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 MeV near iron and nickel (A ≈ 56–62), and falls slowly to 7.6 MeV for uranium. The 7 MeV that binds a nucleon in helium is about 5 × 10⁵ times the 13.6 eV that binds the electron in hydrogen.

Some nuclei are unstable and decay spontaneously. This *radioactivity* was discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896, in radiation from uranium salts. When a given nucleus will *decay* cannot be predicted; quantum mechanics gives only a probability, in the sense of the [[born|Born rule]]. Each [[nuclide|nucleus]] of a given kind has the same probability λ dt of decaying in the next interval dt, whatever its age, where λ is the *decay constant*. Of N nuclei, λN dt decay, so −dN/dt = λN, and integration gives the [[decaylaw|radioactive decay law]]. The *half-life* T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ is the time in which half of any sample decays, and the mean *lifetime* is 1/λ. The *activity* A = λN, the number of decays per second, falls in the same way. Its SI unit is the *becquerel*, 1 Bq = 1 decay/s; the older *curie* is 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

Because decay proceeds at a known rate, the fraction of a radioactive isotope that remains measures time. Inverting the [[decaylaw|decay law]] gives t = (1/λ) ln(N₀/N), the basis of [[dating|radioactive dating]]; it needs the initial amount N₀. In *carbon-14 dating*, cosmic rays keep making ¹⁴C in the atmosphere, so living organisms, which exchange carbon with the air, hold a nearly constant ratio of ¹⁴C to ¹²C. After death the exchange stops and the ¹⁴C decays with a half-life of 5730 years. A sample whose ¹⁴C activity per gram of carbon is 60 % of that in living matter is 5730 y × log₂(1/0.60) ≈ 4.22 × 10³ years old. The method works up to several half-lives, roughly 50 000 years. Rocks are dated with longer-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, whose half-life is 4.5 × 10⁹ years.

Nuclear radiation comes in three kinds, first told apart by how far they penetrate matter and how a magnetic field bends them. *Alpha (α) rays* are helium nuclei, ⁴He, and are stopped by a sheet of paper. *Beta (β) rays* are electrons or, in some decays, *positrons*, the *antielectrons* that have the electron's mass and the opposite charge; they penetrate a few millimetres of aluminium. *Gamma (γ) rays* are high-energy photons, and stopping them takes centimetres of lead. The electrons of β rays are not present in the nucleus beforehand. By the [[uncert|Heisenberg uncertainty principle]], an electron confined within 10 fm would have pc of order 10 MeV or more (Δp ≥ ħ/2Δx), well above the energies of β electrons, so they are created in the decay.

In the [[decay|nuclear decays]] a *parent nucleus* turns into a *daughter nucleus*. *Alpha decay* lowers Z by 2 and A by 4, as in ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He. In *beta decay* a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton and emits an electron and an *antineutrino*, as in ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻ + ν̄; in β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron and emits a positron and a *neutrino*. In *gamma decay* a nucleus in an excited state emits a photon, and Z and A are unchanged. Every decay conserves [[qcons|charge]] and nucleon number. The energy released is Q = (m_{parent} − m_{products})c²; for α decay it equals the [[BE|binding energy]] of the products minus that of the parent [[nuclide|nuclide]]. For the α decay of ²³⁸U, the atomic masses give Q = 4.27 MeV.
eqs: ᴬ_{Z}X → ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z−2}Y + ⁴₂He,   ᴬ_{Z}X → ᴬ_{Z+1}Y + e⁻ + ν̄

paragraphs.text: Alpha half-lives range from less than a microsecond to more than 10¹⁰ years, while α energies span only a few MeV. Classically an α particle could not escape at all. Inside the nucleus the strong force holds it in a well; outside, the Coulomb repulsion of the daughter forms a barrier about 30 MeV high for uranium, far above the 4.27 MeV available. Quantum mechanically the α particle tunnels through the barrier, with a [[Ttun|tunneling probability]] that falls exponentially with the barrier's width and with the square root of its height above the particle's energy. A higher energy meets a thinner and lower barrier, so the [[decay|decay]] is far faster. Thus ²³⁸U, with Q = 4.27 MeV, has a half-life of 4.5 × 10⁹ years, while ²¹²Po, with Q = 8.95 MeV, has a half-life of 0.30 μs, more than 10²³ times shorter.

A daughter nucleus may itself be unstable, so heavy nuclei decay through a *decay series*. Uranium-238 reaches stable lead-206 after eight α decays and six β⁻ decays: A falls by 8 × 4 = 32, and Z falls by 16 and rises by 6, from 92 to 82. Elements beyond uranium, the *transuranic elements*, occur in nature only in traces and are made artificially. Plutonium-239, for example, forms when ²³⁸U captures a neutron and the resulting ²³⁹U undergoes two β⁻ decays, through neptunium-239.

In the 1930s several groups, starting with Enrico Fermi's, bombarded uranium with neutrons. In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium, a medium-mass element, among the products: the uranium nucleus had split. In [[fission|fission]] a heavy nucleus such as ²³⁵U absorbs a slow neutron and divides into two fragments of unequal mass plus two or three neutrons, for example n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n. About 200 MeV is released, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments. The new neutrons can cause further fissions, a *chain reaction*. If on average each fission leads to exactly one more, the multiplication factor is k = 1 and the system is in a state of *criticality*. Neutrons escape through the surface, whose area grows more slowly than the volume, so k = 1 is reached only above a *critical mass* of fissile material.

Niels Bohr and John Wheeler explained fission in 1939 with the [[liqdrop|liquid drop model]]. Nuclear density is nearly constant, like that of a liquid, because the [[strong|strong force]] is short-range and saturates, as do the forces between molecules in a [[fluid|fluid]]. Nucleons at the surface have fewer neighbours, which acts like a surface tension and favours a spherical shape, while the [[coul|Coulomb repulsion]] of the protons acts across the whole drop and favours breaking it. When ²³⁵U absorbs a neutron, the excited drop oscillates; if it stretches far enough, the Coulomb repulsion between its two ends wins and it splits. The energy release follows from the [[BE|binding energy]] per nucleon: about 7.6 MeV for uranium against about 8.5 MeV for fragments of medium mass. A gain of about 0.9 MeV for each of 236 nucleons gives roughly 200 MeV per [[fission|fission]].

A *nuclear reactor* holds the chain reaction at k = 1. Fission of ²³⁵U is most likely with slow neutrons, so a moderator such as water or graphite slows the neutrons, and control rods that absorb neutrons adjust k. Natural uranium is only 0.72 % ²³⁵U, and most reactors use fuel enriched in it. The first reactor, built under Enrico Fermi's direction in Chicago, went critical in 1942. An *atomic bomb* instead assembles a mass with k > 1 so quickly that many generations of fission occur within about a microsecond, before the material blows apart. A *breeder reactor* uses neutrons to turn ²³⁸U into fissile plutonium-239 and so produces more fuel than it consumes.

Light nuclei lie on the rising side of the curve of [[BE|binding energy]] per nucleon, so joining them releases energy. In [[fusion|nuclear fusion]] such as ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n, the masses before and after give a released energy, the *Q value*, of 17.6 MeV. Fusion is hard to start because the nuclei must come within a few femtometres against their Coulomb repulsion, a barrier of several hundred keV for two protons. In the Sun's core, at about 1.5 × 10⁷ K, the mean thermal energy is only about 2 keV. Fusion still occurs for two reasons. The high-energy tail of the [[mbd|Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution]] contains a small fraction of much faster protons, and these pass the rest of the barrier by [[Ttun|tunneling]]. The product of the falling tail and the rising tunneling probability sets the rate.

In the late 1930s Hans Bethe worked out how stars release energy by fusion. In the Sun the main route is the *proton–proton chain*. Two protons fuse to deuterium, ¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν, a slow step because it needs the weak interaction that also causes β decay. Then ²H + ¹H → ³He + γ, and two ³He nuclei form ⁴He and two protons. The net result, 4¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν, releases 26.7 MeV, part of it carried off by the neutrinos. Older stars fuse helium into carbon and continue toward iron, beyond which fusion no longer releases energy; heavier elements form by neutron capture. This *nucleosynthesis* made the carbon, oxygen, iron and other heavy elements around us. A *nuclear fusion reactor* would fuse deuterium and tritium in a plasma above 10⁸ K, confined by magnetic fields or compressed by lasers; such reactors remain under development.

Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine because their radiation can be detected from outside the body. A *radiopharmaceutical* is a compound that an organ takes up and that carries a *radioactive tag*. Iodine-131 collects in the thyroid, and technetium-99m, which emits a 140 keV γ ray with a half-life of 6.0 h, is the most widely used tag. In *single-photon-emission computed tomography* (SPECT), detectors rotating around the patient record the γ rays from many directions, and a computer reconstructs a three-dimensional map of the tracer. *Positron emission tomography* (PET) uses positron emitters such as fluorine-18. Each positron annihilates with an electron into two 511 keV photons travelling in opposite directions, and detecting both at once fixes a line through the point of emission.

The same radiation damages tissue. Each α particle, β particle or γ photon from [[decay|nuclear decays]] carries an energy of order 1 MeV, while ionizing a molecule takes about 10 eV, so one particle can ionize tens of thousands of molecules and break bonds in DNA. The effect grows with the energy absorbed per unit [[m|mass]], the [[dose|radiation dose]]. Its SI unit is the gray, 1 Gy = 1 J/kg; the older *radiation dose unit*, the *rad*, is 0.01 J/kg. Equal doses of different radiations do unequal harm, so the dose is multiplied by the *relative biological effectiveness* (RBE), about 1 for X-rays, γ rays and electrons and up to about 20 for α particles. The product is the equivalent dose, in *sieverts* (Sv) for a dose in grays and in *roentgen equivalent man* (rem) for a dose in rad; 1 Sv = 100 rem.

Effects depend on the dose and on how quickly it is received. *Low doses*, below about 0.1 Sv, cause no immediate symptoms; their main risk is a small increase in the chance of cancer years later. *Moderate doses*, from about 0.1 to 1 Sv, can cause temporary changes in blood counts. *High doses* of more than about 1 Sv received at once cause radiation sickness, and about 4–5 Sv without treatment is fatal to roughly half of those exposed. Natural sources, mainly radon gas, cosmic rays and radioactive potassium in the body, give a typical person about 2–3 mSv per year. As an example, 2.0 mJ of γ-ray energy absorbed by 1.0 kg of tissue is a dose of 2.0 mGy and an equivalent dose of 2.0 mSv; the same energy deposited by α particles would give about 40 mSv.

Atoms are built from electrons and nuclei, and nuclei from protons and neutrons held by the [[strong|strong nuclear force]]. Particle physics asks what these are made of and which interactions act between the smallest constituents. The answer so far is a short list of elementary particles, a set of conservation laws that decide which reactions occur, and one theory for three of the four fundamental interactions. The chapter then turns to the largest scale. Galaxies recede from one another, and the universe has cooled from a hot, dense early state in which particle physics decided what formed. [[GR|General relativity]] describes the expansion.

All known forces reduce to four [[forces4|fundamental forces]]. The [[strong|strong nuclear force]] binds nucleons and, at a deeper level, the quarks inside them; its carriers are *gluons*. The electromagnetic force, described for static charges by [[coul|Coulomb's law]], is carried by photons. Gravity, described by [[ngrav|Newton's law of gravitation]], acts on all mass and energy; its proposed carrier, the graviton, has not been observed. A fourth force, the *weak nuclear force*, is needed for β [[decay|decay]], in which a neutron turns into a proton; its carriers are the massive *W and Z bosons*. The strengths differ enormously: between two protons, gravity is weaker than the electric force by the factor Gm_{p}²/(ke²) ≈ 8 × 10⁻³⁷. At energies near 100 GeV the electromagnetic and weak forces merge into one *electroweak force*. A *grand unified theory* would join the strong force to it at much higher energies, and a *theory of everything* would include gravity; neither has been confirmed.

These forces act on a small set of particles. The electrons and protons that are the [[atom|charge carriers]] of matter, the neutron, the neutrinos and positrons of β [[decay|decay]], and many short-lived particles found since are sorted first by [[spin|spin]]. *Fermions* have half-integer spin and *bosons* integer spin, and their *exchange symmetry* differs. The state of two identical fermions changes sign when they are exchanged, so fermions obey the [[pauli|exclusion principle]]; that of two identical bosons does not, and any number of bosons can share one state. Among the [[particles|elementary particles]], the fermions form two families. *Leptons*, the electron, muon and tau and a neutrino for each, feel no strong force. *Quarks* feel it and occur only inside composite particles, the *hadrons*: *baryons*, such as the proton and neutron, contain three quarks, and *mesons*, such as the pion, a quark and an antiquark. Every particle has an *antiparticle* with the same mass and opposite charge; the *positron* is the electron's.

Some reactions that conserve energy, momentum and [[qcons|charge]] are never observed. The decay p → e⁺ + γ, for example, has never been seen, and the proton's lifetime exceeds 10³³ years. Such absences are explained by further additive quantum numbers carried by [[particles|particles]]; these are the [[pcons2|particle conservation laws]]. *Baryon number* B is +1 for baryons, −1 for antibaryons and 0 for leptons and mesons. *Lepton number* is +1 for leptons, −1 for antileptons and 0 otherwise. It is counted separately for the electron, muon and tau families, and only neutrino oscillations, in which a neutrino changes family, alter these family numbers. In neutron decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ, B is 1 before and after, and the electron's lepton number +1 is cancelled by the antineutrino's −1. *Strangeness* S is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic interactions but not by the weak one. The Λ⁰, with S = −1, therefore decays to p + π⁻ only weakly and slowly, with a lifetime of 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ s.

In 1964 Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig independently proposed that hadrons are made of quarks, constituents listed among the [[particles|elementary particles]]. Six are now known: up, charm and top, with charge +⅔e, and down, strange and bottom, with charge −⅓e, each with baryon number ⅓. In the [[quarkmodel|quark model]] the proton is uud, with charge (⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓)e = +e; the neutron is udd, with charge 0; and the π⁺ meson is ud̄, with charge (⅔ + ⅓)e = +e. The [[pcons2|conserved quantities]] of a hadron are sums over its quarks; a strange quark has S = −1. The Ω⁻ baryon, sss with spin 3/2, has three identical quarks in the same state, which the [[pauli|exclusion principle]] forbids. A new quantum number, *colour*, with three values, removes the conflict: the three quarks differ in colour. Only colourless combinations occur, and no free quark has been seen. Electron scattering at high energy reveals point-like charges inside the proton, the main evidence for quarks.

Particles are studied by accelerating them and recording what their collisions produce. A *particle accelerator* gives charged particles energy with electric fields: a *Van de Graaff accelerator* uses one large static [[dV|voltage]], a *linear accelerator* a long row of oscillating fields. A *cyclotron* bends the particles into [[helix|circular orbits]] in a fixed magnetic field so that they cross the same gap many times. A *synchrotron* raises the field as the [[prel|momentum]] grows, keeping the radius fixed; its particles lose energy as *synchrotron radiation*, far more for electrons than for protons of equal energy. Colliding beams head-on makes their whole energy available: the *Large Hadron Collider*, a 27 km ring, collides protons at 13.6 TeV. In a *particle detector*, a track of radius r in a field B gives p = qBr, or p ≈ 0.3Br in GeV/c for a singly charged particle, with B in teslas and r in metres.

The [[sm|Standard Model]] describes three of the [[forces4|fundamental forces]] as the exchange of bosons. *Quantum electrodynamics* (QED) treats the electromagnetic force as the exchange of [[photon|photons]] between charges; *quantum chromodynamics* (QCD) treats the strong force as the exchange of gluons between the colour charges of [[quarkmodel|quarks]]; the electroweak theory adds the W and Z bosons. A *Feynman diagram*, named after Richard Feynman, draws such a process with time running upward, lines for particles and vertices where a boson is emitted or absorbed. The exchanged boson is a *virtual particle*. Creating it violates energy conservation by ΔE = mc², which the [[uncertE|energy–time uncertainty]] relation tolerates for a time Δt ≈ ħ/(mc²). Moving at most at c, the boson travels R ≈ cΔt = ħ/(mc), which sets the range of the force. For the W boson, mc² = 80.4 GeV and R ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁸ m; the massless photon gives the electromagnetic force an infinite range.

The Higgs boson, found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, completes the [[sm|Standard Model]]; its field gives the W and Z bosons, the quarks and the charged leptons their masses. The model does not include gravity, and it does not account for dark matter. The strengths of the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces change with the energy of a collision and approach one another near 10¹⁵ GeV. This is the main motive for a grand unified theory, in which the three would be one force. Such theories predict that protons decay, which has not been observed.

Light from distant galaxies arrives with its spectral lines shifted to longer wavelengths, a *redshift* z = (λ_{obs} − λ_{emit})/λ_{emit}. Read as a [[relDop|relativistic Doppler effect]], it gives the recession speed, v ≈ cz when z ≪ 1. Distances come from standard candles, objects of known luminosity such as Cepheid variable stars, whose apparent brightness falls as 1/d² with the distance d, a [[L|length]] of millions of light-years. In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that the speed grows in proportion to the distance. This is [[hubble|Hubble's law]], with *Hubble's constant* H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc, where 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m. A galaxy 100 Mpc away therefore recedes at about 7000 km/s, and its redshift is z ≈ 0.023.

Hubble's law has no centre: if every distance grows by the same factor, every galaxy sees all others receding with v ∝ d. Dots on an inflating balloon behave the same way, and no dot on the surface is special. *Cosmology*, the study of the universe as a whole, assumes the *cosmological principle*, that on large scales the universe is the same everywhere and in every direction. In [[GR|general relativity]] the expansion is a stretching of space itself, not a motion of galaxies through space, and the stretching also lengthens light waves, which is the cosmological redshift. Running the expansion of [[hubble|Hubble's law]] backward brings all matter together. The [[bigbang|Big Bang model]] holds that the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state. At a constant rate the time since then would be 1/H₀ = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years; detailed models give 13.8 billion years.

The early universe was hot, and as it expanded it cooled, so its history is a sequence of stages set by temperature. At the highest energies the electromagnetic and weak [[forces4|fundamental forces]] acted as one electroweak force, and they separated as the temperature fell. Within about the first ten microseconds, quarks combined into protons and neutrons. During the first few minutes, [[fusion|nucleosynthesis]] built about a quarter of the mass of ordinary matter into helium-4, with traces of deuterium and lithium, the abundances found today in the oldest gas. Until about 380 000 years after the [[bigbang|Big Bang]], at temperatures above about 3000 K, matter was a plasma of nuclei and electrons, opaque to light. Then the electrons joined the nuclei into neutral atoms, and the universe became transparent.

The radiation released then still fills the universe. Expansion has stretched its wavelengths by a factor of about 1100, so [[bbrad|blackbody radiation]] at 3000 K now has a temperature of 2.7 K and peaks at a wavelength near 1 mm, in the microwave range. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected this [[cmb|cosmic microwave background]] in 1964, reporting it in 1965, as a faint signal arriving equally from all directions. Satellite measurements show that its spectrum is a blackbody to high precision, as the hot early universe of the [[bigbang|Big Bang model]] predicts, and that its temperature varies over the sky by only about one part in 10⁵. Maps of these variations, made by satellites such as the *Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe* (WMAP), record the small density differences from which galaxies later grew.

Stars far from the centre of a spiral galaxy should orbit more slowly, with the [[vorb|orbital speed]] v = √(GM_{visible}/r) once r encloses most of the visible mass. Measured speeds stay nearly constant out to large r, so the galaxy must contain more mass than it shows. The motions of galaxies in clusters, and the bending of light by clusters predicted by general relativity, called gravitational lensing, lead to the same conclusion. This *dark matter* emits no light and is about five times as abundant as ordinary matter. Observations of distant supernovae, which extend [[hubble|Hubble's law]] to great distances, show that the expansion described by the [[bigbang|Big Bang model]] is speeding up; the cause is called *dark energy*. Together, [[dark|dark matter and dark energy]] make up about 95 % of the energy content of the universe, roughly 27 % and 68 %, and the nature of neither is known.

nodes.label: Order of magnitude
nodes.description: Rounds a value to the nearest power of ten so that very different scales can be compared multiplicatively.

nodes.label: SI system of units
nodes.description: The convention that fixes base quantities and their units and builds every other unit as a product of powers of them.
properties: seven base units (s, m, kg, A, K, mol, cd)
derived unit = product of powers of base units

nodes.label: Time
nodes.description: Read from a clock. SI unit the second, fixed by the caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency.

nodes.label: Length
nodes.description: Read from a ruler. SI unit the metre, fixed by the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299 792 458 s.

nodes.label: Mass
nodes.description: Inertial measure of the amount of matter, read from a balance. SI unit the kilogram, fixed since 2019 through Planck's constant.

nodes.label: Unit conversion
nodes.description: Multiplies a quantity by a ratio equal to one, so the number changes and the quantity does not.

nodes.label: Dimensional analysis
nodes.description: Tracks the powers of base dimensions in a quantity; an equation is admissible only if both sides carry the same dimension.
properties: dimensions form a multiplicative group generated by L, M, T, …
only like dimensions add or equate
arguments of exp, sin, log are dimensionless

nodes.label: Estimation (Fermi)
nodes.description: Obtains an order-of-magnitude answer from rough inputs combined in a dimensionally consistent way.

nodes.label: Discrepancy
nodes.description: Difference between a measured value and the accepted value; a small discrepancy means high accuracy.

nodes.label: Uncertainty
nodes.description: The spread of a measured value; percent uncertainty δA/A·100 % compares it with the value itself. Small spread means high precision.

nodes.label: Uncertainty propagation
nodes.description: For products and quotients the percent uncertainties add (to first order), which bounds the uncertainty of a result.

nodes.label: Significant figures
nodes.description: Bookkeeping rule that keeps only the digits supported by the uncertainty of the inputs.
properties: × and ÷ keep the fewest significant figures
+ and − keep the fewest decimal places

nodes.label: Scalar
nodes.description: A quantity fixed by one real number and a unit; scalars obey ordinary arithmetic.
properties: addition and multiplication commutative and associative
equations between scalars are scalar equations

nodes.label: Vector
nodes.description: A quantity with magnitude and direction; displacement is the model case. Two vectors can be parallel, antiparallel or orthogonal.
properties: a vector equation fixes magnitude and direction at once

nodes.label: Vector addition
nodes.description: Combines vectors head to tail (or by the parallelogram) into a resultant; subtraction adds the antiparallel vector.

nodes.label: Multiplication by a scalar
nodes.description: Stretches a vector by |α| and reverses it if α < 0; dividing a vector by its magnitude gives a unit vector.
properties: distributive over vector and scalar sums

nodes.label: Vector components
nodes.symbol: A⃗ = A_x î + A_y ĵ + A_z k̂
nodes.description: Writes a vector in the orthonormal basis of a Cartesian coordinate system; vector equations become one scalar equation per axis.

nodes.label: Polar coordinates
nodes.description: Locates a point in a plane by its distance from the origin and an angle from the x-axis.
properties: x = r cos φ, y = r sin φ

nodes.label: Scalar product
nodes.description: Multiplies two vectors into a scalar, AB cos φ; it projects one vector on another and vanishes for orthogonal vectors.

nodes.label: Vector product
nodes.description: Multiplies two vectors into a vector perpendicular to both, of magnitude AB sin φ, oriented by the right-hand rule.
properties: not associative (obeys the Jacobi identity instead)

nodes.label: Position
nodes.description: Coordinate of the body on an axis of the frame at a given instant.

nodes.label: Reference frame
nodes.description: An origin and axes against which positions are measured, together with a clock.
properties: choice of origin and axes arbitrary

nodes.label: Motion on a line
nodes.description: The kinematic state of a body on a line: its position at every instant.
nodes.math_structure: function t ↦ x(t), ℝ → ℝ

nodes.label: Displacement
nodes.description: Change of position between two instants; signed. A total displacement is the sum of successive displacements.

nodes.label: Distance traveled
nodes.description: Total length of path covered, never negative; it can exceed the magnitude of the displacement.

nodes.label: Average velocity
nodes.description: Displacement divided by the elapsed time; it depends only on the end points of the interval.

nodes.label: Elapsed time
nodes.description: Duration of an interval between two clock readings.

nodes.label: Time derivative
nodes.description: The limit of a difference quotient as the interval shrinks; turns a quantity known at every instant into its rate of change.

nodes.label: Instantaneous velocity
nodes.description: Rate of change of position at an instant: the slope of x(t).

nodes.label: Average speed
nodes.description: Distance traveled divided by elapsed time.

nodes.label: Speed
nodes.description: Magnitude of the instantaneous velocity.

nodes.label: Average acceleration
nodes.description: Change of velocity divided by elapsed time.

nodes.label: Instantaneous acceleration
nodes.description: Rate of change of velocity: the slope of v(t) and the second derivative of x(t), which sets the concavity of its graph.

nodes.label: Constant-acceleration kinematics
nodes.description: The motion when acceleration does not change: velocity linear and position quadratic in time.
properties: polynomial of degree two in t

nodes.label: Free fall
nodes.description: Vertical motion with acceleration −g; Galileo's result that the motion does not depend on the mass.
properties: special case a = −g of constant-acceleration kinematics

nodes.label: Free-fall acceleration
nodes.description: Acceleration of a body falling near Earth's surface without air resistance: about 9.80 m/s², the same for all bodies at one place.

nodes.label: Time integral
nodes.description: Accumulates a rate over time; undoes the derivative up to a constant fixed by initial conditions.
properties: ∫ (d f/dt) dt = f + C (fundamental theorem of calculus)

nodes.label: Position vector
nodes.description: Vector from the origin of the frame to the body: r⃗ = x î + y ĵ + z k̂.

nodes.label: Trajectory
nodes.description: The kinematic state in space: the curve traced by the position vector, made of three independent motions along the axes.
nodes.math_structure: curve t ↦ r⃗(t) in ℝ³

nodes.label: Displacement vector
nodes.description: Change of the position vector between two instants.

nodes.label: Velocity vector
nodes.description: Rate of change of the position vector; tangent to the trajectory.

nodes.label: Acceleration vector
nodes.description: Rate of change of the velocity vector; in curved motion it has parts across and along the path (total acceleration).

nodes.label: Projectile motion
nodes.description: Motion under gravity alone: uniform horizontally, free fall vertically, the two independent.
properties: parabolic trajectory y = (tan θ₀)x − g x²/(2v₀² cos²θ₀)

nodes.label: Time of flight
nodes.description: Time a projectile spends in the air.

nodes.label: Range
nodes.description: Horizontal distance traveled by a projectile landing at its launch height.

nodes.label: Circular motion
nodes.description: The state of a body moving on a circle of radius r: its angle at every instant.
nodes.math_structure: curve on a circle S¹ ⊂ ℝ²: r⃗(t) = r(cos φ(t), sin φ(t))

nodes.label: Centripetal acceleration
nodes.description: Acceleration toward the centre needed to keep a body on a circle.

nodes.label: Angular frequency
nodes.description: Rate at which the angle advances, in rad/s; constant in uniform circular motion.

nodes.label: Tangential acceleration
nodes.description: Rate of change of speed; directed along the path.

nodes.label: Relative motion
nodes.description: Converts positions and velocities between two reference frames in relative motion by adding the frames' relative position and velocity.
properties: vector addition of relative positions, velocities and accelerations
time is the same in all frames
acceleration is frame-independent for frames moving uniformly

nodes.label: Relative velocity
nodes.description: Velocity of a body measured in a frame that itself moves.

nodes.label: Force
nodes.description: A push or pull on a body, with magnitude and direction; measured by the stretch of a calibrated spring. SI unit the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

nodes.label: Free-body diagram
nodes.description: Isolates one body and draws every external force on it as a vector from the body; the starting point of every force problem.
properties: separates the system from its surroundings

nodes.label: Net external force
nodes.description: Vector sum of all external forces on a body.

nodes.label: Newton's first law
nodes.description: A body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts; this tendency is inertia, measured by mass.
properties: defines the class of inertial frames
special case F⃗_net = 0 of the second law

nodes.label: Inertial reference frame
nodes.description: A frame in which the first law holds; any frame moving at constant velocity relative to one is also inertial.
properties: closed under constant-velocity changes of frame

nodes.label: Newton's second law
nodes.description: The net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; one equation per component.
properties: second order in time, so r⃗₀ and v⃗₀ fix the motion

nodes.label: Weight
nodes.description: Gravitational force of the Earth on a body near its surface; proportional to mass, unlike mass itself it depends on location.

nodes.label: Newton's third law
nodes.description: Forces come in pairs: when A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two act on different bodies.
properties: internal forces of a system cancel in pairs

nodes.label: Normal force
nodes.description: Contact force perpendicular to a surface, as large as needed to stop the body from moving into it.

nodes.label: Tension
nodes.description: Pulling force transmitted along a string or cable.

nodes.label: Hooke's law
nodes.description: A spring pulls back with a force proportional to its stretch from the relaxed length.

nodes.label: Friction law
nodes.description: Contact force parallel to a surface that opposes relative motion (kinetic) or its onset (static), proportional to the normal force.

nodes.label: Static friction
nodes.description: Friction between surfaces not sliding relative to each other; adjusts up to a maximum μ_s N.

nodes.label: Kinetic friction
nodes.description: Friction between sliding surfaces, opposite to the relative velocity.

nodes.label: Centripetal force
nodes.description: Net force toward the centre that a circular motion requires; supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.

nodes.label: Banked curve
nodes.description: A road tilted so the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal force at a design speed.

nodes.label: Noninertial frame
nodes.description: An accelerating or rotating frame; the laws of motion hold there only if inertial (fictitious) forces such as the centrifugal force are added.

nodes.label: Coriolis force
nodes.description: Inertial force on a body moving relative to a rotating frame, perpendicular to its velocity; deflects winds and projectiles on Earth.

nodes.label: Drag force
nodes.description: Resistance of a fluid to a body moving through it; grows with the square of speed for fast motion, linearly for slow motion in viscous fluid.

nodes.label: Terminal velocity
nodes.description: Constant speed reached when the drag force balances the weight.

nodes.label: Work
nodes.description: Energy transferred by a force acting along a displacement; only the component of force along the path does work. SI unit the joule.

nodes.label: Kinetic energy
nodes.description: Energy of motion of a particle; depends on the frame through the speed.

nodes.label: Net work
nodes.description: Work done by the net force, equal to the sum of the works of all forces.

nodes.label: Work–energy theorem
nodes.description: The net work done on a particle equals its change of kinetic energy.
properties: scalar consequence of the second law
the path enters only through W_net

nodes.label: Power
nodes.description: Rate at which work is done; P = F⃗·v⃗ for a force acting on a moving body. Average power is work over elapsed time.

nodes.label: Potential energy
nodes.description: Energy of a system stored in its configuration; only differences are physical, so the zero can be chosen freely.

nodes.label: Gravitational potential energy (near Earth)
nodes.description: Potential energy of the body–Earth system for a height y near the surface.

nodes.label: Elastic potential energy
nodes.description: Potential energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring.

nodes.label: Conservative force
nodes.description: A force whose work between two points is independent of the path; equivalently zero around every closed path, and derivable from a potential energy.
properties: gravity and springs conservative, friction not

nodes.label: Work of nonconservative forces
nodes.description: Work by forces such as friction or air resistance, which depends on the path and changes the mechanical energy.

nodes.label: Mechanical energy
nodes.description: Kinetic plus potential energy of a system.

nodes.label: Conservation of mechanical energy
nodes.description: Mechanical energy changes only through the work of nonconservative forces; without them it is a conserved quantity.
properties: follows from the work–energy theorem with W_cons = −ΔU
energy lost to friction becomes thermal energy

nodes.label: Potential-energy diagram
nodes.description: A plot of U(x) with the total energy as a horizontal line; motion is allowed only where E ≥ U, and reverses at turning points.

nodes.label: Equilibrium point
nodes.description: A position where the force vanishes; stable at a minimum of U (small disturbances oscillate), unstable at a maximum.
nodes.math_structure: point x₀ with U′(x₀) = 0; stable if U″(x₀) > 0

nodes.label: Momentum
nodes.description: Mass times velocity; a vector.

nodes.label: Impulse
nodes.description: Time integral of a force; for a short collision, average force times duration.

nodes.label: Impulse–momentum theorem
nodes.description: The impulse of the net force equals the change of momentum.
properties: integral form of the second law
independent of the detailed force history

nodes.label: System of particles
nodes.description: A chosen set of bodies; forces split into internal (between members) and external. A closed system has no net external force.
nodes.math_structure: N labelled trajectories r⃗_j(t) ∈ ℝ³ with masses m_j

nodes.label: Conservation of momentum
nodes.description: The total momentum of a closed system does not change, whatever happens inside it.

nodes.label: Collisions
nodes.description: Collisions conserve momentum; they are classified by kinetic energy: elastic (kept), inelastic (lost), perfectly inelastic (bodies stick together), explosion (gained).
properties: kinetic energy conserved only in elastic collisions
perfectly inelastic loses the most K compatible with P

nodes.label: Center of mass
